title: Encyclical letter Magnifica Humanitas
description: Magnifica Humanitas is an encyclical issued by Pope Leo XIV in 2026 that sets out a comprehensive framework for addressing the impact of artificial intelligence on human dignity and society. It forms part of the broader Social Doctrine of the Church and positions AI as a major transformation requiring moral, social and political discernment rather than a purely technical response. The initiative responds to the rapid expansion of digital technologies, highlighting both their potential benefits and their risks. It recognises AI as “a valuable tool” that can improve living conditions and support decision-making, while stressing that it is not neutral and can “shape decision-making processes” and society itself. The text identifies key concerns, including the concentration of technological power in private actors, the opacity of algorithmic systems, and the risk of exclusion, inequality and manipulation. A central component of the initiative is the call for governance mechanisms to ensure that AI serves the common good. It emphasises the need for “responsibility, transparency and the governance of AI”, arguing that technological systems must remain subject to ethical oversight and public accountability. The initiative highlights the importance of regulatory frameworks, independent oversight and participatory processes, as well as international cooperation to address the global nature of digital technologies. It also underlines that responsibility must be shared across developers, policymakers and users. The encyclical further examines the societal implications of AI, particularly in communication, education and the labour market. It warns that automation and digital systems may disrupt employment, create new forms of inequality and reduce human agency if not carefully managed. At the same time, it stresses the role of education in fostering critical thinking, responsible use of technology and an “educational alliance” adapted to the digital age. Finally, the initiative frames AI within a broader vision of integral human development. It rejects purely technocratic or efficiency-driven models, advocating instead for a human-centred approach that prioritises dignity, solidarity and social justice. The encyclical calls for a balance between innovation and ethical reflection, ensuring that technological progress strengthens, rather than undermines, human relationships and the common good.

title: IPS Córdoba Assistant — AI Policy Analysis Agent for Social Progress Governance (Subnational: Province of Córdoba)
description: The Province of Córdoba measures the Social Progress Index across all 427 of its localities over two census periods, producing one of the most granular subnational quality-of-life datasets in Latin America. Despite the richness of this data, a persistent and well-documented gap existed between data production and data use in public administration: mayors, municipal officials, and local planners often lacked the time, technical capacity, or analytical tools to translate 57 social indicators into concrete policy decisions. Complex statistical products were being generated but not acted upon. The IPS Córdoba Agent was developed specifically to close this gap — not by simplifying the data, but by building an intelligent analytical layer on top of it that is capable of reasoning across indicators, localities, time periods, and policy frameworks simultaneously. The initiative has three core objectives. First, to democratise access to complex social intelligence: any local official — regardless of technical background — should be able to query their territory's social performance in natural language and receive a rigorous, grounded analysis in return. Second, to support evidence-based policy design at the local level by connecting social diagnoses directly to actionable intervention options drawn from provincial development frameworks. Third, to strengthen a culture of data-driven governance across Córdoba's municipalities, embedding AI-assisted analysis as a routine part of local decision-making rather than an exceptional resource. The IPS Córdoba Assistant is designed and should be understood as a policy analysis agent, not a retrieval chatbot. The distinction is substantial and consequential. A conventional chatbot answers discrete questions by retrieving pre-existing text. This agent, by contrast, performs multi-step analytical reasoning: it interprets a locality's indicator-level results, identifies patterns of improvement or deterioration across dimensions and sub-dimensions, benchmarks performance against provincial averages, infers which population groups are most affected by specific social gaps, and generates policy recommendations grounded in a curated knowledge base that includes academic literature on human development, the provincial development model, and validated intervention frameworks. The agent synthesises all of this into a coherent, contextualised policy narrative — a form of analytical output that would otherwise require a trained policy analyst.

title: Digitalization & AI Introduction Subsidy 2026
description: The Digitalization & AI Introduction Subsidy 2026 is the 2026-cycle successor to the IT Introduction Subsidy (IT導入補助金), Japan's primary SME digitalisation grant since 2017. For the 2026 cycle, the programme was renamed to explicitly incorporate AI, reflecting a strategic shift by the Small and Medium Enterprise Agency (SMEA) and METI towards prioritising AI adoption. The programme subsidises the purchase of pre-registered software and tools from a registry maintained by the secretariat (SMRJ), with AI-enabled tools explicitly prioritised and flagged with a dedicated AI filter for 2026. Applications are handled through accredited IT Introduction Support Businesses, who serve as mandatory implementation partners. The programme offers four streams: a Standard Stream for business process digitalisation; an Invoice Stream for e-commerce and invoice-compliance tools; a Security Stream for cybersecurity services; and a Multi-Party Stream for consortia of 10 or more SMEs pursuing joint DX initiatives. Grant amounts under the Standard Stream range from JPY 50,000 to JPY 4,500,000, covering 50% of costs for standard SMEs and up to 80% for micro-enterprises. A new wage growth requirement introduced for 2026 means repeat applicants must demonstrate a pay increase plan, with partial repayment triggered if targets are unmet. Multiple application rounds run throughout the year from 30 March 2026.

title: Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of Foundation for Trustworthiness ("AI Basic Act")
description: The AI Basic Act followed over four years of legislative discussion, having first been tabled in the National Assembly in July 2020. The 22nd National Assembly merged 19 separate bills through bipartisan agreement, passing the consolidated legislation through the Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee on 26 November 2024, the Legislation and Judiciary Committee on 17 December 2024, and finally the plenary session on 26 December 2024. Korea is the second country in the world to enact such foundational AI legislation, following the US Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (October 2023) and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (June 2024). The Act rests on three main pillars. First, it creates a framework for AI development and trust-based infrastructure: the Minister of Science and ICT may establish and implement an AI Master Plan every three years after gathering input from relevant ministries and local governments, and the Act provides the legal basis for the National AI Committee, chaired by the President and launched in September 2024, as well as the AI Safety Institute, a specialised body protecting citizens' lives, bodies and property from AI risks. Second, it supports the AI industry through government backing for research and development, standardisation, training data policies, and the promotion of AI adoption. It stipulates the designation of AI clusters, the establishment of AI data centres, and the promotion of AI convergence, alongside measures for securing AI experts, special support for SMEs, and fostering of startups. Third, it establishes a safe and trustworthy foundation for high-risk and generative AI, defining these categories as regulatory targets and setting obligations around transparency, safety, and operator responsibilities, alongside a legal basis for voluntary safety and trustworthiness certification and AI impact assessments.

title: Agentic AI Hub
description: The Agentic AI Hub is the central interface between public administration and AI start-ups, translating bureaucratic problems into technical prototypes that are safely piloted and, where successful, scaled to what works. Autonomous AI agents take over administrative routines: checking applications for completeness, requesting missing documents, analysing documents and preparing proposals for official decisions. The BMDS leads the initiative, supported by DigitalService. Pilots are organised around five fields of application: simplifying citizen interaction, supporting citizen-oriented administrative processes, supporting internal administrative processes, building digital tools, and building infrastructure for agentic AI. Selection was carried out by the BMDS and DigitalService, supported by an advisory board from science and industry including representatives of the German Association of Cities, UnternehmerTUM and Merantix, based on strategic fit, representativeness and scalability. The application phase ran from the end of January to the end of February 2026, drawing around 400 start-up and almost 200 municipal applications. Ten start-ups and 17 municipalities deliver 18 separate pilot projects, each addressing a different use case: forml automates housing eligibility checks in Frankfurt and Düsseldorf; Celonis applies process mining to receivables management in Nuremberg and naturalisation in Munich; Summ AI models processes via voice recording across seven municipalities; LeistungsLotse digitises housing benefit applications in Nettetal; Myosotis/formfix supports care-assistance applications in Cologne and Berlin districts; deepset builds an AI orchestration layer in Borken; lector.ai automates mail sorting in Neckar-Odenwald; and Tucan Systems with Speechmind pilot meeting documentation in Bielefeld. Over the three months following the March 2026 launch, the BMDS and DigitalService examine each pilot for effectiveness and scalability, with the goal of supporting employees rather than replacing them. In April 2026, parliamentary members raised questions about the limits of automation, transparency and costs, with concrete guidelines and best-practice examples identified as next steps.

title: SPARK - "Accelerating Planning and Approval through AI"
description: SPARK is a central project of the Federal Government to modernise public administration through artificial intelligence. It addresses challenges in planning and approval procedures. The software was developed through an innovation partnership with the Federal Ministry for Digital and State Modernization developing the solution and the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy initiating and financing it as the department responsible for the development of Germany's hydrogen infrastructure. The modules are modular, scalable and transferable to a variety of administrative procedures. First agents are already working in Hamburg for the approval of hydrogen core grid lines. The modules published so far cover the extraction of relevant information from application documents, formal completeness and plausibility checks, and supporting functions for process overviews, subsequent submissions and comments. Their basis is AI-supported legal dogmatics connected to legal databases, enabling automated deconstruction of norms and legal evaluation; further modules on substantive examination, legal assessment and decision-making are to follow during the year. Following the "Best Use of AI in Government Services" award at the World Government Summit in Dubai in February 2026, the modules were made available under the "Public Money, Public Code" principle, allowing municipalities, companies and civil society to use and further develop them without licence fees. A Parliamentary State Secretary stated that approval durations could be halved, while the Federal Digital Minister referred to an estimated 80 percent acceleration of approval procedures based on the project's stage in 2026. For citizens and companies, this is stated to mean shorter waiting times, more transparency and more reliable processing. Human oversight is central: the AI prepares information and proposals, while the final decision and legal responsibility remain with the responsible employees. The published code is to be understood as a reference and basis for integration rather than a finished security configuration, and a dedicated security review is stated to be mandatory before the AI is involved in productive approval procedures.

title: AI for Care – Artificial Intelligence Strategy for Healthcare in Ireland 2026–2030
description: The strategy is designed to respond to key pressures on Ireland’s health system, including rising demand, workforce constraints, and the need to improve efficiency and patient experience. It identifies artificial intelligence as a core enabler of healthcare transformation, capable of improving diagnostics, automating workflows, and supporting clinical decision-making, while also addressing administrative burdens and resource limitations. Implementation is supported by a dedicated AI Implementation Framework, which provides guidance on how AI projects should be deployed across the health service. This framework includes processes for project design, validation, scaling, and continuous evaluation, ensuring that AI solutions are introduced in a controlled and structured manner. It also ensures alignment with regulatory requirements, including the EU AI Act, and promotes robust governance, safety, and ethical standards in all deployments. The strategy is built on extensive stakeholder engagement, involving the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive, public bodies, clinicians, academic partners, regulators, and patient representatives. A working group with over 30 stakeholders was established to guide its development, and ongoing collaboration with patients and the public is identified as essential for implementation. This participatory approach reflects the emphasis on transparency, trust, and the inclusion of lived experience in decision-making. A central element of the strategy is the development of enabling conditions for AI adoption, particularly digital and data infrastructure. The strategy highlights the importance of high-quality, secure, and interoperable data, supported by initiatives such as electronic health records, the National Shared Care Record, and the Health App. A complementary national data strategy is expected to ensure that AI systems are built on reliable data foundations and that data can be accessed, shared, and reused effectively. The strategy also establishes mechanisms to ensure sustainability and measurable impact. AI initiatives will follow a phased approach, starting with proof-of-concept trials, followed by pilot projects and, where successful, national scaling. Progress will be monitored through defined success factors and evaluation processes, with continuous learning and adaptation built into the implementation model. This approach aims to ensure that AI deployment delivers tangible improvements in patient care, operational efficiency, and healthcare outcomes over time

title: Sweden’s AI Strategy
description: Context Sweden’s first comprehensive AI strategy addresses the need for a coordinated national approach to artificial intelligence to strengthen competitiveness, public sector efficiency, and research capacity. It responds to previously fragmented efforts and seeks to leverage AI to drive societal benefit, sustainable development, and innovation, while managing risks related to privacy, security, and intellectual property. It also aims to position Sweden in an increasingly competitive global AI landscape. Objectives The overarching objective is for Sweden to become one of the top ten countries globally in AI. The strategy aims to: Promote responsible, secure, and trustworthy AI Increase AI adoption across society, particularly in the public sector Strengthen research, innovation, and business competitiveness Deliver tangible societal benefits, including improved public services Enhance Sweden’s global position and technological capability Sweden also aims to become world-leading in the use of AI in public administration. Implementation and future development The strategy will be implemented through an action plan with ongoing and planned measures, including: AI and data related assignments across government agencies Reforms to enable more efficient data sharing Appointment of a national AI coordinator Strengthened international cooperation Implementation is supported by annual follow-up, with the Swedish Agency for Digital Government and the Swedish Post and Telecom Authority responsible for monitoring progress, analysing developments, and proposing additional measures. This approach enables continuous adaptation and supports scaling across sectors, as well as alignment with EU and international frameworks. Process and evaluation The strategy builds on earlier policy work, in particular: The AI Commission’s report Roadmap for Sweden (SOU 2025:12) Sweden’s Digitalisation Strategy 2025–2030 Going forward, it will evolve through regular follow-up, policy adjustments, and international benchmarking, including within the OECD framework.

title: European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU)
description: Under the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU), access to AI compute is provided primarily through the AI Factories programme, which makes AI‑optimised supercomputing capacity available to European researchers, startups, SMEs, industry and public bodies. The initiative focuses on enabling the training and deployment of large‑scale AI models by offering tailored access to high‑performance computing resources combined with technical support. Rather than offering cash-based cloud credits, EuroHPC provides what functions as an in‑kind compute subsidy. AI startups and SMEs can access supercomputing capacity free of charge for innovation activities through the Industrial Innovation track. This access replaces costs that would otherwise arise from commercial cloud GPU usage, while larger or non‑eligible industrial use cases can obtain compute through pay‑per‑use arrangements. AI Factories also support publicly funded research and collaborative projects by offering free access to AI compute for scientific applications, including machine learning, foundation models and generative AI. This applies in particular to projects funded under Horizon Europe or the Digital Europe Programme, ensuring that advanced AI workloads can be developed without direct infrastructure costs for eligible users. Access is organised through structured allocation modes that scale from small experimental use to very large GPU‑intensive workloads.

title: GPU provision measures under the National AI Project to support SMEs and startups
description: Korea's National AI Project, coordinated through the 6th Science and Technology Minister's Meeting, allocated approximately 3,000 of the 10,000 GPUs procured via the 2025 supplementary budget across ministry-level programmes. The Ministry of SMEs and Startups submitted two project proposals, both of which were approved, securing a combined 264 GPUs exclusively for smaller firms and founders. The manufacturing-focused project supports consortiums of technology firms and manufacturing companies, providing end-to-end assistance from R&D through to on-site deployment. Participating consortiums may apply GPU resources to AI training on manufacturing process data, dataset development, and technology validation. The initiative aims to accelerate AI transformation in Korea's SME manufacturing sector and lay the groundwork for a sustainable manufacturing innovation ecosystem. The larger startup incubator operates across three tracks. The Strategic AI Development track (85 GPUs) combines university and government-funded research institute expertise with startup proprietary technologies. The Industry-Specific AI Solutions track (85 GPUs) fosters inter-company collaboration on sector-focused innovation. The Startup for All track (30 GPUs) targets aspiring entrepreneurs, pairing computing access with AI incubation, mentorship, and investment linkage. The initiative responds directly to the persistent barrier that high computing costs represent for smaller firms and first-time founders, reflecting a policy commitment to ensuring AI transformation is not the exclusive domain of large corporations.

title: Zimbabwe National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026–2030
description: The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026–2030 establishes a national framework to harness artificial intelligence for inclusive growth, innovation and digital sovereignty, aligned with Vision 2030 and national development strategies. It addresses the opportunity presented by advances in AI while recognising risks such as inequality, skills shortages, fragmented data systems, infrastructure limitations and weak governance. The strategy seeks to ensure Zimbabwe shapes the adoption of AI in line with local values, national priorities and the Ubuntu philosophy. The strategy is structured around six strategic pillars: AI Talent and Capacity Development; AI Infrastructure and Computational Sovereignty; AI Adoption and Service Transformation; AI Governance, Ethics and Regulatory Framework; AI Research, Development and Innovation; and Strategic International Collaboration and Diplomacy. These pillars focus on strengthening AI literacy and education, expanding research capacity, building secure compute and data infrastructure, promoting responsible and widespread sectoral adoption, and establishing ethical and regulatory safeguards. The strategy builds on identified national strengths, including high literacy levels, indigenous knowledge systems and an emerging digital ecosystem, while addressing gaps such as brain drain, limited institutional resources and data silos. Target sectors include agriculture, mining, healthcare, education, financial services, manufacturing, transport and logistics, energy, public services, environment and climate resilience, and defence and security. AI is positioned as a tool to improve productivity, service delivery, governance transparency and economic diversification, with particular attention to inclusion of rural communities, women, youth and small and medium enterprises. The strategy was developed through a multi‑stakeholder process involving government, academia, the private sector, civil society, the diaspora and international partners. Implementation, oversight and accountability are supported through defined governance mechanisms. Strategic direction is provided by the National AI Council, while day‑to‑day coordination, execution and monitoring are led by the AI Strategy Implementation Office, supported by sector‑specific Technical Working Groups. A dedicated Monitoring and Evaluation Framework defines indicators, targets and reporting processes across the strategy’s lifecycle, supported by public reporting and periodic reviews. Ethical considerations are integrated throughout, with commitments to human dignity, privacy, transparency, inclusivity, safety and accountability guiding AI development and deployment in Zimbabwe.

title: Use of AI in Business Intelligence System Skrinja
description: Skrinja is operating in a secure GDPR-compliant government environment since 2020 and integrates major national datasets, including the Common Agricultural Policy (covering over 90,000 farms), Administrative Procedures (more than 1 million cases annually), Market and Health Inspections, Public-Sector Salaries (over 180,000 employees and 2,000 budget users), Public Procurement, the Central Personnel Registry and Public Funding Programmes. In 2026, Skrinja Open was launched to provide citizens, businesses, researchers and journalists with direct access to public procurement analytics, strengthening transparency, accountability and data-driven governance. Skrinja as Business Intelligence (BI) platform (with data warehouse and UI ML supported predictive analytics) contributes to public value by enabling more transparent, accountable and evidence-based governance. It addresses the need for integrated and reliable data to support strategic decision-making, transforming administrative data into actionable insights for better public policies and more effective use of public resources. Beyond transparency, Skrinja supports proactive policymaking through AI-powered predictive analytics. For example, machine-learning models help identify farms at risk of abandonment, enabling authorities to implement targeted measures before problems materialise. Combined with real-time monitoring of operational workloads and performance indicators, Skrinja allows public bodies to respond more quickly to emerging challenges, optimise resource allocation, and improve service delivery for citizens. By transforming complex data into accessible and actionable information, Skrinja Open strengthens transparency and evidence-based governance (https://ejn.gov.si/skrinja.html , https://ejn.gov.si/skrinja/skrinjaeng.html ). Skrinja also incorporates advanced AI and machine-learning capabilities, currently supporting the Common Agricultural Policy through predictive analytics covering more than 90,000 farms - over 80% of all farms in Slovenia. A predictive model based on XGBoost has been successfully implemented to identify farms at risk of abandonment, enabling early intervention and the development of targeted policy measures. The model analyses historical data and key farm characteristics to estimate risk levels, providing decisionmakers with valuable foresight through dedicated analytical dashboards. Building on this approach, similar predictive models are planned for other domains, including public procurement, administrative procedures, and inspection activities, further enhancing data-driven policymaking across the public sector.

title: High-Tech Agenda Germany – Roadmap for AI
description: The German Federal Government adopted the High-Tech Agenda Germany in July 2025. The agenda serves as a guideline for technological and economic objectives. It reflects the common understanding of the measures required to consolidate Germany's position as a nation of technological innovation, ensure technological sovereignty and maintain economic strength. The focus of the agenda is on the further development of six priority key enabling technologies, one of them artificial intelligence, and the strengthening of five research fields. In addition, nine levers are used to increase the innovation potential in key enabling technologies and research fields. With a concrete roadmap for artificial intelligence and defined milestones published in May 2026, research and application-oriented development are being driven forward in a targeted and transparent manner. Its four key objectives „increasing value creation through AI, improving AI capabilities, becoming a key player in AI innovation and expanding the use of AI in healthcare“ aim to strengthen innovative power, maintain competitiveness and secure prosperity while addressing key challenges facing society and promoting technological potential.

title: Voluntary AI Code of Ethics (AICE)
description: The Voluntary Artificial Intelligence (AI) Code of Ethics (AICE) was developed by AI Malaysia Berhad, Malaysia’s national AI lead agency, to support the practical implementation of Malaysia’s ethical AI principles across the AI ecosystem. While the National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE) establish seven overarching AI Principles, organisations require practical guidance on how these principles can be applied in the design, development, deployment and use of AI systems. AICE serves as an operational bridge between these principles and real-world implementation across sectors. AICE is a voluntary, non-binding guidance document intended for organisations, AI developers, deployers, researchers and other stakeholders involved in AI. It aims to support the adoption of responsible, human-centred and trustworthy AI practices throughout the AI lifecycle, while encouraging practical, consistent and accountable approaches to implementing ethical AI. AICE complements existing legal and regulatory frameworks and does not replace or modify legally binding requirements. Launched in July 2026, the initiative is designed to remain relevant as Malaysia’s AI ecosystem and the wider AI governance landscape evolve. AICE takes into consideration emerging ethical AI principles, including potential future sector-specific and national principles.

title: National AI Action Plan 2026–2030 (AI Nation 2030)
description: National AI Action Plan 2026–2030 (AI Nation 2030) sets out Malaysia’s strategic direction for becoming an AI Nation by 2030. It positions Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a core driver of Malaysia’s next phase of national development, building on the aspiration under the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan (RMK-13) for AI technologies to be integrated holistically across socioeconomic development, public administration and the daily lives of citizens. By 2030, Malaysia aspires to become a Regional Digital Technology Hub and a producer of globally competitive Made by Malaysia AI products and services that are inclusive and sustainable. The Plan responds to the rapid transformation of the global AI landscape, which presents significant opportunities alongside emerging risks for Malaysia. It recognises that technological advances are accelerating AI adoption across sectors, while competition for AI talent, compute capacity, investment and technological capabilities is intensifying. At the same time, AI development has become an increasingly strategic consideration, with implications for national competitiveness, economic resilience and Malaysia’s ability to shape its own AI future. AI Nation 2030 therefore seeks to strengthen national capabilities and enable AI to deliver broad-based value, while ensuring that technological progress remains balanced with trust, effective governance and positive societal outcomes. The Plan is centred on the vision of an Inclusive and Sustainable AI Nation and a mission to deploy AI systematically across Government, Business and the Rakyat, translating technological capability into tangible and measurable benefits. It brings together national priorities across human capital, market-driven innovation and adoption, data and compute infrastructure, responsible governance and sectoral AI adoption. Through this approach, AI is positioned not as an end in itself, but as a means to deliver inclusive growth, national resilience, sustainability and long-term value for Malaysia.

title: Incorporation of Artificial Intelligence into the Electronic Administrative Records System
description: The obligation of public administrations to resolve administrative procedures within the legal timeframe, the right of citizens to effective judicial protection, and the increasing volume of appeals against decisions issued by the General Treasury of Social Security (TGSS) have made it necessary to consider technological alternatives to expedite the processing and resolution of appeals. In this project, the first phase involved using AI to summarise the content of appeals received and processed through the SIMAD-SIEE (Electronic Administrative File System) application. These appeals were then classified for proper processing or redistribution to the appropriate management area. This first phase was implemented in January 2026. In a subsequent phase, the plan is for AI to suggest resolution proposals to the case manager regarding the issues raised in the appeal document, as well as for AI to process the information on appeals collected in our computer application. This will allow the Administration to anticipate future actions aimed at reducing administrative burdens and costs, better redistributing workloads, or preparing for future increases in workload. Results, outcomes and impacts Since its implementation in January 2026, the initiative has enabled the automatic summarisation and classification of appeals received by the Social Security administration, supporting caseworkers in the initial review of each file. This has reduced the time needed to understand the content of appeals and has facilitated their faster and more consistent routing to the appropriate management area. Results are measured through operational use of the system, review of generated summaries by caseworkers, and monitoring of processing workflows within the electronic administrative file system. In the future, the initiative is expected to support greater efficiency in appeal handling, better workload distribution and improved capacity to manage cases.

title: Data Sharing AI (DSAI) - Proof of Value
description: The Data Sharing Artificial Intelligence (DSAI) Proof of Value explores how governed AI agents can responsibly support the drafting of Data Sharing Agreements (DSAs) under Ireland’s Data Sharing and Governance Act 2019 (DSGA). The Act sets out a transparent, legally defined process for sharing personal data between Public Service Bodies, requiring public consultation and publication of DSAs, with oversight by the Data Governance Board (DGB). While this framework strengthens trust and accountability, it also introduces significant administrative and coordination demands. In 2022, the DSGA process was formalized through a nine‑stage DSA Playbook. Stage 3 of this playbook—drafting the DSA itself using a standardized legal template—is particularly challenging. Public bodies must ensure compliance with GDPR and DSGA requirements while coordinating multiple stakeholders and managing legal, technical and policy considerations. In practice, this stage often involves manual drafting, inconsistent ethical and compliance checks, version‑control issues, limited traceability between drafting bodies and OGCIO reviewers, and little structured guidance during document preparation. The DSAI Proof of Value focuses specifically on simplifying Stage 3 by applying AI to support—and not replace—the drafting process. Governed AI agents assist with generating traceable draft sections, applying ethical prompts, and orchestrating workflows that guide users through complex requirements. Full human oversight is maintained throughout: Public Service Data Officers remain human‑in‑the‑loop, and the OGCIO remains human‑in‑command. The AI does not make autonomous decisions but instead produces legally grounded, auditable outputs that reviewers can validate and refine. This approach demonstrates how AI can safely replace a manual process while preserving transparency, accountability and institutional control. Early results indicate reduced administrative burden and improved quality of draft DSAs, measured through staff time and resource‑use surveys. The AI‑assisted process supports the faster creation of plain‑English, legally accurate DSAs with consistent definitions, resulting in agreements suitable for public consultation and typically requiring fewer DGB recommendations. Beyond individual agreements, the initiative establishes a reusable AI governance pattern that can improve service delivery, enhance customer experience, strengthen compliance and risk management, ensure consistent application of OGCIO principles, and improve traceability for both drafting bodies and reviewers.

title: AI Safety and Security Institute Deutschland
description: The AI Safety Security Institute Deutschland is a national competence and evaluation center for Frontier AI models. It combines technical, strategic, and security policy expertise within a single central institution. The institute’s primary goal is to evaluate the opportunities and risks that advanced AI models present for Germany and to sustainably strengthen resilience in the field of artificial intelligence. The AISI Deutschland is currently in the process of being established., where a phased and modular approach is being followed: - In the first step, a “virtual nucleus” is set up by drawing on existing expertise, particularly from the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) and the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA). - In a second step, the AI Safety and Security Institute will be further expanded in terms of both scope and capacity. It is intended to advise the Federal Government on fundamental issues of technical evaluation, development scenarios, and strategic action requirements in the field of AI policy, and to ensure a structured transfer of safety and security-relevant knowledge regarding artificial intelligence to the Federal Government, the public administration, the private sector, and civil society. Its core tasks include, in particular - the technical evaluation of Frontier AI models (including cyber capabilities, levels of autonomy, robustness, and potential for misuse), - analyzing the safety and security-related impacts of AI on state, economy, and society, - providing strategic advice to the Federal Government on AI-related safety, security and sovereignty issues, - monitoring international technology trends and analyzing the global situation, - building national expertise and fostering international cooperation in the field of AI safety and security. From the outset, the AISI Deutschland institute will be internationally oriented and will work closely with corresponding institutions in other countries as well as with multilateral organizations. The institute will also actively participate in the international network of AI safety/security institutes, which serves to facilitate the exchange of knowledge and the development of common positions among the participating countries, and will work together with international partners to establish uniform standards for the effective and safe use of cutting-edge AI.

title: Responsible AI Policy
description: The Responsible AI Policy is developed to address the growing need for a comprehensive framework that enables the responsible adoption of AI while managing associated risks. As AI technologies continue to evolve and expand across sectors, they introduce significant opportunities for economic growth, innovation, and improved public services, alongside risks related to bias, privacy, safety, and misuse. The policy seeks to strike a balance between fostering innovation and ensuring that AI systems are developed and deployed in a safe, ethical, and trustworthy manner. The primary objective of the policy is to establish clear governance principles and regulatory direction for AI across sectors. It provides guidance for government entities, private sector organisations, developers, and users to ensure alignment with national priorities and ethical standards. The policy promotes accountability, transparency, fairness, and human-centric AI, while supporting innovation through enabling mechanisms such as data access, infrastructure, and capacity building. It also aims to harmonise practices across entities and reduce fragmentation in AI adoption and oversight. Looking ahead, the policy is expected to evolve into a more institutionalised and enforceable framework through the development of supporting regulations, standards, and compliance mechanisms. This includes integrating a risk framework, sector-specific guidelines, and monitoring and evaluation tools to track implementation and impact. The policy can scale through continuous updates, stakeholder engagement, and alignment with international best practices, ensuring it remains adaptive to technological advancements and emerging risks while strengthening national AI governance and resilience. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has established a baseline to enable proper AI maturity across entities, enabling improved visibility and benchmarking. Early outcomes include increased alignment on definitions, greater awareness of AI governance practices, and limiting potential risks associated with this technology. Results are measured through surveys, maturity assessments, and periodic reporting across participating entities to improve consistency in reporting and gradual adoption of the policy. In the future, the initiative is expected to drive higher AI adoption maturity, improved efficiency in government services, and stronger national benchmarking capabilities, with measurable improvements in data quality, compliance rates, and alignment.

title: AI-Specific Evaluation Framework for Public Procurement in Korea
description: Public procurement plays a strategic role in Korea’s AI ecosystem, representing a large-scale demand-side policy instrument. At the same time, Korea became the first country in the world to enact a comprehensive AI Basic Act, establishing overarching principles for trustworthy and responsible AI. However, despite this landmark legislation, clear operational definitions and classification criteria for AI-enabled products and services have remained underdeveloped in the procurement context. Existing public procurement evaluation systems—designed primarily for conventional goods and services—have therefore proven inadequate for assessing AI-enabled offerings, particularly with respect to algorithmic performance, data dependency, model reliability, and potential risks. This initiative responds to that institutional and practical gap by developing an AI-specific evaluation framework tailored to public procurement. Rather than applying a single, uniform assessment model, the framework introduces procurement-instrument–specific AI evaluation approaches across major programmes, including innovation procurement, excellent product designation, and multi-supplier framework contracts. Each procurement scheme incorporates AI-relevant evaluation criteria aligned with its policy objectives and operational characteristics, recognising that AI products require different assessment logics depending on the purchasing mechanism. Instead of relying solely on legal definitions, the framework provides practical and evaluative criteria to identify and assess AI-enabled products and services within procurement processes. New assessment dimensions include AI model appropriateness, robustness, transparency, lifecycle risk management, and alignment with public sector use cases, complementing existing criteria on public value, performance, and innovation. This approach allows contracting authorities to more accurately distinguish genuinely AI-enabled solutions from conventional products, while ensuring that AI-specific risks are systematically considered.

title: AI in Digital Health
description: The main objectives are to support safer care, reduce manual work, and improve how health information flows across the system. This includes testing practical AI tools that can summarise information, detect patterns and help people find what they need more easily. The initiative also focuses on strong governance, transparency and safeguards so that AI is used in ways that protect privacy and maintain public trust. Over time, the initiative is expected to grow from early exploration into more structured, systemwide solutions. Future work includes developing standards, guidance and processes that help health organisations adopt AI safely and consistently. As confidence increases and successful solutions are identified, the initiative could scale to support national services, clinical environments and consumerfacing tools. The initiative continues to evolve based on feedback from the sector, advances in technology and lessons from early trials. This iterative approach helps ensure that the Agency’s work remains aligned with community expectations, government policy and the real needs of clinicians and consumers. Results, outcomes and impacts Looking ahead, the initiative is expected to deliver broader impacts across the health system as tools mature and adoption increases. These expected outcomes include reduced administrative burden, faster access to relevant information, and more consistent application of policy and standards. The initiative aims to support safer and more connected care by ensuring people have access to clearer, more timely insights. Future evaluations are expected to include measurable improvements such as reductions in processing time, increased accuracy of information outputs, and broader uptake of AI supported services within partner organisations. These impacts will help guide where AI investments can deliver the greatest value across the national health system. Challenges and lessons learned From this work, several lessons have emerged. One is that early and ongoing engagement with clinicians, consumers and technical specialists helps build trust and leads to better solutions. Another is that high-quality data and clear policies are essential for safe AI use. A final lesson is that AI initiatives need clear problem definitions—tools work best when they are targeted at specific, well understood tasks rather than broad ambitions. Success in initiatives like this depends on a few conditions: strong governance, access to reliable data, skilled teams, clear communication, and a willingness to learn and adapt. Support from leadership and partners across the health system is also critical to ensure AI is used responsibly and delivers real benefits for clinicians and consumers.

title: National Office of Information Technologies (ONTI) AI Agents Guidelines
description: The initiative consists of a standard guideline developed by the National Office of Information Technologies (ONTI), as the governing body, to guide the design and sizing of projects that incorporate Artificial Intelligence Agents in public administration. It arises from the lack of common criteria for the development of these systems and the risk of isolated implementations with proprietary standards, design flaws, or deficiencies in security and governance. It also responds to the need to organise the growing adoption of generative AI-based tools within the National Public Administration. The guideline aims to establish a common framework that promotes open standards and interoperability, incorporates security, governance, and human-in-the-loop oversight criteria, and facilitates informed decisions regarding the levels of autonomy of the agents. It also seeks to optimise the use of public resources, strengthening the efficiency and effectiveness of technology projects through best practices in architecture, risk assessment, and results measurement. While not mandatory, its use is recommended as a best practice guide for the design and sizing of initiatives involving AI Agents. It will be integrated into formal, non-binding technical evaluation processes and updated based on technological advancements. Furthermore, it is complemented by dissemination and training activities targeting technical, legal, and procurement areas, and can serve as a reference for other levels of government, given the guiding role currently played by ONTI's technological standards.

title: SOPHOS
description: The Problem and Opportunity The federal public service faces a critical gap in bilingual service delivery due to the high cost and limited availability of official language training. Traditional classroom models cost upwards of $70,000 per employee annually, resulting in long wait times and supply constraints. Simultaneously, the Government of Canada requires high language proficiency to deploy agile diplomats abroad. The SOPHOS initiative addresses these pressures by introducing a secure, agentic AI-enabled platform. It provides personalised, consistent learning for both official and foreign languages, ensuring linguistic capacity is no longer a barrier to operational readiness or career advancement. Objectives of the Initiative SOPHOS modernises training via a 24/7 AI-driven platform aligned with Public Service Commission (PSC) and Interagency Language Roundtable (ILR) standards. Key objectives include: Accessibility & Personalisation: Providing real-time feedback, oral practice, and learner-driven maintenance tailored to individual needs. Cost Reduction: Complementing traditional instruction with AI-supported modules to allow for more targeted, affordable language acquisition. Security: Operating within a secure environment to ensure data sovereignty. Diplomatic Capacity: Strengthening international engagement by calibrating foreign language training to ILR proficiency levels.

title: Prompting Guide for Public Administration
description: The Prompting Guide for Public Administration was developed to support professionals across Argentina’s National Public Administration as the use of generative AI tools rapidly expanded within government. As public servants increasingly rely on large language models for drafting, analysis and information processing, the guide provides a shared institutional framework to ensure that prompting practices are safe, effective and legally compliant. The guide addresses both skills development and governance. It introduces a practical, structured methodology for prompt design—most notably the ROCLET framework (Role, Objective, Context, Limitations, Style and Output type)—to improve the quality, clarity and reproducibility of AI‑assisted work. At the same time, it establishes clear safeguards covering data protection, confidentiality, intellectual property, transparency and bias mitigation. AI‑generated outputs are explicitly defined as preliminary inputs that support, but do not replace, human judgment or legal, technical and administrative responsibility. Although the guide has not yet been formally published, its expected impact is clear. It is designed to strengthen institutional AI literacy, standardise prompting practices across agencies and reduce risks such as data exposure, hallucinations and overreliance on automated outputs. By embedding mandatory human supervision and traceability into AI‑assisted workflows, the initiative aims to increase confidence, accountability and compliance with Argentina’s legal and administrative framework. Key challenges emerged during the design phase. Balancing innovation with strict legal and security requirements—particularly around data protection and institutional responsibility—required careful framing. Another challenge was ensuring that the guide discourages dependency on AI outputs while promoting their responsible use. The main lesson learned is that practical, operational methodologies are more effective than abstract principles alone. Clear boundaries, institutional endorsement, targeted training and regular updates are essential for sustainable adoption. The central purpose of the guide is to professionalise how public servants interact with AI systems, enabling consistent, transparent and responsible use across government. Following formal publication, it is expected to be institutionalised through internal dissemination, training programmes and integration into broader digital transformation and AI‑governance initiatives. Over time, the guide may be updated to reflect technological advances, regulatory changes and feedback from practical implementation.

title: GOV.BR Chatbot
description: The Chat Gov.BR was built as a secure platform to manage government AI chatbots using LLMs and RAG technology. This ensures millions of Brazilians get accurate and safe answers to public policies. It is essential because 144 agencies are preparing their own assistants. Our central infrastructure saves costs, protects data, and improves services. In the pilot, the GOV.BR Chat helped high school students to enroll in graduation, clarifying doubts about the ENEM (the national exam, similar to "SATs") and SISU (the University selection system after ENEM results). The primary goal of this pilot project was to support high school students throughout their academic journey by providing clear guidance on the SISU system and other public policies. This initiative aimed to increase citizen confidence in official government communications while testing the ability of AI tools to handle massive peaks of demand when millions of people use the system simultaneously. Furthermore, the chatbot collected performance metrics and interaction data, which allowed leaders to make better, evidence-based decisions to continuously improve digital public services. The initiative then evolved from a simple idea into a functional tool with a dedicated knowledge base. In January 2026, the government sent a proactive message to students to announce the ENEM results. This was a significant evolution because the chatbot moved from a passive tool to a proactive one. Instead of waiting for the student, the government started the conversation to clarify the next steps for SISU. This test showed that the government can share accurate information on a massive scale. Looking ahead, this pilot is the foundation for a more modern and inclusive digital governance model. After the team assesses the final performance of this project, the goal is to institutionalize the use of AI in government communication. By using the lessons learned from this education case, the government aims to create "transactional chats." In the future, citizens will not only receive information but will also be able to request benefits and complete government tasks directly through the chatbot. The initiative has yielded measurable results. In the Education case, we reached 6 million students, with a 3.5% interaction rate and an average of 5 messages per user. With Gov.br support, the chatbot independently resolved 65% of queries, significantly reducing human escalation. We measure these impacts using real-time platform analytics and resolution metrics. Developing the GOV.BR chatbot brought several challenges. The main risk was the possibility of incorrect or confusing answers due to flaws in the knowledge base. To address this, we implemented a phased testing strategy: we started with internal checks and followed with a pilot group of students. These tests were essential to build the confidence needed for a large-scale launch.

title: 7th Basic Plan for the Promotion of Science and Technology
description: The 7th Basic Plan was developed through a consultative process launched by Cabinet Office referral to the Council for Science, Technology and Innovation (CSTI) in December 2024, with a dedicated Expert Committee leading drafting through 2025 and a Cabinet decision adopted in March 2026. The Plan is structured around three strategic pillars. First, reviving Japan's research power: recognising a decade of declining research competitiveness, the Plan prioritises reform of the research environment through increased KAKENHI grants, postdoctoral support and university management reform. Second, innovation and industrial competitiveness: AI, semiconductors, quantum technologies, fusion energy, robotics and biotechnology are identified as strategic technology areas requiring end-to-end support from basic research through to social implementation. AI for Science is a prominent cross-cutting theme, covering AI-enabled research data infrastructure, autonomous laboratory systems and AI integration into research methodology; both GENIAC and the Japan AI Safety Institute operate under the mandate the Plan sets. Third, economic security integration: breaking from previous plans, the 7th Plan explicitly aligns science and technology strategy with economic security objectives, identifying strategically sensitive technology domains, introducing research security and integrity requirements for universities, and adopting a selective rather than uniformly open approach to international collaboration. Attracting global talent and positioning Japan as an international innovation hub are also explicit goals.

title: R&D Tax Credit System
description: The Japanese R&D Tax Credit System (試験研究費の税額控除) is a long-standing element of Japan's innovation policy, administered by METI and the NTA. The system operates through blue-form corporate tax returns. Core credit (general category): 6–14% of total qualifying R&D expenses, with the rate sliding upward as R&D intensity increases (R&D expenses as a percentage of total expenses); the credit ceiling is 25% of annual corporate tax liability, extendable to 20–30% depending on changes in R&D spending. SME special rate: 12–17%, with a higher base rate to compensate for limited access to other innovation incentives. Open innovation add-on: an additional up to 10% credit for R&D expenses related to joint or commissioned research with universities and certified research institutions; credit ceiling of 10% of corporate tax. From FY2026, a new strategic technologies track was introduced under the FY2026 Tax Reform: 40% credit for R&D expenses related to six 'national strategic technologies' designated by the Cabinet Office (including AI and robotics; semiconductors and communications; quantum technology; space; bio and healthcare; fusion energy); 50% for joint/commissioned research in these areas with certified institutions; ceiling of 10% of corporate tax. In FY2023, approximately JPY 950B in deductions were claimed under the R&D credit system across all categories. Target audience: all Japanese companies conducting qualifying R&D, from SMEs to large enterprises.

title: AI-Enabled Curbside Analytics in Bergen (Subnational: Bergen)
description: Bergen is experiencing increasing pressure on curbside and shared urban spaces. Growth in micromobility, urban deliveries, flexible loading needs, pedestrian prioritisation, and dynamic public space regulations requires more adaptive and data-driven management tools. Traditional curbside regulation—based on static signage and manual enforcement—does not provide sufficient insight into how space is actually used, where conflicts arise, or how capacity should be adjusted over time. To address this, we are developing an AI-enabled curbside analytics tool that combines CDS/MDS-based regulation software with privacy-preserving video analytics in public streets. The foundation of the system is a digital Curb Data Specification (CDS) framework, aligned with standards developed by the Open Mobility Foundation. This enables us to digitally define and manage geofenced curb zones—such as loading areas, micromobility parking, short-term stopping zones, pedestrian-priority areas, or flexible shared-use spaces—and adjust regulations dynamically. On top of this regulatory layer, we plan to integrate AI services that process blurred video streams from public-space cameras. The system will not identify individuals; instead, it will classify movement patterns and user categories such as delivery vans, private cars, buses, pedestrians, cyclists, and micromobility devices. CDS-defined geofenced areas will be mapped directly into the video image, enabling the AI to monitor how specific zones are used in near real time. By combining regulation data with observed behaviour, the system will allow us to measure intensity of use, dwell times, availability rates, peak load periods, modal distribution, and potential conflicts between user groups. It will also support identification of capacity bottlenecks, safety risks, congestion dynamics, and patterns of non-compliance. We are currently planning a pilot analysis near the city square. A key focus will be loading zones that shift function during the day, assessing how real-world behaviour aligns with intended regulations. The objective is to generate improved insight into curb turnover rates, better understanding of micromobility parking patterns, and more precise identification of conflicts between delivery traffic, cyclists, and pedestrians. The broader ambition is to establish a scalable methodology for AI-supported curbside planning. By combining geofencing, standardised digital regulation, and privacy-conscious video analytics, Bergen aims to move towards more adaptive, evidence-based management of shared urban space—supporting safer streets, more efficient logistics, and better allocation of limited curb capacity.

title: AI for Mapping regulatory mechanisms and Estimating Regulatory Compliance Costs
description: The initiative addresses two linked challenges in regulatory systems. First, Israel does not currently have a single map of prior approvals across regulation. These requirements are spread across laws, regulations and administrative procedures, and may also include “approval within an approval” cases, where one approval is needed to obtain another. This fragmentation creates uncertainty, duplication, inconsistencies and unnecessary costs for regulated entities. Second, regulators and the public often face difficulty quantifying direct compliance costs, which limits better regulatory design and review. The initiative’s objectives are to build a practical foundation for smarter regulation in Israel and to strengthen transparency and public trust. It is designed to support the Israeli Regulatory Authority (the national regulatory oversight body), government regulators conducting economic analysis of proposed or existing regulation, and, at a later stage, the wider public, who may benefit from easier estimates of the costs of complying with specific regulatory requirements. The initiative follows a phased approach. In the first stage, a Hebrew AI engine will scan public regulatory texts (laws, regulations, procedures and guidance) using uploaded files or links, identify regulatory instruments or requirements (the first module will scan for prior approval requirements, such as licences, permits and approvals), and extract structured information on each requirement (including approval type, validity period, and the exact legal citation and source reference). The planned output is a structured database. This stage is also the foundation for the second stage, which will develop an automated tool to quantify direct compliance cost components, based on the Standard Cost Model methodology (for example: fees, tests, professional advice and waiting time), and generate cost estimates for the regulation being reviewed. The initiative is currently in the development phase. It is being advanced through a partnership between the Israel Regulatory Authority (IRA) and the Center for Citizen Empowerment in Israel (NGO). The work is expected to take place over the coming year, with an initial version planned within approximately five months. The Center for Citizen Empowerment in Israel is responsible for IT development, while the Authority provides professional guidance and economic methodology. The workplan includes data collection and cleaning, development of the extraction logic and a first prototype, economic calibration, a pilot in a selected regulatory field, and implementation through a dashboard for Authority staff. If the pilot is successful, the system could scale to additional regulatory fields, broader types of regulation (beyond prior approvals), and additional users, including the public.

title: Digital Twins AI
description: The initiative develops an AI-powered digital twin of the City of Catania, a metropolitan area of approximately 1.2 million inhabitants. Catania is characterised by the presence of a major commercial port, an international airport, and its proximity to Mount Etna, one of the most active volcanoes in Europe. The city also experiences significant daily mobility flows, with around 800,000 vehicles entering from the surrounding Etna municipalities. These factors create complex challenges in terms of mobility management, environmental monitoring, infrastructure resilience, and emergency preparedness. The digital twin integrates data from transport systems, environmental sensors, public services, and urban infrastructure into a unified virtual model. It enables public authorities to simulate scenarios related to traffic congestion, volcanic risk, port and airport operations, climate events, and infrastructure maintenance. By providing predictive analysis and real-time monitoring, the system supports more informed and co-ordinated decision-making. The main objective is to strengthen urban planning, optimise resource allocation, and enhance risk management in a city exposed to natural hazards and high mobility pressure. By testing policy options in a virtual environment before real-world implementation, the initiative reduces costs, limits unintended consequences, and increases transparency for citizens and stakeholders. In the future, the initiative is expected to expand through the integration of additional data sources and AI capabilities, becoming a permanent decision-support system within public administration. It may be scaled at regional level and connected with other territorial platforms, fostering collaboration between public institutions, research centres, port and airport authorities, and private operators. Over time, the digital twin will contribute to making Catania more resilient, sustainable, and efficient. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has improved data integration and co-ordination across municipal departments, reducing analysis time for urban planning scenarios by an estimated 30%. Pilot simulations on traffic flows and emergency response have supported more efficient decision-making and risk assessment. Results have been measured through performance indicators such as response time, data processing speed, and scenario comparison accuracy. In the future, the initiative is expected to reduce congestion, improve infrastructure maintenance planning, and enhance resilience to volcanic and climate-related risks.

title: Custom machine translator
description: OBJECTIVE : Develop a machine translator for StatCan products, trained on public StatCan products, metadata, and other internal documents. It outputs initial translation drafts for various texts, including sensitive and pre-release material, that language experts will review and edit. OBSERVATION : Blind test results reveal that customised machine translators outperform off-the-shelf options in translation quality. TARGET GOAL : Integrate StatCan’s custom machine translator into Translation Services’ existing computer-assisted translation tools to generate initial translations for language experts to review and edit. The tool will be accessible through a user interface that can (a) translate sentences, (b) translate full documents and reproduce the initial format, and (c) be used within existing tools. It is intended to increase operational efficiency and reduce manual workload when and where it is fit for use. The tool operates in a protected environment accessible to StatCan’s internal language experts. It supports the consistent use of terminology, international standards, and StatCan’s writing style. Machine-translated texts are not perfect, but provide a draft that can be easily edited. DATA & METHODS : Azure neural machine-translation models were fine-tuned on 395,000 segments of public StatCan products. They were evaluated through expert review using four quality metrics and automated metrics. Quality is planned to be monitored by reviewing translations of recurring StatCan documents, calculating post-editing scores, and collecting quality issues in a form. All machine-translated texts are reviewed. The language expert is at the core of decision-making, and the tool’s versatility allows the expert to choose the best tool and process for each text. Results, outcomes and impacts The current baseline of 1,500 words translated per day could increase to 2,500 words per day, which would equal a 66.7% increase, in addition to cost savings from reduced use of external translators. The work distribution strategy is still being fine-tuned, and more data will be available as time progresses and as the tool is fully implemented within the Language Services teams. Data on the number of words post-edited are available, and we expect to see a sharp increase over time. We are working on integrating time metrics as well.

title: Codebridge
description: CodeBridge supports StatCan’s shift from proprietary applications to open-source software alternatives and aligns with modern data practices for using open-source tools. CodeBridge helps in the skills development of analysts and developers as it provides explanatory text for code and explains legacy “black box” code, facilitating the transition of statistical code to Python or R. CodeBridge provides fast, accurate conversions with clear explanations that help users learn as they go. It allows users to customise prompts, choose their preferred open-source packages (R or Python), and keep control of their code. It provides line-by-line explanations, so users understand what’s happening, like having a mentor built into their workflow. Code is processed in a protected-data environment, so data stays secure. The tool is offered to users in both English and French. Two education surveys focused on secondary and post-secondary education finance underwent significant modernisation efforts since 2022. Both surveys were successfully transitioned to open-source platforms and have since completed multiple cycles using these new tools. Production in open-source tools has been completed for the 2023, 2024, and 2025 cycles. Since the initial migration process, additional tools were built in Python for digital collection tools, including automated mail-out processes and materials. The Blaise application, previously used for hard-copy questionnaires, became unavailable. Rather than allowing this disruption to impede progress, the teams proactively transitioned to R and Python for questionnaire development and data processing. Through the adoption of these flexible and powerful tools, the digital questionnaire processing environment was recreated using R, with early migration efforts supported via StatCan GitLab. Results, outcomes and impacts The migration effort began roughly three years ago on Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) due to the absence of a designated Zone environment. This allowed the teams to establish processes and workflows in a cloud-based setting. Subsequently, work is transitioning to the Zone environment for enhanced stability and integration. One cycle has been completed using Python, which is used for data cleaning and verification. This open-source tool has been chosen to align with production partners in the Centre for Social Data Processing (CSDP), where migration is also underway.

title: National Artificial Intelligence Agenda
description: The ANIA, which corresponds to Action #20 of the 2026–27 Action Plan of the National Digital Strategy, has the objectives of using AI as a driver of competitiveness at the service of society and ensuring that the use of technology translates into economic opportunity, productivity, and public value. It is based on six guiding principles: Responsible innovation, ensuring a focus on the ethical and safe use and development of technology; Focus on strategic bets, concentrating resources on areas with the greatest potential; Public Administration as a catalyst, leading by example; More than technology, recognising that AI adoption is also an organisational and human effort; Product-driven AI, with concrete, useful, and scalable use cases; and Build on what already works and ensure continuous evaluation. The Agenda is structured around four areas of action: Infrastructure and Data (computational capacity and a robust data economy); Innovation and Adoption (accelerating adoption across the economy, with a focus on SMEs and Public Administration); Talent and Skills (training, attracting, and retaining AI talent); and Responsibility and Ethics (protecting citizens and promoting responsible innovation). The ANIA is implemented through 32 initiatives, covering the entire ecosystem — universities, research centres, companies (including start-ups), and Public Administration (PA). Also, this agenda is aligned with the AI Continent Action Plan and the Apply AI strategy, positioning Portugal to contribute to the goals and objectives of the European Union in this area. A central deliverable is Action 2.7, consisting of the development of AMÁLIA, the first Portuguese large language model (LLM). Other key projects comprise investments in shared enabling infrastructure, with the expansion of the national supercomputing capacity (action 1.1) and the establishment of an AI Gigafactory in collaboration with Spain (action 1.2); the development of AI skills for the workforces of both the public and private sectors (actions 3.1 and 3.2); and the promotion of responsible AI research and the AI ecosystem, with specialised support for start-ups (action 4.2), the co-ordination of critical ecosystem initiatives through the Center for Responsible AI (action 4.3) and the implementation of the AI Act (action 4.4). Together, ANIA’s initiatives provide a time-bound route to develop the national AI ecosystem, models, data and computing infrastructure and to embed them into public services and businesses.

title: Red Roofs – Green Roofs - Extended Digital Twin – National Programme Metro Plus 21-27 (Subnational: Milan)
description: Red Roofs In order to accelerate the achievement of carbon neutrality by advancing the 2050 deadline, and in compliance with the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (PAESC), the Municipality of Milan started developing a GIS-oriented web application, supported by AI algorithms for the automatic analysis and classification of geospatial data. This application is capable of identifying the morphology of buildings’ roofs and grouping them by type (flat roofs and pitched roofs), identifying the optimal roof pitches, i.e. those exposed to a suitable orientation, for simulating the installation of photovoltaic panels. The calculation has been based on the available classified "point cloud" generated by the LiDAR flight, with an average density of over 20 points per square metre. The goal is to address municipally owned buildings first, in order to encourage interventions on private buildings to increase self-consumption of electricity produced by photovoltaic panels with the presence of storage systems. The next step will be to incorporate this initiative into the broader Air and Climate Plan (PAC), inspired by the municipality, promoting public-private partnerships (PPP) with a project financing mechanism that will leverage the financial contribution already made available. This initiative will also allow for similar interventions on privately owned buildings, promoting them with tax breaks. Green Roofs Green roofs and green walls can generate a multitude of benefits, such as reducing the "heat island" effect; increasing the energy efficiency of buildings; improving stormwater management by reducing sewerage; improving air quality; increasing biodiversity in urban areas; improving the microclimate by reducing temperatures; and, where possible, by creating social spaces that improve human psychological well-being. Using a similar methodology and with the support of AI algorithms, a GIS-oriented web application for the identification of flat roofs was created. This application is suitable for the installation of plant-based structures that require reduced nutritional and energy input, low thickness and weight, and low management and installation costs. The application also uses the identification and delineation of urban heat islands, within which the Building Regulations guarantee a bonus for reducing the RIC (Climate Impact Reduction). Looking ahead, this initiative will allow the Municipality to address a technical issue: verifying the building's static stability, in order to ensure the effect of additional loads that were not foreseen in the building's design. It could address a legal issue as well: defining an administrative approach capable of managing the public use of undivided private property.

title: AI-based “iDost” Digital Assistant
description: The “iDOST” initiative is an AI-enabled digital assistant integrated into the “e-Social” portal, a unified platform for social services developed by the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of Population of the Republic of Azerbaijan. It facilitates access to public services related to labour, social protection, employment and all other related issues while addressing challenges such as fragmented information, complex administrative procedures, and limited accessibility for citizens, especially those facing time, mobility, or information barriers. It benefits a wide range of users, including jobseekers, pensioners, persons with disabilities, employers, and residents of remote areas. Through the “iDOST” section located on the platform’s main page, citizens can directly access relevant electronic services or obtain detailed information about them simply by typing their requests, without searching through the site menu. For example, based on queries such as “I want to check my pension” or “I need to obtain an e-reference”, the AI directs users to the appropriate service within seconds. “iDOST” is capable of promptly answering citizens’ questions related to pension provision, social payments, disability, references, and other social services. Users can freely type their questions and receive the necessary information and service links. One of the key advantages of the system is its interactive communication mechanism with citizens. To enhance the quality of responses generated by the AI, a dedicated evaluation function has been introduced, allowing users to rate answers using a star-based system and provide feedback or suggestions. This participatory approach enables continuous learning and improvement of the system. Moreover, the initiative is being further developed to deliver tailored, context-aware responses through citizens’ personal cabinets, accessed via Digital Login, which serves as a nationwide single sign-on point for social services. Results, outcomes and impacts Since its launch, iDOST has processed 41,168 requests from 25,477 conversations, averaging 5.87 seconds per response, with 2,283 requests daily and 1,414 active conversations. The tool has improved access to social and labour services, expanded 24/7 availability, and lowered administrative work. Impact is measured through usage metrics and a 1–5-star satisfaction rating. Expected future impacts include further efficiency gains, higher user satisfaction, and continued reduction in service delivery time and operational costs.
