title: One Million Coders Programme (OMCP)
description: Following a 2025 pilot across four cities, Accra, Kumasi, Sunyani, and Tamale, which attracted approximately 94,000 applications within 48 hours and ultimately trained 859 participants (52% female), lessons from the pilot informed the design of the national rollout to ensure the programme delivers practical digital skills and meaningful employment pathways. The national rollout began on 10 April 2026 with the distribution of laptops to institutions and training centres, with each of the 130 learning centres across all 16 regions equipped with 50 customised laptops configured specifically for coding and digital training. A total of 130 constituency-level coordinators have been recruited to oversee training centres and provide technical support, with plans to expand coverage to all constituencies nationwide. Registration is linked to the Ghana Card through a simplified verification system, and the application portal was announced to reopen to allow both previous and new applicants to complete registration. Key implementing partners include the Ghana Investment Fund for Electronic Communications (GIFEC), Ghana Digital Centres Limited, and the Ghana-India Kofi Annan Centre of Excellence in ICT, where the programme was originally launched. Twelve universities are participating in the initial phase, including the University of Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, and the University of Cape Coast. Private sector support includes MTN Ghana, which contributed approximately US$2 million towards laptop procurement, alongside partners such as Google, Telecel, and the Data Protection Commission. Courses span a wide range of disciplines, including AI essentials, coding, cloud computing, cybersecurity, data analytics, software development, digital marketing, and UI/UX design, offered at beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels, both online and in person. The programme is inclusive by design, targeting a 50/50 gender split, and is positioned as a central pillar of Ghana's digital transformation agenda, building a skilled workforce for emerging opportunities in software development, artificial intelligence, and remote digital employment. President Mahama stated that the government aims to train 300,000 Ghanaians under the programme in 2026 alone, describing it as "a national commitment and a social contract."

title: MERaLiON (Multimodal Empathetic Reasoning and Learning in One Network)
description: MERaLiON is designed with features that understand Southeast Asia's diverse languages, cultures, and nuances. The model incorporates code-switching capabilities to handle natural language mixing across the region, and is emotionally intelligent, able to detect emotional tone, gender, and paralinguistic features in speech. It is also fine-tuned with industry-specific data to ensure contextual relevance and accuracy. Additional capabilities include multilingual speech transcription and translation, speech summarisation, audio scene understanding, and local speech recognition covering regional accents, dialects, and colloquialisms. To ensure broader impact and accelerate adoption, the Singapore government announced the establishment of a Consortium led by A*STAR, bringing together private sector partners (DBS Bank, Grab, ST Engineering, NCS, and SPH Media Trust), alongside the Ministry of Health. The Consortium aims to harness ecosystem expertise and share learnings across sectors. Further Southeast Asian language coverage is planned for future releases.

title: Artificial Intelligence Governance for Indonesian Banking
description: Artificial Intelligence Governance for Indonesian Banking sets out a comprehensive framework to guide the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence within the banking sector. The initiative addresses the rapid adoption of AI in banking and the associated risks, including bias, limited transparency, cybersecurity threats, and potential impacts on financial system stability. It emphasises that the use of AI by banks must align with prudential principles, customer protection, and the safeguarding of banking and financial stability, and should be managed throughout the entire AI lifecycle. The initiative outlines key elements of AI governance, including guiding values and principles, risk identification and classification, and structured risk management processes. It identifies major risks such as deepfakes, black box models, algorithmic bias, data quality weaknesses, over-reliance on AI, and cyber threats. These risks are discussed in relation to core banking activities, including credit assessment, fraud detection, customer services, compliance, and operational functions. While recognising opportunities from predictive, generative, and agentic AI, the initiative stresses that these technologies must be implemented in a controlled, accountable, and responsible manner. Governance arrangements focus on the responsibilities of banks to establish effective oversight, leadership involvement, clear roles for AI developers and users, documented internal policies, and integration with existing risk management, compliance, and internal control frameworks. The initiative promotes alignment with national strategies, ethical principles, and international standards, and highlights the importance of collaboration among banks, regulators, third-party providers, and other AI actors across the AI lifecycle. It also identifies challenges related to skills, leadership, AI literacy, and organisational readiness. The initiative further provides guidance on supervision and audit, including expectations for monitoring, documentation, auditability, transparency, and human oversight. AI governance is presented as a continuous process that must adapt to technological developments, emerging risks, and evolving regulatory approaches. The overall objective is to ensure that AI systems used in Indonesian banking remain trustworthy, secure, explainable, and accountable, while supporting innovation and improving efficiency without compromising prudence or financial stability.

title: National Supercomputer "DAEDALUS" and Lavrio Data Center
description: The National Supercomputer "DAEDALUS" is a Greek government initiative to build one of Europe's most powerful computing systems, with a total budget of €58.9 million. Implemented by GRNET SA under the Ministry of Digital Governance and co-funded by EuroHPC JU, it is expected to be operational in early 2026. With a power of 89 PetaFlops, DAEDALUS will serve as the computing core of the Greek AI Factory "Pharos".

title: Enterprise Compute Initiative (ECI)
description: The ECI is structured around three key actors working in coordination. Digital Industry Singapore (DISG) administers the programme, assesses company applications, and awards grants to consultant partners on behalf of the government. Cloud service providers, Google Cloud, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, and Oracle, provide access to compute, cloud platforms, and AI tools, and connect participating companies with nominated consultant partners. Consultant partners, selected by cloud service providers for their platform expertise, work directly with companies to develop an AI roadmap and support the development of a minimum viable product and change management processes. Each participating company receives cloud credits and consultancy services. Google Cloud offers up to SGD $200,000 in training licences; Amazon Web Services provides a baseline of SGD $350,000 in cloud credits with up to SGD $600,000 through complementary programmes; Microsoft offers up to SGD $250,000 in Azure credits and up to SGD $700,000 in co-development services for select businesses; Oracle provides up to SGD $250,000 per company, and up to SGD $1.9 million for enterprises requiring private cloud infrastructure. The total supportable consulting cost is capped at SGD $150,000, with DISG covering 70% of actual costs, capped at SGD $105,000 per company. Participating companies are expected to fully commit manpower and technical resources for approximately six months, and to deliver an AI roadmap and a minimum viable product tested with at least five end-users. The programme runs one year from the launch date of each cloud service provider, with multiple cohorts launched on a rolling basis. Companies that progress quickly and demonstrate readiness for broader AI plans may be considered for further support by DISG.

title: HumAIn
description: Saudi Arabia's strategy bets on models and software but also on the physical underpinnings of AI: energy, data centres, semiconductors, and connectivity, leveraging its unique comparative advantage in abundant oil, expanding renewables, and a cost-effective compute infrastructure. HumAIn is assembling a network of strategic partnerships. A deal with Qualcomm includes co-developing AI data centres, building a semiconductor design centre, and integrating HumAIn's Arabic large language model ALLaM into Qualcomm's ecosystem of AI edge devices. A deal with NVIDIA includes plans to build AI factories with 500 megawatts of computing capacity, while AWS is investing over $5 billion to develop an "AI Zone", a dedicated cluster of data centres optimised for training and deploying AI systems at scale.

title: SPRIND Next Frontier AI
description: Announced by SPRIND at EurIPS in Copenhagen on 3 December 2025, the Next Frontier AI Initiative is a DARPA-style challenge programme designed to build at least three European Frontier AI Labs capable of developing their own foundation models and competing with US and Chinese AI leaders. Applications are open until 31 May 2026; successful teams begin in July 2026 and are funded for 24 months. Up to 10 teams receive non-dilutive funding in staged tranches totalling up to EUR 27M per team (from the EUR 125M total pool), plus compute access, infrastructure, MLOps support, legal and strategic company-building support, and structured investor/partner matching. In autumn 2028, up to 3 winning labs are selected and positioned to raise EUR 1B scale-up rounds from a pre-aligned investor and corporate partner ecosystem. The programme explicitly targets new model classes, modalities, agentic systems, and efficient training regimes — not AI application layers. title: Guidance for AI Adoption: Implementation Guidance
description: The Guidance for AI Adoption: Implementation Guidance is an Australian Government initiative released in October 2025 to support organisations in adopting AI responsibly across the economy. It responds to the need to build confidence, trust and capability in AI use by providing structured, practical practices aligned with Australia’s AI Ethics Principles and international standards. The initiative targets both AI developers and deployers, including businesses, government bodies and non-profits, and offers detailed governance and technical guidance. It is designed to be accessible to varied audiences, with a focus on integrating AI practices into existing organisational governance systems while enabling experimentation and scaling of AI initiatives. It addresses risks arising from AI systems, such as bias, lack of transparency and potential harm to individuals, communities and organisations. The framework promotes a human-centred approach, ensuring fairness, inclusion and respect for rights, and encourages organisations to assess impacts, engage stakeholders and monitor harms throughout the AI lifecycle. Implementation is structured around six practices: defining accountability, understanding impacts, managing risks, ensuring transparency, testing and monitoring systems, and maintaining human oversight. These are supported by processes such as stakeholder engagement, risk assessments, incident reporting, AI registers, and continuous monitoring, enabling organisations to prevent, identify and mitigate AI-related risks while meeting legal and ethical obligations.

title: HHS AI Strategic Plan
description: The HHS AI Strategic Plan presents a high-level framework to guide the adoption and use of artificial intelligence across health, human services, and public health in the United States. It emphasises that AI will affect nearly all aspects of these systems and should be deployed to deliver tangible benefits for individuals, including better health outcomes, improved service delivery, and increased efficiency. The plan is structured around four overarching goals: catalysing AI innovation and adoption, promoting trustworthy and responsible AI use, democratising access to AI technologies and resources, and cultivating an AI-ready workforce. These goals are intended to improve quality, safety, accessibility, equity, and outcomes across health and human services, while ensuring that AI is used as a support tool rather than a replacement for human decision-making. The strategy is organised across several domains covering the full ecosystem, including medical research and discovery, medical product development, healthcare delivery, human services delivery, and public health, as well as cross-cutting areas such as cybersecurity and internal operations. For each domain, the plan outlines opportunities for AI use, current trends, risks, and action plans, including policy, funding, infrastructure, and education measures. A key feature of the plan is its emphasis on balancing innovation with risk management. It identifies risks such as algorithmic bias, data privacy breaches, and potential safety concerns, and highlights the need for governance frameworks, regulatory oversight, transparency, and human oversight. Ensuring equitable access, protecting sensitive data, and maintaining public trust are presented as central conditions for successful AI deployment. Finally, the plan adopts an adaptive and evolving approach, recognising that AI technologies are rapidly advancing. It proposes continuous monitoring, stakeholder engagement, and iterative updates to policies and actions, with the objective of coordinating efforts across public and private actors and ensuring that AI contributes to improved health, well-being, and service outcomes for all Americans.

title: AI and Health Data Strategy 2025–2028
description: The strategy addresses structural challenges in the French health data ecosystem, particularly fragmentation, limited interoperability, and complex access procedures. It seeks to unlock the potential of existing datasets by improving their organisation, quality, and reuse, while ensuring compatibility across systems and supporting large-scale data-driven innovation. A major focus is the preparation for the European Health Data Space framework, which introduces new obligations for data sharing and reuse across the EU. The strategy outlines concrete steps to align national systems with these rules, including defining national bodies responsible for data access, setting up standardised procedures, and creating coordinated infrastructures to enable secure and efficient data exchange at both national and European levels. The initiative also defines a comprehensive governance model to oversee the use of health data and AI. This includes strengthening institutional coordination, creating mechanisms for stakeholder participation, and establishing oversight structures to monitor compliance, security, and ethical standards. Particular emphasis is placed on protecting individuals’ rights, improving transparency around data use, and ensuring accountability in the management of sensitive health information. In addition, the strategy introduces operational measures to accelerate innovation, such as the development of open tools, shared resources, and experimental environments to test new data uses and AI applications. It supports the emergence of new use cases while encouraging collaboration between public and private actors, including in research, healthcare delivery, and industrial development. Finally, the strategy incorporates mechanisms for long-term sustainability, including financial planning for data infrastructures and the introduction of economic models governing data access and reuse. It also establishes monitoring tools, indicators, and evaluation processes to assess the effectiveness, impact, and equity of data and AI use in healthcare over time.

title: AI Ecosystem in Social and Health Services (SOTE) – AI Vision 2035
description: The SOTE AI Vision 2035 is built around four principles: individual self-direction, active prevention for populations and individuals, personalised medicine and tailored treatments, and automation of care, services, decision-making and support functions. Over five to ten years, healthcare and social welfare AI is expected to evolve from supporting professionals to becoming collaborative intelligence and increasingly autonomous automation that initiates, directs and supervises entire service and care processes. Citizens and clients are increasingly expected to utilise AI themselves to maintain their wellbeing, with a personal AI wellbeing coach acting as a guide to services, initially with simple features but evolving into a more versatile and interactive assistant. Self-measurement is noted as needed to provide comprehensive data for training AI models, enabling AI to produce personal forecasts and tailored care pathways. The roles of healthcare and social welfare professionals will diversify, with more time freed from routine tasks for direct client work. Professionals may specialise either in physical, in-person care requiring direct interaction or in remote, knowledge-based supervisory roles monitoring and guiding clients' health as well as the activities of AI agents and robots in service provision. Leadership is described as increasingly about managing the technological transformation within the system, with leading people through change becoming a key skill as knowledge-based management and services become more automated. The recommended actions are organised around five areas: national and regional guidance and legislation, including identifying opportunities for autonomous AI decisions and necessary legislative amendments; education and competence for professionals, leaders and citizens, including guaranteeing access to AI for all through devices, connections and AI literacy; standardising healthcare and social welfare data structures and facilitating their shared use for developing large AI models; identifying service and care paths suitable for automation and developing the use of AI in genetic data analysis and disease prediction; and supporting public-private collaboration and reforming procurement. A Wellbeing AI Ombudsperson is proposed to oversee the rights of clients and professionals and to monitor impact, equity, ethics and environmental effects in the long term.

title: AI Basic Plan
description: Japan’s Artificial Intelligence Basic Plan , adopted by Cabinet decision on 23 December 2025, sets out the basic policy framework for promoting the research, development and utilisation of artificial intelligence-related technologies. The plan defines the overall concept, policy directions and measures to be implemented by the government. The document is structured into four main components. First, it presents the basic concept, including the positioning of AI as a technology underpinning economic and social development and the objective of enhancing its use and development. Second, it sets out basic policies for promoting AI innovation. Third, it details government measures, organised into four areas: accelerating AI utilisation across sectors; strengthening AI development capabilities; advancing AI governance; and supporting transformation of economic and social systems. The plan also establishes provisions for implementation, including coordination across ministries and agencies, follow-up and monitoring, and mechanisms for revision. It provides for alignment with related strategies in science, technology and digital policy, and identifies the need for comprehensive and systematic promotion of AI-related measures.

title: Act on Promotion of Research, Development, and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Related Technologies
description: Japan’s Act on the Promotion of Research and Development and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Related Technologies (AI Act), enacted on 28 May 2025, is the country’s first law specifically addressing artificial intelligence. It establishes a national framework to promote AI research, development, and use, and sets out general principles and governance arrangements. The Act functions as a “fundamental law,” defining broad policy directions rather than detailed regulatory requirements. It provides for the development of a “Basic AI Plan” to guide and coordinate government action, alongside institutional structures for centralised policy oversight. It outlines roles for public authorities and private actors involved in AI, including expectations that businesses align with government policies and principles. It also enables future legislative, financial, and administrative measures to support AI. The Act does not establish detailed compliance obligations or penalties, focusing instead on principles, coordination, and policy frameworks.

title: Genesis Mission
description: The Genesis Mission was launched by President Trump via Executive Order on 24 November 2025, building directly on EO 14179 (Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, January 2025) and advancing the America's AI Action Plan (July 2025). The Mission's central infrastructure deliverable is the American Science and Security Platform: an integrated, secure national platform combining the DOE's 17 national laboratories, world-class supercomputers, federal scientific datasets, and AI systems into a unified discovery environment. The Executive Order sets a series of firm deadlines: within 60 days, DOE must identify at least 20 national science and technology challenges spanning priority domains including advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, critical materials, nuclear energy, quantum information science, and semiconductors; within 120 days, DOE must identify initial datasets and model assets for Platform integration; within 240 days, DOE must inventory robotic laboratory and AI-directed experimentation capabilities across national laboratories; and within 270 days, DOE must demonstrate an initial operating capability of the Platform for at least one identified challenge. The Executive Order also directs DOE to establish standardised frameworks for public-private partnerships. Prize competitions, fellowships, internships and international scientific collaboration are also mandated. The Mission's three headline priority areas are American energy dominance (accelerating advanced nuclear, fusion and grid modernisation), advancing discovery science, and ensuring national security through AI-enabled nuclear stockpile reliability and strategic deterrence.

title: DOL AI Workforce Guidance (TEGL 03-25)
description: Issued in August 2025 by the Employment and Training Administration (ETA) as Training and Employment Guidance Letter No. 03-25, implementing Executive Order 14277 ('Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth'). The guidance encourages state and local workforce development boards (LWDBs) to use Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) Title I Youth, Adult, and Dislocated Worker programme funds to: provide AI literacy training; integrate AI learning into existing programmes; partner with employers, education providers, and other organisations to expand access; and create AI skills development pathways for participants facing barriers to employment. Guidance is non-prescriptive, preserving local flexibility. A complementary AI Literacy Framework (Training and Employment Notice No. 07-25) was released in February 2026, defining five foundational AI literacy content areas and seven delivery principles. The framework aligns with the White House AI Action Plan (July 2025) and the America's Talent Strategy (August 2025, joint DOL/DOC/DoEd). Target audience is the entire US public workforce system and its participants.

title: Executive Order 14179: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in AI
description: Executive Order 14179 represents a fundamental reorientation of US federal AI policy away from the risk-management and safeguard-oriented approach of the Biden era towards an explicit focus on removing regulatory barriers, promoting competition and ensuring American global leadership in AI. Key provisions include: the immediate revocation of Executive Order 14110 ("Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence") and all actions taken under it; a direction to all agency heads to identify and begin repealing or modifying regulations, guidance and policies that may inhibit American AI innovation; the establishment of an interagency AI Action Plan to be developed within 180 days by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), the National Security Council and the National Economic Council; a reaffirmation that AI policy must sustain American global leadership and prevent adversary nations from gaining advantage in AI; and the principle that AI systems developed in the US must be "free from ideological bias or engineered social agendas". The EO served as the mandate for the subsequent OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22 (April 2025) on federal AI use and procurement, and for the America's AI Action Plan published in July 2025.

title: AI Pioneers
description: Launched in September 2025 within France's national AI strategy (Phase 3) and France 2030 investment plan, the 'Pionniers de l'IA' programme is operated for the State by Bpifrance and the Agence de programmes Numérique (Inria). The programme targets projects developing breakthrough ('rupture') AI technologies with high economic impact and national sovereignty significance, particularly in five priority sectors: industrial design and manufacturing, biomedical and health, ecological transition, cybersecurity, and energy. Projects progress through three selective phases: Phase 1 — technical feasibility (100% grant, EUR 100K–EUR 200K, 6–12 months); Phase 2 — prototype and demonstrator development (50% grant/advance for enterprises, 100% for research, EUR 400K–EUR 800K, 6–18 months); Phase 3 — market application and MVP development (up to 50% for enterprises, EUR 3M–EUR 8M, 1–3 years). Passage between phases is selective. International consortia with European partners are eligible; European partners may access funding from the Current AI Foundation. 23 first-round laureates were announced in February 2026. The programme succeeds earlier France 2030 AI calls (Communs numériques pour l'IA générative, 2023; Accélération des usages de l'IA générative, 2024).

title: Artificial Intelligence Boost Loan
description: The Prêt Boost Intelligence Artificielle is part of Bpifrance Flash's suite of online SME loans (alongside Prêt Boost Transformation Numérique, Prêt Boost Industrie, etc.). It is delivered entirely online through Bpifrance's digital platform with a response within 48 hours and disbursement within 7 days. The loan requires no personal or corporate guarantee (sans garantie ni caution personnelle) and operates on a co-financing basis: the applicant must have an existing bank loan with a remaining repayment period of more than 3 years. Loan duration is 3 to 5 years, with a repayment deferral period of up to 12 or 24 months to allow the business to realise AI benefits before repayments begin. Eligible expenses include AI software acquisition, implementation costs, consulting fees, and AI project costs. To be eligible, a company must: be a VSEs or SME under the EU definition with fewer than 49 employees; be incorporated and operating in France (metropolitan and DROM (overseas)); be at least 3 years old; and be financially sound.

title: Cambodia AI Readiness Assessment (RAM) Report 2025
description: Cambodia is taking exciting steps in the policy and legal dimension by actively participating in ASEAN discussions on AI governance and working on important legislation such as Personal Data Protection, Cybersecurity, and AI Ethics Guidelines. However, there's still work to be done, as the country does not yet have a finalised national AI strategy, experiences some fragmentation in institutional roles, and has room to grow in cybersecurity maturity and open data performance. Additionally, there is a need for specific laws surrounding AI procurement and access to information. The social and cultural aspects show encouraging progress in bridging the gender gap in internet usage, along with good PISA results for girls in science and reading. Many initiatives are working hard to close the STEM gender gap, and CADT is making strides by developing Khmer language datasets. Despite these positive steps, Cambodia still faces several challenges, including connectivity issues, a persistent gender gap in STEM fields within higher education and the workforce, low performance in e-government services, and the need to integrate AI ethics into its developing strategies for Digital Health and Cultural Heritage. The scientific and educational landscape reveals a promising growth in AI publications, emphasising the importance of ethics. Excitingly, new AI and Data Science Master's programs are starting to incorporate ethics into their curricula, and there is a flourishing collaboration with UNESCO to enhance AI education. However, Cambodia still faces several challenges: R&D spending remains on the lower side, many schools lack adequate digital and AI infrastructure, and there is an urgent need to refresh curricula to better equip students with digital skills. Additionally, the demand for advanced AI talent is critical. Cambodia faces a challenge in having limited data to assess AI's economic aspects thoroughly. However, the assessment identified some promising examples, such as pilot AI projects in the public sector, like Sarika and Khmer Braille, as well as studies on the economic potential of AI to increase GDP by 2030. While AI adoption is still in its early stages, there is a risk of job displacement, so data on AI's impact on the labour market and investments is needed. The technical and infrastructure dimension highlights potential improvements in mobile connectivity and near universal access to electricity. Cambodia has established statistical standards and is developing draft policies for Cloud First and Data Governance. Nonetheless, there is a pressing need to enhance internet access and speed, as modern data centre capacity is currently limited. Additionally, Cambodia is not represented in AI standardisation bodies, and the statistical infrastructure requires further strengthening.

title: Government Communication Service Assist
description: In 2023, the Government Communication Service (GCS) identified "lack of time" as a key barrier to innovation for its 6,500-strong communications profession, with members spending large portions of their working day on routine tasks such as producing first drafts of content. Assist is a secure, generative AI tool built by government communicators, for government communicators. It supports users to brainstorm ideas, produce first drafts, and review work through communications-specific pre-built prompts spanning all seven GCS disciplines. Outputs are grounded in GCS policies, frameworks, and best practice guidance. Responsible use and human oversight are central to its design: Assist produces suggested drafts that communicators develop further, applying their own critical thinking and judgement. Assist saves the average user around three hours per week, contributing to projected annual efficiency savings of £5.5 million. More than 90% of the 6,500-strong GCS profession are now using Assist, across 210 government organisations. Over 30% of users log in each week, with both users and usage growing weekly, 98% of surveyed users find it useful in their role, and 88% report applying its outputs in their work. Finally, over 70% of all potential users have completed the bespoke 'AI for Communicators' training course, which is mandatory to gain access to the tool. After completing the course, users report a 23% improvement in confidence using AI at work. Lessons Learned Build for your users, not just for technology: Assist was designed around the real daily tasks of government communicators, with discipline-specific prompts shaped by user research. Relevance drives adoption. Make responsible use structural, not optional: mandatory training, ethical frameworks, and human oversight were built into the tool from the outset, not added afterwards. Scale with a people-centred approach: GCS published "The People Factor" guide and the Mitigating Hidden AI Risks Toolkit, drawing on its own rollout experience to help other organisations scale AI tools safely. Overall, government communicators spend less time on routine drafting and more time on strategic, creative, and high-impact work. By embedding GCS standards directly into its outputs, Assist also improves the consistency and quality of government communications at scale, whilst building AI capability and confidence across the profession.

title: PALOMA: Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection of Unwanted Loneliness in Older Adults (Subnational: Madrid)
description: Unwanted loneliness affects older adults over 75 who live alone in Madrid and can lead to isolation, declining health, and loss of autonomy. Early detection is difficult, as many do not seek help and traditional channels—postal mail or in person visits—are not sufficient to identify those who may be at risk. To address this challenge, the Madrid City Council launched a pilot initiative using artificial intelligence to proactively contact this population group and better understand their situation through brief telephone conversations. PALOMA uses natural language processing technology capable of maintaining conversations with a natural sounding synthetic voice and administering a short questionnaire designed by social services professionals. The AI analyzes responses to detect signs of loneliness, classify risk levels, and offer follow up calls or information about municipal services. Cases flagged as relevant are always reviewed by professional staff, ensuring safe, ethical, and tailored intervention. This combination of AI and human oversight expands municipal capacity without replacing the professional role, aligning with principles of trustworthy and human centred AI. The project has three main goals: improving early detection of unwanted loneliness, enabling more personalized interventions, and increasing access to activities and support services. It also modernizes the relationship between citizens and the administration, showing how AI can support social services in an efficient, accessible, and respectful way. Automated calls make it possible to reach thousands of people quickly and at a cost far lower than traditional alternatives such as call centers, significantly increasing the reach and effectiveness of social policies. PALOMA carried out 5,163 calls, completed 2,071 conversations, and enabled 646 people to request municipal follow up. Of these, 602 were referred to social programs and 236 accepted a home visit; 84% showed signs of loneliness. The system identified 44 clear high risk cases and reached individuals who would not have contacted the city through other means. AI expanded reach, accelerated detection, and optimized resources. Results were measured through call analysis, conversion rates, referrals, and professional follow up. A key strength of PALOMA is its capacity to scale. Traditional outreach programmes are limited by staff time, whereas AI enabled calling can reach thousands of people quickly and at low cost. The pilot contacted 5,000 people in only two weeks, leading to 646 individuals requesting follow up and enabling targeted support for those experiencing loneliness. These results demonstrate the potential for broader deployment and for replication in other municipalities facing similar demographic challenges.

title: Messina Urban Digital Twin (GDU) – AI-enabled Urban Intelligence Platform (Subnational: Municipality of Messina)
description: The Messina Urban Digital Twin (GDU) was developed to address the fragmentation of urban data across multiple systems and the lack of integrated tools for evidence-based decision-making in local government. Cities generate large volumes of data through IoT sensors, administrative processes and external systems, but these data are often siloed and underutilised. The initiative integrates heterogeneous data sources, including IoT infrastructure, environmental monitoring, mobility systems and administrative datasets, into a unified digital representation of the urban environment. AI techniques are used to analyse data patterns, support predictive insights and enable simulation of complex urban scenarios, such as traffic flows, environmental impacts and resource allocation. The system enables public officials to explore “what-if” scenarios and supports strategic planning, operational management and policy evaluation. It is designed as a modular and scalable architecture, allowing progressive integration of new data sources and services. The initiative is part of the broader investment framework of the PN METRO Plus 2021–2027 programme, ensuring alignment with national and European urban innovation priorities and supporting its long-term sustainability and scalability. The GDU is also aligned with national and European digital strategies and integrates with the municipality’s Open Data ecosystem, promoting transparency and enabling future reuse by developers, researchers and other public administrations.

title: Agent MIA (Argentine State's Artificial Intelligence Assistant)
description: The initiative seeks to address inefficiencies in public services by modernizing them to achieve a more transparent, efficient, and citizen-centered government. Specifically, it addresses the following points: It aims to reduce waiting times and simplify digital processes for citizens. It solves the problem of misinformation by drawing on a closed knowledge base that uses only official data, thus ensuring accuracy and avoiding bias. Unlike traditional chatbots that only respond, MIA can act: query data, generate reports, and perform administrative tasks under human supervision. MIA's main objectives focus on improving the interaction between the government and society: Supporting SMEs and assisting the 26 million users of the Mi Argentina app with their digital transactions. Offer a more agile, efficient, simple, and secure conversational experience. Save time for both users and government support teams. MIA is expected to evolve from a consultation assistant to a comprehensive government management tool: • We are working to expand the initiative and achieve integration into critical environments such as the Electronic Document Management System (GDE), Online Procedures (TAD), and the official portal Argentina.gob.ar. MIA has been designed to scale to a wide range of topics and services. In the next 12 to 18 months, the goal is for these AI agents to significantly simplify people's lives and make public administration more efficient at all levels. Currently, it already registers more than 1.5 million conversations per month. Impacts are measured using internal performance metrics for continuous improvement and the exploratory application of UNESCO's RAM Methodology. In the future, MIA will evolve from conversational to agentic, executing administrative tasks and generating reports in systems such as GDE and TAD. Over the next 12-18 months, it is expected to be the cornerstone for positioning Argentina as a regional AI hub, enabling a government that not only responds but also acts to simplify citizens' lives and optimize public administration.

title: Guideline for Japanese Government’s Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
description: As AI-related technologies advance rapidly, and their utilization expands across the public and private sectors, the Japanese Government recognized the necessity to establish rules and frameworks to promote the proper procurement and utilization of generative AI within its administrative operations, while ensuring appropriate risk management. Accordingly, the “Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration” was approved by the Council for the Promotion of a Digital Society Executive Board on 27 May 2025. The Guideline was developed by referring to domestic and international initiatives, including the AI Guidelines for Business, the outcomes of the Hiroshima AI Process, and discussions in frameworks such as the OECD and the G7. The Guideline applies to the national government staff and covers text-generating AI systems, including those incorporating large language models (LLMs), used as components of government information systems, excluding systems handling classified or national security–related information. Under the Guideline, each ministry or agency should appoint a Chief AI Officer (CAIO) responsible for promoting utilization while ensuring AI governance, risk management, and, enhance AI literacy among government staff. Based on the “Model User Rule for Generative AI” the CAIO develops rules for users within each ministry or agency. The Guideline also establishes a government-wide Advanced AI Utilization Advisory Board to provide advice on projects likely to be classified as high-risk, share best practices, and consider revisions of the Guideline. It introduces the “High-Risk AI Project Finder” assessing risks based on factors such as users, operations, confidential information or personal data, and staff judgment on outputs. Given rapid technological advancement, the Guideline is to be reviewed and revised in a timely manner, with planned revisions from fiscal year 2026 onward, including scope expansion, enhancements to procurement check sheets, updates reflecting institutional and regulatory developments, and revisions to the High-Risk AI Project Finder.

title: MencIA: Sovereign AI Strategy for Territorial Cohesion (Subnational: Lugo)
description: MencIA addresses the dilemma of “Digital Feudalism”, in which public administrations hand control of their data to proprietary “black box” technologies. The strategy proposes a different path, which it calls realistic technological sovereignty: open-source and open-weight AI models running on the Provincial Council’s own infrastructure. Small towns would then be able to use secure, publicly controlled AI, with privacy by design and energy efficiency, without depending on large technology vendors. The model rests on three rules: Data control and privacy: sensitive information never leaves the Council’s servers. Real adaptability: tools are designed around local needs, not the other way round. Economic sustainability: recurring licence costs give way to investment in assets and talent that stay under public control. Sovereignty here is realistic, not dogmatic. Commercial models may be used as a testing ground for non-critical tasks, provided no sensitive data is ever involved. The guiding principle is “AI as assistant”. AI augments the work of public employees and does not replace them. Human oversight cannot be waived for any administrative act with legal consequences, and the final decision and the responsibility always rest with a person. The technical stack combines Ollama and vLLM for inference, Docker for containerisation, LangChain for orchestration, Open WebUI for general chat and Streamlit, React and others for purpose-built interfaces. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) works only on the Council’s own documents. A key pillar is “Green by Design” efficiency, delivered through the “3 clicks, one task” paradigm. Each application solves a single, well-defined task and returns a short, structured output, so in practice it behaves like a small language model. This lowers the inference load and avoids the cumulative consumption of conversational chatbots. The strategy is organised around four pillars: Governance and compliance, internal transformation, service to municipalities, and territorial ecosystem It creates three new bodies: AI Governance Committee: it includes the Data Protection Officer, the legal and audit services, and one representative of each political group in the Plenary. Provincial AI Office: the Committee’s executive body. Provincial Register of AI Systems: publicly accessible from the Transparency Portal. Each entry records the system’s risk classification under the EU AI Act.

title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
description: The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 is the primary legislative vehicle through which the UK government has sought to address concerns about market concentration in AI and digital platform markets. The DMCC Act creates the Digital Markets regime, administered by the CMA's Digital Markets Unit (DMU), which enables the CMA to designate specific large technology companies as having Strategic Market Status in a designated activity. SMS designation triggers a suite of obligations including conduct requirements (preventing self-preferencing, data access barriers and interoperability restrictions), pro-competitive interventions (structural or behavioural remedies), and enhanced merger scrutiny. The CMA has identified foundation model markets — including AI model APIs, AI-integrated search, and cloud infrastructure underpinning AI services — as priority areas for the Digital Markets regime. The CMA published its AI Foundation Models review in 2024, identifying concentration risks among a small number of US hyperscalers and AI labs. The DMCC Act also significantly strengthens consumer protection enforcement and streamlines merger review processes in a manner directly applicable to the wave of AI-related acquisitions and investments. SMS designation processes for the first cohort of technology companies began in 2025. Internationally, the DMCC approach is frequently compared with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA).

title: UK National Data Library (NDL)
description: The National Data Library was announced as part of the UK Government's AI Opportunities Action Plan in January 2025, based on recommendations from entrepreneur and AI advisor Matt Clifford. Its creation is overseen by DSIT, with close involvement from the Government Digital Service (GDS). The NDL completed an extensive discovery phase in 2025, including public attitudes research, consultation with over 200 organisations and expert bodies (including the Open Data Institute, Wellcome Trust, Public Digital, The Tony Blair Institute and The Startup Coalition), and five 'kickstarter' projects designed to test approaches to systemic data reform. An architecture design contract of £650,000 was awarded to esynergy in November 2025 to produce a federated architecture blueprint for the NDL. The NDL's design principles prioritise: (1) public benefit and ethical data use; (2) data security and privacy safeguards; (3) a federated model that does not centralise data but provides shared infrastructure for access; (4) AI-readiness, with guidelines for making government datasets AI-ready published by GDS; and (5) public trust through ongoing citizen engagement. Economic analyses suggest a fully developed AI-ready data ecosystem underpinned by the NDL could generate £40 billion annually in productivity gains by 2030.

title: GovAI Chat
description: GovAI Chat is a secure, government-controlled generative AI tool developed specifically for the Australian Public Service (APS). It is different from commercial tools (for example, ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot) because it is designed to: Operate within secure onshore infrastructure with vendors who are compliant with the Australian Government Hosting Certification Framework which ensures data remains securely within Australia and under government control. Meet the highest standards of security and compliance, including meeting the Australia’s Protective Security Policy Framework, enabling safe handling of sensitive and PROTECTED-level information. Offer equitable access to all APS staff, with usage costs covered during the pilot phase. Allow access to a range of AI models providing choice and flexibility and limiting the risk of vendor lock-in. Enable the APS to build digital capability, drive innovation, and maintain public trust in the responsible use of AI. GovAI Chat will increase the capability of the APS to deliver more for the Australian public, while maintaining standards and complying with legal frameworks for cyber security and data sovereignty. The result will be a safer and smarter way to work that supports operational integrity and delivers value through time saved and reduced rework. GovAI Chat will continue to evolve throughout Alpha and Beta trial stages based on user feedback, security requirements and technical capability. The delivery team will regularly incorporate feedback, distil insights, prioritise for future implementation and adjust the product roadmap as required. The GovAI trial will consider a range of potential enhancements and continue to seek feedback on these, considering impacts to key themes such as scale, scope, schedule, budget, usability and trust. We will embed a continuous observability and evaluation process to review all relevant metrics. Initial trials of GovAI Chat with APS staff are expected to begin in April 2026.

title: OMB AI Acquisition Guidance (M-25-22)
description: Issued on 3 April 2025 by the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), M-25-22 ('Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government') replaces the Biden-era M-24-18 and implements Executive Order 14179 ('Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence', January 2025). It applies to AI systems and services acquired by covered federal agencies under contracts awarded pursuant to solicitations issued from 30 September 2025 onwards (excluding National Security Systems and AI used incidentally). Three core policy themes: (1) fostering a competitive American AI marketplace — agencies must prioritise US-developed AI solutions; (2) safeguarding taxpayer dollars by tracking AI performance and managing risk — contracts must include performance monitoring, regular risk assessments, and minimum risk management practices for high-impact AI; (3) promoting effective AI acquisition through cross-functional engagement — agencies must involve legal, privacy, IT, and programme officials in acquisition. Key contract requirements include: data-use restrictions preventing vendors from training public AI models on non-public government data; IP and data ownership protections; vendor lock-in protections; privacy safeguards; and mandatory AI disclosure provisions. GSA was directed to release AI procurement guides by August 2025 and establish a best-practices repository by January 2026. Complements OMB M-25-21 on federal AI use governance.

title: Fraud Risk Assessment Accelerator
description: FRAs are a critical safeguard in public spending, yet their production is slow, specialist-intensive, and inconsistent across departments. This bottleneck means fraud controls are often underdeveloped at the point of implementation. The UK's experience during the COVID-19 pandemic illustrated this risk at scale: emergency schemes were exploited extensively before adequate fraud assessment was in place. In the year to April 2025, UK anti-fraud teams recovered a record £480 million in fraudulent payments, over a third of which related to pandemic-era schemes. This recovery underscored the need for a more proactive, prevention-led approach. Developed by the PSFA Data Science team and powered by GPT-4.1, the Accelerator enables qualified fraud assessors to upload draft policy and scheme documentation and automatically generate a structured FRA covering potential fraud actors, actions, and outcomes. Critically, the tool analyses policy documents, not individual citizen data, positioning it as a policy design tool rather than a surveillance or targeting mechanism. By automating the research and initial drafting stages, it redirects specialist time towards review and validation. Human oversight is embedded throughout: all outputs are reviewed and enriched by qualified Fraud Subject Matter Experts before use, with automated PII detection and redaction built in. Early testing indicates the tool could reduce fraud risk identification time by up to 80%, and it has already led to £480 million recovered in fraudulent payments in the year to April 2025, the highest single-year recovery by UK anti-fraud teams. Following Cabinet Office Technical Design Authority assurance in October 2025, the tool is entering public beta rollout across UK government, with international licensing underway for Five Eyes partner nations. Lessons Learned Prevention over recovery: integrating fraud controls at the policy design stage is significantly more cost-effective than pursuing recovery after exploitation has occurred. Human oversight is non-negotiable: qualified assessors validate and enrich every FRA before use, ensuring professional accountability throughout. Automate the routine, preserve the judgement: directing automation at research and drafting, rather than evaluative stages, maximises efficiency without compromising quality. Govern from the start: involving legal, ethics, and data privacy specialists from discovery through to rollout builds the trust necessary for responsible scaling. Overall, the Accelerator represents a deliberate shift from reactive recovery to proactive prevention, embedding fraud assessment earlier in the policy design process.

title: AMALIA – Automatic Multimodal Language Assistant with Artificial Intelligence
description: AMALIA is the first Large-Scale Language Model (LLM) designed specifically for European Portuguese language, using AI to process and generate natural language, with the ability to understand the linguistic diversity, cultural context, and historical references unique to Portugal. The main objective of AMALIA is to promote digital sovereignty, ensuring that sensitive national data can be processed securely and independently. It also aims to strengthen the national AI ecosystem by supporting innovation in key sectors such as education, culture, speech, media, science and public administration. AMALIA will be a multimodal model, capable of interpreting not only text but also speech, images and video, and its development implies an investment of €5,5 million, led by national research institutions and coordinated by the State Technological Reform Agency (ARTE). AMALIA shows strong performance in European Portuguese, outperforming other open models in lexicology and semantics. The base version is complete, and developed by over 60 researchers, reinforcing national digital sovereignty. Results are measured through technical benchmarking reports and evaluations in public services. Future impacts include broader use in education, public administration, and science, with the final version expected in mid-2026. Key risks associated with AMALIA include establishing secure and compliant protocols for sharing non-public data, ensuring adequate funding and timely development of user interfaces for the defined use cases, and preventing data obsolescence. The critical conditions for the success of an initiative such as AMALIA include the effective productization of its use cases, ensuring that they move beyond prototypes into scalable, user-ready solutions, and the establishment of a robust inference infrastructure capable of supporting its widespread deployment across Public Administration. All versions of the model, along with the training data, will be released as open source, making them freely available to researchers, public institutions, companies, and citizens. This initiative is the first major project under Portugal’s National Artificial Intelligence Agenda, reinforcing Portugal’s commitment to ethical, inclusive, and sovereign development. The current version is already available through the IAedu platform of the Foundation for Science and Technology (FCT), while the final version of AMALIA is expected to be launched in mid-2026.

title: AI Learning Pathway (AILP)
description: The AI Learning Pathway was developed in response to a diagnostic conducted through the Public Innovation Capabilities Radar, which identified significant gaps in digital competencies across the Public Administration. The assessment revealed heterogeneous levels of digital literacy, challenges in data use and governance, and the persistence of manual processes with strong potential for improvement. At the same time, growing interest in Artificial Intelligence (AI) among public employees presented a strategic opportunity to strengthen institutional capacities and accelerate the State’s digital transformation through an ethical, evidence-based approach. The initiative was designed as a strategic capacity-building intervention to reduce internal training gaps and provide accessible, profile-adapted learning opportunities. Its objectives are to equip public employees with both conceptual foundations and practical tools in AI, public data management, information security, and public-sector use cases; promote the ethical, strategic, and responsible adoption of emerging technologies; and foster cross-departmental collaboration while consolidating a culture oriented toward innovation and data-driven decision-making. The program follows a blended format, combining asynchronous modules with in-person practical sessions, structured around four thematic pillars: Digital State and AI; Public Data and Decision-Making; Information Security; and AI Use Cases and Adoption. After initial editions reaching over 200 employees, the Pathway scaled to train more than 600 public officials, with the participation of specialists from both public and private sectors. Participant evaluations reported high satisfaction and strong relevance to day-to-day responsibilities, reinforcing the initiative’s institutional value. Looking ahead, the initiative is evolving toward a second level focused on soft skills and organizational capabilities for AI integration. This phase emphasizes the design of adoption models for automation and augmentation, drawing on academic research on AI agents and human–AI collaboration. By institutionalizing training as a continuous, multi-level pathway, the program seeks to scale across government, embed AI competencies into long-term workforce development strategies, and ensure sustainable, responsible integration of AI into public administration.

title: AI Experience Lab
description: The AI Experience Lab was created to address a growing gap in the public sector between the potential of artificial intelligence and the actual capacity of public organisations to use it safely, effectively and responsibly. Many public bodies face limited technical skills, fragmented data and uncertainty about risks, which makes it difficult to move from interest in AI to informed decision-making. The Lab responds to this challenge by offering a protected environment where public organisations can explore AI through real use cases without immediate pressure to procure or deploy solutions. The main objective of the AI Experience Lab is to build lasting capacity in public administration. It supports organisations through a structured journey that combines ideation, certified training and practical application, enabling participants to better understand AI, its limitations and its value for public services. A key goal is to ensure that public entities are able to make informed choices about if, when and how AI should be used, while reinforcing trust, responsibility and alignment with public values. To date, the Lab has supported the development of 10 AI projects across different public sector domains, including employment services, financial inspection, public management, regional administration and public sector training. These use cases address concrete challenges such as improving service delivery, supporting decision-making, reducing administrative burden, strengthening risk analysis and improving planning. Each project is developed in collaboration with leading national universities in technology, business and management, and major technology consulting firms, ensuring both scientific rigor and practical relevance. Looking ahead, the AI Experience Lab is expected to evolve as a permanent capacity-building framework within the National Institute of Administration. Its results — certified skills, tested solutions and practical knowledge — create a foundation for scaling successful approaches across the public sector. Over time, the Lab aims to strengthen a community of practice (CoP), support the institutionalisation of AI capabilities in public organisations and contribute to a more capable, autonomous and future-ready public administration.

title: UK Health Data Research Service (HDRS)
description: The HDRS was announced following the Sudlow Review ('Uniting the UK's Health Data: A Huge Opportunity for Society'), which identified the fragmented, slow and complex landscape for health data access as a critical barrier to research and innovation. At its core, the HDRS is built on a national network of Secure Data Environments (SDEs), expanding the existing NHS Research SDE Network. The HDRS will provide a 'single front door' through which researchers make standardised access requests, enabling them to access linked primary care, hospital, prescribing, mortality, genomic and diagnostic imaging data at national scale, while keeping data in secure environments and maintaining privacy through encryption, anonymisation and synthetic data techniques. The service has six stated goals: (1) providing secure access to linked national-scale health data; (2) leveraging major UK cohort studies and biobanks; (3) enabling access to diagnostic images, genomics and laboratory data for precision medicine; (4) supporting innovative data linkage; (5) streamlining governance; and (6) building public trust.

title: UK Sovereign AI Unit
description: The Sovereign AI Unit was established in DSIT in 2025 as a core pillar of the UK AI Opportunities Action Plan. Chaired by venture capitalist James Wise (Balderton Capital), the Unit operates as a novel government fund structure designed to be the first choice for founders building essential parts of the UK's AI infrastructure. The Unit's mandate covers the full AI value chain: investing in compute infrastructure, supporting data assets, backing frontier model development, and enabling AI application companies. Key activities include launching open calls to researchers and companies through the AI Research Resource (AIRR), supporting 'Autonomous Labs' combining robotics and AI, and forging Memoranda of Understanding with leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI to advance responsible AI development aligned with UK values. The Unit works alongside the British Business Bank and UKRI, and collaborates with the UK Compute Roadmap to build a world-class compute ecosystem. It complements AI Growth Zones and the National Data Library as part of a broader national AI infrastructure strategy.

title: UK AI Skills Hub
description: The UK AI Skills Hub is a flagship component of the government's TechFirst initiative, launched in June 2025 and significantly expanded on 28 January 2026 (coinciding with the anniversary of the AI Opportunities Action Plan). The programme offers free AI training to all UK adults, delivered online through a government-backed platform developed in partnership with 23 major technology companies. Its stated ambition is to upskill 10 million workers by 2030, with 2 million of those targeted from the SME workforce. Courses range from foundational AI literacy modules (some under 20 minutes) suitable for non-technical staff, to professional-level qualifications for those in AI-adjacent roles. Completions are recognised through a government-backed AI Foundations digital badge, providing portable evidence of skills for employees and assurance for employers. The January 2026 expansion also introduced a £27 million TechLocal scheme to connect people with tech jobs in their local area, and a £7.8 million TechLocal AI Professional Degree and Traineeship Accelerator, which funds universities and colleges to develop new AI-focused higher education courses created with industry input.

title: APS AI Plan - Artificial Intelligence (AI) Plan for the Australian Public Service (APS)
description: The Australian Government is focused on capturing the opportunity of AI and, to ensure the benefits of this technology are shared equitably, creating a higher standard of living for all Australians. The APS AI Plan positions the government to improve service delivery, policy outcomes, efficiency and productivity by substantially increasing the safe and responsible use of AI in government. The APS AI Plan is built around three core pillars that work together to enable the safe, effective and scalable use of artificial intelligence across the Australian Public Service. Trust Pillar. Focuses on ensuring AI is used safely, ethically and transparently. It builds on existing security and privacy safeguard governing the use of ICT and data and strengthens governance and improves transparency to maintain public trust, manage risk, and ensure AI use aligns with APS values and community expectations. People Pillar. Focuses on building capability and supporting the public service workforce by ensuring ensures public servants are equipped with the right skills to use AI responsibly and effectively. This includes access to training, consultation and engagement, and other support to use AI confidently and responsibly, recognising the impact of AI on roles, skills and ways of working. Tools Pillar. Focuses on empowering the public service workforce through access to secure, fit for purpose AI technologies. It supports the rollout of shared platforms and tools that enable efficient adoption of AI, collaboration across government, and reuse of solutions where possible. APS AI Plan Objectives: Improving AI literacy. As AI becomes increasingly widespread and available, everyone in government needs basic AI literacy and training. Leading by example. The government has an important role to play in modelling responsible and ethical AI adoption. Expanding generative AI use. Current levels of AI adoption are inconsistent. Improving our AI maturity means broadening the safe, responsible use of generative AI to all agencies. Coordinating the government’s approach. AI transformation needs to be coordinated across the pillars of trust, people and tools. Driving systemic adoption. Advancing AI maturity requires a coordinated program of projects and investments Implementation of the APS AI Plan.

title: Automated Multi-agent Analysis of Occupational Licensing
description: Occupational licensing serves legitimate purposes, but requirements that exceed what public interest justifies prevent people from entering occupations and reduce labor market competition. Czechia regulates more than 300 professions, and for several professions regulatory restrictiveness has been found to exceed the EU average, yet no systematic assessment has been made of whether the requirements are still justified across the board. The Government Analytical Office developed an automated multi-agent system to conduct this assessment at scale. For each profession, specialized AI agents independently search online legal sources, official government databases, and EU-level registers to research six dimensions: the legal basis under Czech law, EU-level constraints, whether requirements are proportionate to documented risks, how Czech requirements compare to those in other member states, labor market effects, and how regulation is enforced in practice. The system synthesizes these findings into a structured assessment with a ranked simplification recommendation. This analysis would take months to complete manually; the automated system might reduce it to weeks, making comprehensive reform easier. Where the system identifies a simplification candidate, findings will be shared with the Ministry of Industry and Trade and relevant social partners to assess whether sufficient justification exists. Where it does not, a formal proposal will be submitted to the government. Poland's experience with simplifying access to professions between 2005 and 2015 is instructive: empirical literature suggests such reforms are associated with increased labor market entry and employment growth in affected occupations, though effects vary by profession. Workers currently blocked from entering regulated professions, as well as businesses and the broader economy, stand to benefit from a successful reform. The methodology relies on publicly available legal sources and EU-wide databases accessible to any member state, making it directly replicable by other governments. The system is currently being scaled to cover all regulated professions in Czechia, and the same approach can be extended to other regulatory domains, such as identifying gold-plating across Czech legislation more broadly. The system has been piloted on 15 professions, with 5 outputs validated in detail. In several cases, analysis found no EU requirement to regulate the profession and no equivalent licensing requirement in comparable member states such as Poland and the Netherlands, indicating concrete simplification potential. Output quality is assessed through a structured evaluation pipeline in which an LLM judge scores agent responses against predefined criteria — a methodology designed to scale validation across all professions. The full analysis is underway, and validated findings will be submitted to relevant ministries to inform concrete proposals to the government.

Where it does not, a formal proposal will be submitted to the government. Workers currently blocked from entering regulated professions, as well as businesses and the broader economy, stand to benefit from a successful reform. The methodology relies on publicly available legal sources and EU-wide databases accessible to any member state, making it directly replicable by other governments. The system is currently being scaled to cover all regulated professions in Czechia, and the same approach can be extended to other regulatory domains, such as identifying gold-plating across Czech legislation more broadly. The system has been piloted on 15 professions, with 5 outputs validated in detail. In several cases, analysis found no EU requirement to regulate the profession and no equivalent licensing requirement in comparable member states such as Poland and the Netherlands, indicating concrete simplification potential. title: OTT2 : Dynamic Data-Driven Personalisation of Employment Services and Counsellor Decision Support
description: Estonia’s public employment service faces the same challenge seen worldwide: allocating limited support to jobseekers with very different needs. Before 2020, counsellors relied on rules of thumb, personal experience and the manual profiling of roughly 45 indicators ranging from demographic characteristics and work history to health status and local labour‑market conditions. In practice, this volume of information was difficult to process consistently, making it hard to reliably identify people at risk of long‑term unemployment and in need of more intensive support. This changed with the introduction of OTT1 in 2020, Estonia’s first data‑driven decision‑support tool for counsellors. Using a machine‑learning model, it assessed each jobseeker’s employment prospects at the point of registration. Over several years of operational use, the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund (EUIF) strengthened the model, built organisational confidence and gathered the evidence needed to expand its approach. OTT2 represents this next step. Whereas OTT1 produced a single assessment at registration, OTT2 generates dynamic, regularly updated assessments that reflect changes in a jobseeker’s situation—such as completing training or missing an assigned activity—so counsellors can make decisions using the most current information. The model is retrained periodically on new data but does not change autonomously, ensuring stability, transparency and auditability in a high‑stakes service. OTT2 also explains the main factors shaping each prediction and how these evolve over time, helping counsellors interpret results and offer more personalised support. OTT2 builds on the strong performance of its predecessor, which achieved over 95% prediction accuracy. By updating assessments as circumstances change, accuracy is expected to rise above 98%; this is being tested in a 2026 pilot. The pilot also introduces a targeted service change: the approximately 20% of newly registered jobseekers identified as lowest‑risk will no longer receive mandatory counselling, allowing counsellors to focus more time on individuals at higher risk of long‑term unemployment. Even small reductions in unemployment duration have significant fiscal impact—one day less is estimated to save around 3.8% of annual expenditure.

title: AI Opportunities Action Plan
description: Published in January 2025, the AI Opportunities Action Plan represents the most comprehensive articulation of UK AI ambitions since the 2021 National AI Strategy and was received with a formal Government Response that committed to acting on all 50 of Clifford's recommendations. The Plan is structured around three strategic pillars. First, foundations for AI: securing the physical and data infrastructure necessary for AI development, including a UK Compute Roadmap targeting GBP 1.5 billion in public compute investment, the National Data Library, the Sovereign AI Unit, and AI Growth Zones. Second, unleashing AI across the economy: accelerating AI adoption in key sectors including healthcare, education, energy, finance and public services, with specific recommendations for NHS AI deployment, an AI for Science Strategy, and the expansion of BridgeAI's regional adoption hubs. Third, securing the UK's future in AI: ensuring the UK benefits economically and secures domestic capability in frontier AI development, including through investment in UKRI's AI research programme and partnerships with leading AI laboratories. The Plan also includes a specific chapter on international AI leadership and positions the UK as a bridging actor between the US and EU approaches to AI governance.

title: EU General-Purpose AI (GPAI) Code of Practice
description: The GPAI Code of Practice is one of the most consequential instruments under the EU AI Act for frontier AI model developers, as it directly operationalises the obligations in Chapter V of the Act for providers of general-purpose AI models. The Code was developed through an unprecedented multi-stakeholder drafting process coordinated by the EU AI Office, running from November 2024. It involved over 1,000 stakeholders including AI developers (OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, Anthropic, Mistral, Aleph Alpha and others), academic researchers, civil society organisations, standards bodies, and national competent authorities. Draft versions were published iteratively with a final adopted version targeted for May 2025. The Code is structured across four substantive chapters: transparency and copyright obligations (requiring model documentation, training data disclosure, compliance with EU copyright law, and reservation of rights mechanisms); safety and security for non-systemic-risk models; additional systemic risk obligations (covering adversarial testing, red-teaming, cybersecurity measures, serious incident reporting, and model evaluations against safety benchmarks); and governance and accountability. The Code includes specific "measures" and "key performance indicators" for each obligation, enabling both self-assessment by providers and external verification by the AI Office. Compliance with the Code creates a presumption of conformity under the AI Act, substantially reducing legal uncertainty for GPAI providers. Non-compliance with GPAI obligations under the AI Act (where the Code applies) can result in fines of up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global annual turnover.

title: EU AI Continent Action Plan
description: The AI Continent Action Plan was announced by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 11 February 2025 at the Paris AI Action Summit alongside the InvestAI initiative. It operates around five pillars. Pillar one (computing and data): mobilise EUR 200 billion in AI investment through InvestAI, build five AI gigafactories, expand the 19 AI Factories network through EuroHPC, and develop the European common data spaces. Pillar two (talent and skills): retain AI researchers and engineers in Europe, attract global talent, and build a pipeline of AI-skilled workers at all levels through actions under the Pact for Skills and the Digital Education Action Plan. Pillar three (regulatory environment): ensure the AI Act is implemented in a way that is clear, predictable and minimises unnecessary compliance burdens for innovators, including SMEs; streamline Member State transposition; and develop harmonised standards rapidly. Pillar four (AI adoption): operationalise the Apply AI Strategy across 11 priority sectors; deploy the European Digital Innovation Hubs network for SME support; and establish the Apply AI Alliance to coordinate public-private uptake. Pillar five (sovereignty and outreach): build European leadership in trustworthy AI; strengthen bilateral AI partnerships with the US, UK, Japan, Canada and others; and promote the EU's regulatory model in multilateral forums.

title: EU Scaleup Europe Fund
description: The Scaleup Europe Fund responds to Europe's well-documented late-stage funding gap, in which promising companies have struggled to access the growth capital needed to compete with US and Asian peers. The fund operates as a market-based, privately managed and privately co-financed growth vehicle, focusing on late-stage and growth capital investments in major European-led investment rounds across strategic deep tech sectors. The Commission is a founding investor alongside a group of leading European institutional investors announced on 28 October 2025, including Novo Holdings, EIFO (Denmark), CriteriaCaixa, Santander/Mouro Capital, Fondazione Compagnia San Paolo/Intesa Sanpaolo/Fondazione Cariplo, APG Asset Management (on behalf of Dutch pension fund ABP), Wallenberg Investments, and BGK (Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego). An independent fund manager is being selected through a public call for expressions of interest (closed February 2026); appointment is expected in April 2026. A second fundraising round will follow to diversify the investor base.
