title: Public Service Commission (PSC) AI Agent for Travel
description: The AI Agent for Travel was launched to address a persistent operational challenge across the public service: navigating federal travel and expense policies is complex, time-consuming, and heavily reliant on manual email support. Employees often wait days for answers to routine questions, leading to delayed approvals, last-minute bookings, inconsistent guidance, and avoidable costs. At the same time, departments face increasing pressure to modernise internal services, improve employee experience, and strengthen financial stewardship. This initiative applies artificial intelligence in a practical and responsible way to reduce administrative burden while improving compliance and service quality. The objective of the AI Agent is to provide employees, managers, and finance teams with clear, consistent, and real-time guidance on government travel rules and expense claims. Developed entirely in-house using existing Microsoft 365 tools within a secure Government of Canada environment, the solution relies exclusively on validated policy documents and approved procedures. It guides users step by step, reducing reliance on email inquiries and manual searches. Since implementation, travel-related email volume has decreased by approximately 90%, response times have improved from several days to seconds, and the organisation is realising an estimated $120,000 in annual savings. Additional indirect savings are achieved through earlier travel planning and reduced last-minute booking costs. Beyond operational efficiencies, the initiative strengthens financial oversight and supports broader transformation objectives. Financial officers are now able to focus on higher-value analysis and risk management rather than responding to repetitive policy questions. The solution operates with clear governance, documentation, and human oversight to ensure responsible and ethical AI use, with all data remaining within secure government systems. By developing the capability internally, the organisation has strengthened its digital expertise while avoiding external consulting costs. The initiative has evolved from a targeted travel support solution into a scalable model for responsible AI adoption. Interest from over 40 federal departments and agencies demonstrates its transferability across government, and additional corporate service areas, including human resources and procurement, are beginning to adopt similar agents using the same framework. As governance, training, and knowledge management processes continue to mature, the AI Agent provides a sustainable and replicable pathway for modernising internal government services at scale. The initiative has also received international recognition, including coverage by Global Government Finance in the article “Canada government agency AI tool tackles ‘bottleneck’ of travel and expense inquiries,” extending its influence beyond the Canadian public service.

title: Use of artificial intelligence for the characterisation of the environmental regulatory burden of projects
description: This initiative addresses the opacity and complexity of Chile's environmental regulatory system. Traditionally, the manual analysis of Environmental Qualification Resolutions (RCAs) has been prohibitively slow and costly due to the sheer length and lack of standardisation within these technical-legal documents. To tackle this, the initiative analysed a sample of 1,336 RCAs, representing all mining and energy projects authorised over the last decade. This analysis identified 220,000 individual enforceable obligations, providing a clear quantification and characterisation of the environmental burden imposed by Chilean regulations on major investment projects. This application of GenAI transforms unstructured documents into auditable, comparable databases with unprecedented efficiency. It enables large-scale analyses that would have previously required an extensive team of experts working for several months. Core objectives Generate systematic evidence: Precisely dimension and characterise the regulatory burden on strategic sectors, mining and energy, by analysing over 220,000 obligations. Explore emerging technologies: Evaluate the capabilities and limitations of GenAI in converting “opaque” regulatory information into actionable insights. Promote transparency and efficiency: Advance towards a more streamlined regulatory system rooted in objective data and aligned with international standards. Streamline enforcement: Identify and classify enforceable obligations to improve traceability and institutional compliance. Evolution, implementation and scalability The initiative is designed to evolve from an exploratory exercise into a permanent public policy tool: Institutionalisation: The findings are expected to strengthen the legitimacy of public action, allowing the State to adapt continuously to a changing regulatory landscape. Technological implementation: The results are already accessible via an interactive dashboard, offering users dynamic and detailed data visualisation. Scalability: While this initial phase focused on mining and energy, the report establishes a replicable methodological framework applicable to any regulated productive sector. Evidence-based reform: By identifying the 146 distinct laws that comprise the environmental inventory, this evidence serves as a foundation for future regulatory quality improvements and legislative discussions on system modernisation.

title: AI Pilot: CV screening in consultants’ recruitment
description: The AI Pilot for CV Screening was developed for Formez PA's internal recruitment of consultants who support project activities commissioned to the agency by public administrations. The introduction of the inPA portal led to a surge in applications: from 11,888 between December 2021 and October 2023 (pre-inPA) to 24,053 for 824 notices from October 2023 to October 2025, a more than 100% increase. This overwhelmed manual screening by three-person committees, requiring 1,500 hours in 2023, 3,000 in 2024, and 2,500 in 2025, with risks of inconsistency and missed talent due to varying committee compositions. Objectives include automating competency extraction from CVs and preliminary ranking via semantic matching to job needs, while providing dashboards for human review. The tool integrates Formez PA's scoring rules and aims to address aspects related to EU AI Act/GDPR compliance through audits. An interdepartmental team from human resources, project managers, ICT, and end users drives the process. The initiative will integrate fully into Formez PA's intranet for all internal consultant selections. Future evolution includes refining models via monitoring, potential expansion within Formez PA projects, and capacity-building for staff. Institutionalisation relies on governance, training, and scalable infrastructure to handle growing internal recruitment needs securely. Results, outcomes and impacts Since May 2025, the pilot has processed thousands of CVs monthly for internal consultant selections. Besides significantly cutting screening time by about 50% from the 2024 baseline of 3,000 hours, it enhances consistency by benchmarking human versus AI rankings, freeing committees for interviews. Measurements include workload logs, deviation analysis, audit trails, and staff feedback. Outcomes are fairer internal evaluations and qualitative focus. Future expectations include 20–30% faster cycles for Formez consultant hiring, data-driven improvements to notices, and sustained efficiency gains.

title: OpenCouncil: AI that makes municipal councils open, searchable and understandable (Subnational: 14 Greek municipalities)
description: Greek municipal council meetings are public by law, but in practice they are hours-long videos and minutes that are published weeks later, if at all. Few residents know what their council decided about their street, and the administration spends days transcribing sessions by hand. OpenCouncil needs only a recording of the meeting (a YouTube link is enough). From it, the platform transcribes every word and attributes it to the right speaker and political group; splits the session into subjects, linked to the agenda, each with a plain-language summary, the decision taken and the location it concerns; publishes a page per subject, session, speaker and party, with full-text search across every municipality and a map of what was discussed where; sends personalised notifications ("Notis") to residents about the neighbourhoods and topics they follow; produces the transcript and draft minutes for the municipality, checked by a person and ready for signature; and exposes all public data through an open API and an MCP server, so residents, journalists and officials can ask AI assistants such as Claude or ChatGPT about their council and get answers that cite the exact moment of the meeting. The municipality changes nothing about how it meets, and sessions are published as soon as they are processed. Objectives : OpenCouncil aims to make every council and committee meeting searchable, readable and linkable. It explains proceedings in plain language, subject by subject, so a resident can follow a three-hour session in minutes. The platform connects discussions to the streets and neighbourhoods they affect and brings this information to the people who live there. It also seeks to replace manual transcription and minute-taking with a faster, cheaper, human-verified service by producing transcripts and draft minutes for municipalities that are checked by a person and ready for signature. Finally, OpenCouncil is designed as a standardised, open-source product that any municipality can adopt using only a recording and without changing its existing procedures. OpenCouncil targets residents, elected councillors from both the majority and opposition, municipal administrations, particularly council secretariats, as well as journalists and civil society organisations. The platform uses speech recognition and speaker identification to produce fully attributed transcripts of council meetings. Large language models are used to identify subjects, generate summaries, extract decisions and locations, and draft meeting minutes. To ensure accuracy, every transcript is reviewed and corrected by trained staff before being used for official minutes, while every summary includes a link to the exact moment in the video so that information can be verified. The system is hosted in the European Union, is GDPR-compliant, and includes a data protection impact assessment for speaker voiceprints.

title: Innovation, Automation, and AI Acceleration (i3A)
description: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada’s Innovation, Automation and AI Acceleration (i3A) is a department-wide initiative designed to accelerate the responsible, practical, and scalable adoption of artificial intelligence and automation across AAFC. Developed in response to rising citizen expectations, capacity pressures, and varying digital readiness, i3A enables employees to move from ideas and perceptions to real-world application through structured experimentation building on our current data ecosystem and workforce investment. The programme combines governance guardrails with hands-on delivery. A dedicated Centre of Expertise and a core enablement team provide architecture, cybersecurity, cloud, data, and governance support, ensuring innovation progresses safely and responsibly. Cross-functional pods bring together IT specialists and employees from across branches to co-design solutions that address operational challenges. Through staged experimentation and ethics and risk check-ins, ideas evolve into tested and scalable solutions that strengthen internal services, organisational performance and data foundation. An external Executive Digital Leaders advisory board provides strategic insight and perspectives from across sectors, helping the programme stay aligned with emerging practices and broader digital transformation trends and an internal AI Ethics Committee is also available for support. Equitable access is central to i3A’s design. Targeted engagement sessions with senior management and Diversity, Equity and Inclusion networks help broaden participation and ensure diverse perspectives shape innovation. Approximately one-third of the workforce is equipped with AI licences, while secure web-based tools extend access to employees without licences, supporting inclusive learning and experimentation at scale. Close to half of AAFC employees have engaged in training, showcases, or experimentation activities, building momentum and strengthening digital confidence across roles. Looking ahead, i3A is institutionalising a repeatable pathway from experimentation to scale through standardised intake, reusable playbooks, and documented impact cases. By empowering those closest to service delivery, reinforcing responsible data practices, and embedding privacy, security, and human oversight into everyday workflows, the program advances trustworthy AI adoption while delivering sustainable, people-centered public value.

title: DaFNE chatbot
description: As part of the DaFNE research platform by the Austrian Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, Climate and Environmental Protection, Regions, and Water Management, there is an extensive collection of diverse information and complex data, particularly report files from various research projects that have been coordinated and published. To efficiently and systematically manage this data while ensuring it is easily retrievable, we utilise a chatbot powered by a vector database and a large language model (LLM). The chatbot addresses the challenges associated with managing and accessing large collections of information from various research projects. It enhances information retrieval processes by moving beyond simple keyword matching, providing context-aware, relevant responses that can be easily accessed and utilised by stakeholders, including academia, administration, and the public. Another key objective of the chatbot is to leverage advanced technology, implementing state-of-the-art AI components to facilitate meaningful interactions and deliver accurate responses to user inquiries. Furthermore, the project emphasises continuous development, committing to an ongoing effort to refine and enhance the chatbot's functionality based on user feedback and evolving needs. Networking and collaboration with similar projects will also be essential to promote development and share best practices in the future. Initially available only to internal users, the chatbot will be made publicly accessible by the end of February 2026, thereby broadening its reach and usability. After its public launch, the focus will shift towards continuous improvement, incorporating regular updates and enhancements based on user feedback to ensure the chatbot remains relevant and effective in meeting users' needs. Results, outcomes and impacts To date, the chatbot’s impact has been driven primarily by the unprecedented speed at which it delivers information and its practical usability. Instead of searching for individual projects, opening their reports, and reading them, the chatbot shortens this process. This is particularly helpful when planning public relations work, knowledge transfer, and events on specific topics. Until now, this impact has only been reported through individual user experiences. Of course, it is hoped that the chatbot will be used as an everyday tool for administration in the future, but the general public and practitioners in agriculture, forestry, and water management should also benefit more from the scientific outputs.

title: PolluSense
description: In July 2025, the Enforcement Branch (EB) of Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) tasked ECCC’s Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technology Centre of Excellence (AI&ET CoE) to investigate the potential use of space-based remote sensing technology in detecting illegal discharges and pollution events in freshwater bodies. Leveraging AI models, the goal is to automate detection and prioritise potential incidents for human validation and inspection referrals. This research supports EB’s mandate to enforce federal environmental laws across Canada’s vast and diverse ecosystems, including remote and protected regions. Given the challenges of monitoring such expansive areas, particularly in remote locations, EB has traditionally relied on company-reported data and toxicity levels described in literature to guide its enforcement activities. These limitations emphasise the need for innovative approaches to maintain compliance. The initial focus of the research is on the mining industry, which falls under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act and the Fisheries Act. Specifically, under the Fisheries Act, EB conducts inspections to ensure compliance with the Metal and Diamond Effluent Regulations (MDMER). MDMER allows the controlled discharge of effluent from metal and diamond mines into fish-bearing waters, provided strict effluent quality standards are met. These regulations aim to protect Canada’s lakes and rivers from harm caused by mining operations. Currently, inspections under MDMER are conducted biennially but involve substantial costs—up to $25,000 CAD for remote sites—with limited revisit frequencies and challenges in detecting non-compliance. The primary aim of the initiative is to transition from an episodic, infrequent, and reactive inspection model to a system of continuous and proactive monitoring of industrial sites. Implementing AI-based monitoring can significantly increase the likelihood of conducting targeted inspections aligned with non-compliance events, which may otherwise go unnoticed. Additionally, the monitoring system—called PolluSense—provides valuable insights into facility operational patterns and risk profiles, helping prevent large-scale environmental damage and reducing cleanup and health costs. The AI&ET CoE has now advanced PolluSense to the prototype phase, which is undergoing experimentation and testing with EB. The initial objective is to develop scalable and proactive monitoring capabilities that enhance EB’s cost-efficiency and strengthen environmental protection efforts. Looking forward, the AI&ET CoE plans to expand geographic training data beyond Ontario and Quebec to cover additional Canadian regions and explore applying the technology to other industries, such as agriculture, oil sands, and pulp and paper.

title: Prototyping AI Apps for Addressing Labor Shortages through Cross-Ministerial Collaboration
description: In Japan, the shrinking workforce is being countered by growing demands for public services, placing the administrative sector in a structural crisis. The country's total population has entered a long-term decline, projected to fall below 90 million by 2070, with the elderly population reaching approximately 39%. While the number of working-age individuals is decreasing and aging populations are straining public services, the shortage of civil servants is compounded by increasingly complex and time-sensitive societal needs. title: Water Sector Costing Forecast
description: The Water Sector Costing Forecast initiative for the Saudi Water Authority was created to provide a forward-looking view of plant costs by plant and by cost category. It was proposed by the Costing Department and delivered with support from the Data Management Office to address a practical challenge: historical cost data existed, but planning future costs remained largely reactive and difficult to scale consistently across plants. By using recent cost records to generate forecasts, the initiative helps finance, costing department, and operations teams make earlier and better-informed decisions. The initiative seeks to improve budgeting quality, strengthen cost control, and make future spending patterns easier to understand. Instead of only reviewing past costs, the solution analyzes historical cost behavior and produces estimates for upcoming periods, allowing teams to anticipate increases in areas such as energy, maintenance, labor, chemicals, and other plant-level expense categories. This supports more proactive budget preparation, improves the accuracy of planning, and helps identify unusual cost deviations before they become larger operational or financial issues. From an implementation perspective, the initiative starts by extracting costing data from the costing system, organizing and cleaning the data, and structuring it into consistent groups suitable for forecasting. The solution inventoried more than 136 cost items across multiple plants, removed older data that did not reflect recent cost patterns, treated missing and out-of-range values, and built a forecasting model using recent years of data. The outputs are then published to a costing dashboard so decision-makers can review expected future costs in a simple and accessible way. The initiative has established a working cost-forecasting capability that supports forward planning for Saudi Water Authority plants. So far, cost data was inventoried across 17 plants and 136 cost items, presenting the result through a dashboard for decision-makers. Results were measured through data quality checks, test-set model evaluation using MASE, and forecast-versus-actual variance tracking. The main impact observed is better visibility of future spending by plant and category. Going forward, the initiative is expected to improve budget accuracy, strengthen cost control, enable earlier detection of cost deviations, and scale to wider plant coverage and more regular forecasting cycles.

title: Generative AI for Engineering Design
description: Water desalination plants rely on highly detailed engineering diagrams known as Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs) to document the equipment, piping, and processes that make up their operations. Manually reading and interpreting these diagrams is time-consuming, technically demanding, and prone to human error. The Saudi Water Authority identified an opportunity to apply generative AI to automate this process, reducing the burden on engineers and technicians while improving the speed and accuracy of information retrieval. The initiative delivers an AI-powered system that automatically processes P&ID documents, extracts key information about equipment and components, and classifies the type of desalination process depicted. The system then generates structured summaries of the workflow for each process, giving engineers a clear and concise overview without needing to manually trace through complex diagrams. A user-friendly dashboard presents this extracted data in a visual and accessible format. Additionally, the system includes a conversational chat interface, allowing users to ask questions directly about the content of specific P&ID documents and receive instant, contextual answers. The core objectives of the initiative are to automate data extraction from P&IDs, improve the accuracy of equipment and process identification, streamline asset management through comprehensive equipment listings, and enhance operational efficiency by reducing manual intervention and minimising downtime. The system is designed to process data with minimal latency, comply with relevant data privacy and security standards, and requires minimal training for end users. Looking ahead, the system is designed with scalability in mind, with the capacity to expand across multiple desalination plants and accommodate increasing volumes of P&ID data. As the tool matures through user feedback from engineers and technicians, it is expected to be institutionalised as a standard part of the Authority's plant management workflow, reducing reliance on manual document interpretation and supporting more informed decision-making across operations.

title: Orientation, Methodologies and Guides for AI in the Public Service
description: The advancement of technology demands an increasingly agile, efficient, and innovative public service. To this end, the Government's AI Center offers public servants the tools and knowledge to master Artificial Intelligence responsibly, ethically, and strategically. Our materials are the path for each public servant to optimise their work, make more assertive decisions, and deliver excellent public services to citizens. Guide 1 - Generative AI in Public Service: This guide aims to support public servants in understanding and responsibly using Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools. It provides an overview of GAI, clear explanations of its challenges and limitations, and practical guidance for the ethical and effective use of these tools in the Brazilian public sector. Guide 2 - Practical Prompt Guide: This material offers recommendations on the effective and responsible use of generative AI tools, as well as assisting in the creation of clear and objective prompts that optimise the daily activities of public servants. The main objective of this document is to guide public servants in: critically selecting and experimenting with available artificial intelligence tools; To build good prompts to obtain useful, ethical, and safe answers; to identify use cases that optimise and increase the efficiency of public service; to provide tools for prompt optimisation. There is also a Glossary of AI-Related Terms, with words applicable to the AI context. Results, outcomes and impacts Dissemination of materials through workshops and events aimed at public servants, with presentations generating significant interest at these times. A significant number of accesses to materials. The guides and booklets are initial materials to spark the interest of public servants in the AI training tracks made available by the agency. Challenges and lessons learned There are still challenges in dissemination, reach, and cultural resistance from some people regarding the use of AI. There is still need for clarification of AI definitions and the indispensable need for human review to bring more security. The use of spaces such as events with "Prompt Courses" demonstrates the effectiveness and limits of the tool and elucidates the functioning of LLMs, which contributes to the understanding of the materials.

title: AI Assistants for Supporting Labor Justice Conciliation
description: The project revolutionises labour conciliation — a pillar of social peace that historically faces backlogs and bureaucracy. Operating within Chat-JT, the tool utilises a writing capacity of 333,092 characters, allowing for extremely detailed prompts and structured criteria. This significantly reduces the probability of "hallucinations" and ensures precise legal analysis, standardisation, and institutional security. The AI does not decide for the parties; instead, it provides the conciliator with a "clear map of what is at stake," organising claims into didactic tables and separating severance pay from salary-based funds to ensure conscious and responsible decision-making. The assistants are: Initial Screening - good cases for settlements Settlement - negotiation by numbers Settlement - negotiation by scenarios Calculation - updates values by the Selic rate and deducts payments made Calculation - updates values and compares indices for settlement (Selic vs. Savings) Results, outcomes and impacts The project founder reported a conciliation rate surge from 54% to 68%, a 25% real increase in settlements. AI assistants reduced staff burnout by replacing full file reviews with structured summaries and objective suggestions. Case review time dropped from 20 to 5 minutes, allowing active listening during 30-minute hearings to expand from 10 to 15 minutes. This shift improved dialogue and party confidence. Currently, over 2,200 users utilise the tools, which hold a 96% approval rating from workshop participants. The initiative was a finalist and received an honourable mention at the 2025 J.Ex Innovation Awards.

title: Air Travel Complaints Artificial Intelligence Initiative
description: The new Air Travel Complaints regime, launched in 2023, was designed to modernise Canada’s air travel complaint process. In FY 2024‑25, the Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA) closed 33,000 complaints, surpassing its target, but annual intake continues to exceed 40,000, leaving a backlog of roughly 90,000 complaints. To address this challenge, the CTA is rolling out AI‑enabled tools that streamline key workflow steps while preserving decision quality and consistency. The first tool supports quality review of drafted decisions, and the second introduces automated document summarisation along with integrated case‑file summaries. Future phases will explore AI‑assisted decision drafting, enhanced triage models, and potential external tools to help passengers' self‑screen their complaints. To support the safe and responsible adoption of AI, the CTA has implemented an AI Governance Framework that provides structured oversight for all AI initiatives. The framework establishes clear expectations for risk management, transparency, and accountability, and incorporates mandatory requirements such as the Algorithmic Impact Assessment. This approach ensures alignment with federal direction, including the Directive on Automated Decision‑Making, and enables secure, privacy‑protective, and ethical deployment of AI across the organisation. Results, outcomes and impact CTA expects reduced time on task, more consistent decisions, and faster resolution of the 90,000‑complaint backlog. Challenges and lessons learned Lessons learned highlight that introducing AI into a high‑volume programme requires both substantial operational change and new organisational capacities. Teams must develop new skills such as prompt engineering while adapting workflows and ensuring that privacy, ethics, and transparency requirements remain at the forefront. Effective change‑management practices, including training, user‑support mechanisms, and clear communication of the costs and benefits of adopting the tool versus maintaining the status quo, are critical for adoption and for reducing resistance Equally important was recognising that AI governance itself represents a major organisational change. Establishing a formal governance structure early clarified expectations for documentation, risk management, and completion of Algorithmic Impact Assessments. This foundation enabled responsible experimentation while ensuring alignment with federal requirements.

title: Unified Intelligent Assistant
description: The Unified Intelligent Assistant is a pilot AI solution launched by the Ministry of Digital Transformation in 2025 to modernise public sector support services. Traditional channels such as phone lines and email are frequently overloaded, leading to delays and lower user satisfaction. The Assistant addresses this challenge by enabling fast, intuitive access to information through natural language conversation, consolidating content that is currently dispersed across multiple government portals. The Assistant supports the strategic goals of the “Digital Public Services 2030” agenda and is part of the broader “Development of New Dynamic e Services (DES)” programme. Its purpose is to provide a unified, reliable, and secure digital helper that improves information accessibility, reduces support workloads, and ensures around the clock availability. The first data source included in the pilot phase is the SI TRUST portal, with planned expansion to additional government portals. The assistant operates as a web based conversational interface that is integrated into existing websites, powered by a large language model, returning answers strictly based on predefined public sector content. Responses always include references and links to original sources. The Assistant functions exclusively in Slovene, using formal address, maintains conversational context within a session, and deletes session data after 30 minutes of inactivity or upon closing. It can recognise questions posed in different languages. It does not require login, does not perform transactions (e.g. filing applications), and serves solely informational purposes. A multi-layer anonymisation mechanism ensures compliance with data protection requirements. Since users might inadvertently share personal data despite warnings, all inputs undergo structured and unstructured personal data detection using regular expressions and named entity recognition (spaCy), followed by automatic removal before being sent to the LLM. Results, outcomes and impacts During the testing phase, the Unified Digital Assistant proved highly effective in providing a wide range of accurate information within the supported domains. It is expected to significantly reduce user calls and emails to the support centre (EKC) and decrease the number of user errors when submitting documents for public services. As the initiative is still in its pilot phase, measurable indicators and formal targets have not yet been defined.

title: ProVerifier
description: The food and drug regulatory landscape involves thousands of products entering the market across four major categories: food, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and medical devices. Inspectors are responsible for verifying that each product is properly registered, contains approved ingredients, carries valid import permissions, and complies with applicable safety standards such as GSO standards approved by the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA). Traditionally, this verification process has been manual and time-consuming, requiring inspectors to cross-reference product labels against multiple government databases and regulatory documents. This creates bottlenecks during inspections, increases the risk of human error, and limits the number of products that can be verified in a given period. This initiative addresses these challenges by building an intelligent inspection assistant powered by artificial intelligence. The tool allows inspectors to use a mobile application to capture product information through images or text input. The system then uses AI vision models to automatically extract product details such as the product name, ingredient list, barcode numbers, and manufacturer name. Once extracted, this data is routed to specialised verification services based on the product type. For cosmetics, the system checks ingredient safety and product listing status. For pharmaceuticals, it verifies drug registration and import permissions validity. For food products, a retrieval-augmented generation system compares product information against SFDA standards to assess compliance. For medical devices, the system confirms registration status. The objectives of this initiative are threefold. First, to significantly reduce the time inspectors spend on each product verification, enabling them to process more inspections per day. Second, to improve accuracy by eliminating manual data entry and cross-referencing errors. Third, to create a centralised audit trail of all verification activities, giving administrators and decision-makers a clear view of inspection patterns, compliance rates, and potential risks across product categories.

title: RASID
description: RASID is an artificial intelligence–based regulatory system developed by the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) to support inspectors at border checkpoints in identifying controlled medicines carried by travelers. The system uses AI technologies to analyse images of medicine packages and automatically extract relevant information such as drug name, quantity, and dosage, and is designed to handle a wide variety of medicines across different brands, formulations, and packaging types. The initiative addresses a key operational challenge in drug inspection processes, where inspectors previously relied on manual checks and personal expertise, leading to inconsistent decisions, longer processing times, and potential errors in identifying controlled substances. RASID reduces this dependency by providing a standardized, AI-driven approach that enhances accuracy and decision consistency. Key features of the system include: Automated detection of controlled medicines using image analysis Comparison against official controlled substances lists Verification of prescriptions and medical reports Assessment of whether the quantity carried is reasonable based on medical need and duration of stay Real-time alerts for restricted or non-compliant medicines By automating several manual inspection tasks, the system significantly improves operational efficiency, reduces reliance on individual experience, and ensures consistent regulatory decisions. During its pilot phase, the system demonstrated a significant reduction in inspection time and improved accuracy in identifying controlled medicines. RASID also has strong potential for scalability and replication. The solution can be extended to other entry points, integrated with additional regulatory databases, and adapted for use in other government sectors or countries facing similar inspection challenges. It represents a scalable AI solution that enhances border inspection processes and supports public health protection. RASID has been awarded the SDAIA “Aware” badge in recognition of its alignment with ethical AI principles and responsible AI practices. The initiative follows national guidelines for trustworthy artificial intelligence and demonstrates the commitment of the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) to deploying AI systems that respect transparency, safety, and ethical standards while supporting regulatory operations and protecting public health.

title: AI Scribe for Emergency Departments
description: The Heidi AI Scribe for Emergency Departments (ED) is an ambient, generative AI clinical documentation resource deployed nationally through the HealthX innovation programme. This AI solution listens to clinician–patient interactions (with appropriate consent), securely records consultations and transcribes in real time. It automatically generates structured clinical notes aligned to documentation standards and clinical terminology. Clinicians review, edit and confirm these notes for the clinical record. Clinical accountability and decision making remain fully with the clinician at all times. The AI scribe is suitable for high pressure ED environments, where clinicians face significant administrative burden alongside acute clinical decision making. The tool is saving clinician time while making sure important information is accurately captured. Nationwide rollout covered 39 sites with over 1,000 licences allocated. This national deployment across all emergency departments in New Zealand represents a significant milestone in responsible AI adoption at scale. The deployment is understood to be one of the world’s first fully national deployments of a public health ambient AI scribe for Emergency Departments. The AI scribe enables more direct patient engagement through by freeing clinicians from manual note taking and documentation. Clinicians also report the ability to see additional patients per shift. The solution improves waiting time through improved patient flow and throughput in high demand ED environments, as well as shorter patient stays. Clinician satisfaction scores exceeded targets, with feedback consistently highlighting reduced cognitive load, improved focus on patient interactions, and less end of shift fatigue. Documentation completed outside rostered hours decreased by up to 81%, reducing unpaid overtime and supporting better roster alignment. Results, outcomes and impacts AI scribe improvements are likely to be resulting in a range of positive impacts for patients and their families including reduced waiting time for assessment and faster processing of referrals. Direct improvements measured include time savings. The AI scribe created a substantial reduction in documentation effort and time. Data captured during piloting and early rollout demonstrated reduction in documentation effort of over 10 minutes per patient assessment on average; equal to improvement of approximately 60%. Clinicians reported the ability to see additional patients per shift, driven by faster documentation processes. Documentation completed outside rostered hours also decreased by up to 81%, reducing after‑hours administration.

title: Pakistan Digital Authority (PDA)
description: The PDA was established under the Digital Nation Pakistan Act 2025 as Pakistan’s statutory institution to spearhead the country’s transition toward a digital nation. It serves as a national governance mechanism to coordinate digital transformation across the public sector while engaging the private sector and civil society. Under Section 8 of the Act, the PDA is mandated to develop and implement the National Digital Masterplan and to carry out digital maturity assessment, monitoring and evaluation of digital initiatives. It reviews digital plans and projects for alignment with the Masterplan and recommends approvals. It also advises on laws, rules, regulations and policies related to the National Digital Masterplan. The PDA’s mandate includes oversight, standards and compliance for data governance, AI, and emerging technologies, alongside development of national strategies such as the National Data Strategy, Digital Economy Strategy and National Citizen Experience Strategy. It also leads the development, implementation and oversight of Digital Public Infrastructure and supports policies and frameworks for digital innovation. This governance model is intended to institutionalise interoperable digital transformation, strengthen foundations for scalable and trustworthy AI use in government, and improve digital service delivery and citizen experience across Pakistan. Results, outcomes and impacts The Act created the PDA as a statutory governance mechanism for national digital transformation. The PDA’s mandate includes developing and implementing the National Digital Masterplan, conducting digital maturity assessments, reviewing digital projects for alignment, and establishing oversight, standards and compliance for data governance, AI and emerging technologies. Near-term results will be measured through Masterplan adoption, project alignment decisions, maturity assessment outputs, and monitoring and evaluation of digital initiatives. Longer-term impacts include improved interoperability, stronger digital public infrastructure, and AI-ready data governance. Challenges and lessons learned Key challenges include coordinating across federal, provincial and local governments; aligning digital plans and procurement with the National Digital Masterplan; and achieving interoperability across legacy systems. Capacity constraints may affect consistent maturity assessment, monitoring and evaluation across agencies, requiring sustained resourcing and skills development. For AI-related oversight, success depends on clear standards, secure data governance practices and workable compliance mechanisms that avoid duplication or unclear overlaps with existing regulators. Lessons include the need for strong political sponsorship, phased implementation priorities, measurable KPIs, inter-agency coordination mechanisms, and a citizen-experience focus so digital transformation delivers practical public value.

title: Cali ResuelVÉ. Knowledge Library (Subnational: Cali)
description: Santiago de Cali, Colombia’s third largest city with approximately 2.5 million inhabitants, faces persistent challenges in reducing delays and inconsistencies in citizen attention. The City’s One-Stop Window operates across in-person, phone, and virtual channels, managing around 1,000 daily requests. The city’s institutional offering comprises 225 procedures, 36 other administrative processes and 3 public information access queries. Fragmented information sources and lack of uniform guidance have historically generated delays, confusion, and reduced trust in public institutions. To address this issue, the City—through the Department of Administrative Development and Institutional Innovation (DADII), with support from the IDB’s Knowledge for Results (K4R) initiative—implemented the Knowledge Library. The solution emerged from a Lean/Kaizen diagnosis of citizen service processes, combining continuous improvement, institutional knowledge management and AI to strengthen frontline staff capabilities. The initiative consists of a virtual assistant powered by large language models (LLM) combined with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). In its first phase, the tool supports public servants working across all citizen attention channels, providing immediate access to consistent and updated official information on procedures and administrative requirements. The system uses artificial intelligence to understand questions posed in natural language and generate relevant, context-aware responses in real time. Its outputs are grounded exclusively in verified institutional data, supporting accuracy and reliability. By design, it is not fully generative, preserving human oversight and maintaining the central role of frontline officials in citizen interaction. This creates an “augmented humanity” approach in which AI acts as a cognitive co-actor, supporting public servants by combining technological efficiency with human judgement and empathy. The initiative aims to reduce response times, improve consistency of information, and strengthen institutional knowledge management. By enhancing the capacity of public officials, it contributes to more transparent and accessible government processes. A second phase, currently under development (by October 2026), will support post-earthquake recovery by integrating information on procedures and assistance pathways established by municipal entities for affected residents. The library may subsequently evolve into a broader digital tool (chatbot) accessible directly to citizens, offering a scalable and trustworthy example of AI adoption in subnational government.

title: Promotion and Integration of AI Technologies in Public Administration
description: This initiative forms part of Greece’s broader effort to modernise public administration through the responsible use of artificial intelligence, combining reforms in human resource management with the systematic simplification of administrative procedures. It is anchored in the National Policy for Administrative Procedures, which provides the unified framework for continuous process improvement, reduction of bureaucracy and improved service delivery to citizens and businesses. On the human resource management dimension, the initiative will support the use of AI-enabled tools across the HRM lifecycle, including workforce planning, recruitment, performance management and skills development. Data analytics and machine learning techniques will be used to support evidence-based decision making, skills forecasting and better alignment between organisational needs, roles and competencies. The initiative aims to strengthen motivation, promote a culture of continuous learning and enhance the adaptability of public sector employees, while ensuring that all decisions remain under human oversight. At the same time, the initiative will address the simplification of administrative procedures through data-driven analysis and AI-supported methods. Administrative procedures are systematically documented and maintained in the National Registry of Administrative Procedures (“Mitos”), creating a comprehensive and continuously updated baseline. AI techniques are applied to identify inefficiencies, repetitive steps and bottlenecks, supporting the redesign and simplification of procedures. This contributes to reducing administrative burden, shortening processing times and improving the accessibility and usability of public services. AI technologies are positioned as enabling mechanisms for systemic administrative redesign rather than isolated automation tools. The initiative is complemented by institutional mechanisms such as the National Programme for the Simplification of Procedures and the Observatory for Bureaucracy, which assesses the impact of simplification actions using common indicators. In parallel, technical assistance under the TSI framework will support the development of AI governance models, methodologies and toolkits, ensuring alignment with national legislation, the forthcoming European AI Act and principles of ethical, transparent and accountable AI use. Building on earlier reforms in performance management and HR digitalisation, the initiative is designed to scale across public administration. By combining AI-supported HRM with AI-enabled process simplification, it will contribute to a more efficient, transparent and user-oriented public sector and will lay the foundations for sustainable institutional change.

title: Tiwi Islands Rangers Ghost Nets Program (Subnational: Northern Territory)
description: The prevailing currents and conditions in the Arafura and Timor Seas and the Torres Strait cause marine debris to accumulate in the Gulf of Carpentaria, which is recognised as a global marine debris ‘hot spot’. Although this area is remote and sparsely populated, it has one of the highest rates of marine debris accumulation in Australia. Numerous marine species are regularly entangled in derelict fishing gear, including four vulnerable or endangered marine turtle species found in Australian waters – olive ridley, hawksbill, green and flatback turtles. Ghost nets that wash up or are left on beaches can re-enter the marine environment during large tidal and storm events. They also have the potential to disturb and displace coastal plant and animal communities, especially turtles and other nesting species. The materials that make up these ghost nets slowly deteriorate to eventually form microplastics, which can damage natural food webs and ecosystems. The first Ghost Nets Initiative (GNI) was delivered by Parks Australia from 2021–2025 in partnership with government agencies, Indigenous groups and other key stakeholders. Over $14 million was delivered to innovative projects aimed at addressing the challenge of ghost nets and plastic waste in the waters and beaches of northern Australia. Building on the efforts of Indigenous communities, environmental groups and private industry, the GNI was focused on the following activities: • Delivering new technology and other projects to better detect, collect and dispose of ghost nets, including the $3 million Ghost Nets Innovative Solutions grant program. • Working with Indigenous ranger groups to collect data on the source of ghost nets and coordinate retrievals and marine debris beach clean ups in the Gulf of Carpentaria, one of the nation’s hot spots for ghost nets drifting from foreign waters. • Conducting new trials in collaboration with the Australian Fisheries Management Authority (AFMA) and Maritime Border Command (MBC) – a multi-agency taskforce, within the Australian Border Force - to attach GPS tracking devices to ghost nets when an initial retrieval is not possible due to unsafe conditions. • Commissioning research into the source and distribution of ghost nets and possible recycling solutions in the Gulf of Carpentaria. One of the program’s key initiatives focuses on tracking and managing marine debris – particularly drift nets and plastics – that wash up along Northern Australia’s remote coastlines. Data collection, model training and platform build has been delivered through First Nations led design workshops, and a labelling platform for rangers has been codesigned to allow drone data to be annotated and labelled so that images captured of marine debris by First Nations rangers can be used to train AI models.

title: RADAR - Early Warning System for Anomalies in Health Claims and Payments
description: Context and problem ADRES manages large-scale public health financing flows. Oversight teams often face fragmented datasets, manual checks and retrospective reviews, which limit early detection of unusual behaviours and slow the feedback loop to improve data quality and payment controls. What the initiative does RADAR-Desviaciones turns routine administrative health data into actionable early-warning signals. It combines (1) data-quality gates and deterministic business rules (e.g. structural validity, internal consistency and known red-flag patterns) with (2) anomaly detection methods based on statistical baselines and, where appropriate, machine-learning scoring. Outputs are presented as ranked worklists and dashboards that explain why a case was flagged. How it is used RADAR is a decision-support system: it does not automate sanctions or final decisions. Alerts are reviewed by human analysts/auditors who confirm findings and provide feedback. The system keeps records of inputs, transformations and rule/model versions, enabling auditability and continuous improvement. How it scales The programme is designed to start with a controlled pilot (selected cohorts, regions or payment lines) and expand as data quality stabilises and operating procedures mature. Governance covers access control, privacy and security safeguards, documentation and monitoring (performance, drift and operational impact). Results, outcomes and impacts Status: Pilot / roll-out (2025–2026). Early deliverables include: (a) an agreed deviation catalogue and risk indicators developed with domain experts; (b) automated data-quality checks and traceable pipelines; and (c) dashboards that rank cases by risk and show key drivers. Impact is measured through: reduction in time to triage, audit confirmation rate (hit rate), coverage (records screened per period) and cycle time from alert to action.

title: Alignment of planning instruments with the National Strategic Development Plan, in accordance with the results chain
description: The initiative involves using artificial intelligence tools to analyse and align the Peruvian State's planning instruments within the SINAPLAN framework, in accordance with the results chain established in the Guide for Institutional Planning. According to the regulatory framework, policies and plans must be vertically aligned to implement the national objectives of the National Strategic Development Plan (PEDN), which embodies the country's strategic development priorities and guides State action. However, in practice, this alignment is not always systematically verified or based on evidence. To address this challenge, a methodology was developed that combines semantic embeddings, vector indexing (FAISS), re-ranking and structured validation using advanced language models (OpenAI API). This identifies levels of alignment between: Objectives and Strategic Actions of the PEDN (27 Strategic Objectives and 163 Strategic Actions); and Priority Objectives of the 43 National Policies approved as of 2025 (209 Priority Objectives). The tool enables the detection of clusters, gaps and potential misalignments between strategic instruments, ensuring that National Policies—and progressively, other planning instruments—effectively respond to the priorities defined in the PEDN. This strengthens the coherence and effectiveness of national planning, directly impacting the quality of public policy monitoring and evaluation, evidence-based decision-making and the State's capacity to direct its interventions towards the effective achievement of national priorities and the generation of public value. Results, outcomes and impacts The benefits of the AI initiative are: a. Systematic and Visual Identification of the level of alignment between the PEDN (Strategic National Development Plan) and National Policies. b. Detection of Strategic Actions with low levels of implementation within National Policies (indicating potential implementation gaps, insufficient programmatic alignment or the need to strengthen interventions to ensure consistency with national priorities). c. Identification of Priority Objectives with high thematic concentration. d. Significant Reduction in Time required for manual comparative analysis, transforming a process that previously took approximately three months into one that can be completed in about three weeks.

title: OptiCrea Elements – Application for the creation and naming of policy and plan elements
description: OptiCrea Elements is a web application developed in R Shiny that integrates artificial intelligence (via the DeepSeek API) to assist planning specialists. Its primary purpose is to create and improve the naming of indicators and strategic elements, ensuring they align with Peru’s Chain of Results and current regulations. Strategic planning in Peru requires indicator names to meet strict criteria: a. Specific Structures: Defined by the type of element (Objective or Action). b. Methodological Alignment: Adherence to the CEPLAN 2024 Guide, SMART criteria and results-based management. c. The Problem: Manual drafting is time-intensive, highly dependent on individual experience, difficult to standardise and prone to structural errors. d. Core Functionalities: Multi-Instrument Support: Covers all planning levels, including Sectoral, Regional, Local and Institutional plans. Dual Operating Modes: IMPROVE: Optimises existing names while maintaining required legal structures. CREATE: Generates new names from scratch based on user-provided context (problem, population, territory). Complex Hierarchical Handling: Manages associations between Objectives → Actions → Indicators, ensuring consistency across different levels of the planning tree. Specialised AI Prompts: Features specific prompt engineering for eight distinct scenarios (improving/creating for objectives, actions and their respective indicators). Dynamic Interface: Built for high usability with dynamic inputs, the ability to add/remove groups of elements and structured visualisation of results. DeepSeek API Integration: Uses asynchronous calls with low "temperature" settings to ensure consistent, non-creative and technically rigorous responses. Efficient Exporting: Results can be copied to the clipboard or downloaded in structured TXT formats for integration into other systems. Technological Stack: Frontend/Backend: R Shiny & shinydashboard. Artificial Intelligence: DeepSeek API (deepseek-chat). Data Processing: jsonlite, httr, glue. Interactivity: shinyjs.

title: Recommendations on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
description: The Recommendations on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence is a national policy guidance document prepared by the Ministry of National Education to ensure the ethical, safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence in education. Developed in alignment with the Artificial Intelligence in Education Policy Document and Action Plan (2025–2029), the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy and the Century of Türkiye Education Model, the initiative establishes a human-centred and value-based ethical framework for AI use. The initiative addresses key ethical risks associated with artificial intelligence, including data privacy violations, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, and the protection of children’s rights. It provides comprehensive recommendations for all education stakeholders, including developers, service providers, students, teachers, school administrators and parents. Core principles include human dignity, fairness, accountability, transparency, data security, proportionality and inclusiveness. The document defines clear guidance on privacy-by-design, human oversight of AI-supported decisions, explainability of algorithms, bias monitoring, child safety measures, and ethical governance mechanisms. It emphasises that AI systems should support, not replace, human judgement in critical educational decisions and must always operate under human supervision. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has established a national ethical reference framework for AI use in education and increased awareness among key stakeholders. It supports safer AI deployment, improved data protection practices and stronger accountability mechanisms. Expected future impacts include reduced ethical risks, increased trust in AI-supported education systems, improved protection of children’s rights and greater alignment with international AI ethics standards. Implementation is supported through institutional guidance, training activities and policy alignment. Challenges and lessons learned Key challenges include ensuring consistent ethical awareness across diverse stakeholder groups, addressing algorithmic bias risks and protecting sensitive child data. These challenges are mitigated through clear ethical principles, stakeholder-specific recommendations and alignment with data protection legislation. A key lesson learned is that ethical AI requires continuous human oversight, institutional commitment and education-wide awareness. Ethical guidance must be practical, inclusive and adaptable to evolving technologies to remain effective.

title: Alberta Responsible AI Policy and Governance Frameworks (Subnational: Alberta)
description: Alberta is strengthening responsible AI adoption through policies, strategies, and governance measures. The Government of Alberta works with federal partners and Alberta’s AI sector to address privacy, ethics, transparency, and safety concerns. The AI Usage Policy, introduced in May 2025, establishes responsibilities and principles for the responsible development, procurement, adoption, and implementation of AI across departments. The Alberta Technology and Innovation Strategy, which is being renewed, sets priorities to grow the technology sector and support AI and quantum technologies. Alberta’s Protection of Privacy Act includes transparency provisions that require public bodies to notify individuals at the time of collection if their personal information will be used in automated systems, including AI. Complementary initiatives, such as the Data and Information Management Framework, the Data Ethics Framework, and the Alberta AI Data Centre Strategy, reinforce ethical, secure, and effective AI implementation. An internal AI Hub centralises approved AI tools, usage policies, training, and resources. Guidance for SharePoint agents emphasises restricting data scope, curating and maintaining datasets, and assigning responsible contacts and data custodians to ensure reliability and accountability. The government continues to monitor and assess regulatory options to protect Albertans from AI misuse while fostering responsible use. Results, outcomes and impacts Government-wide AI governance has been strengthened through clear policy direction, transparency requirements, centralised resources, and practical guidance, including controls for SharePoint agents. Expected impacts include more consistent and human-centred use of AI, reduced risks of misuse, improved privacy safeguards, and increased public trust as adoption scales. Challenges and lessons learned Challenges include rapidly evolving AI capabilities, aligning practices across ministries, and sustaining awareness and training. Alberta is responding through a formal AI Usage Policy, centralised AI Hub resources, and ongoing renewal of its strategies and frameworks. Success depends on continued monitoring, clear roles and accountability, and cross-government coordination with external partners.

title: Text Simplification via GenAI
description: Clear and accessible communication is essential for ensuring that citizens can effectively navigate public services. This work examines the use of generative AI models to simplify administrative texts on the INPS, Italy’s National Institute of Social Security, web portal, which provides nearly 500 digital services related to pensions and welfare. As Europe’s largest welfare institution, INPS serves approximately 45 million citizens, making the clarity of its service descriptions crucial for accessibility and user experience. INPS has been running a structured simplification programme aimed at making its content understandable to users with a middle-school education level. To date, over 700 texts have been manually simplified, using the Gulpease index to measure readability. The average score improved from 57 to 64, reflecting a substantial increase in accessibility. Currently, INPS relies on a manual process to simplify the language of its Service Pages, a time-consuming and resource-intensive approach that requires specialised expertise. The need for clearer bureaucratic language has been recognised in Italy for decades. A 2002 directive, still in force, states that “all texts produced by administrations must be designed and written to be understood by those who receive them.” Despite this, institutional communication often remains complex, limiting citizens' ability to fully understand and access essential services. While simplification enhances transparency and public trust, a major challenge is maintaining the legal precision required for official documentation. This work explores how Large Language Models (LLMs) can support INPS in transforming its manual simplification process into a semi-automated system that is both efficient and scalable. The goal is to develop a solution that can process large volumes of text while ensuring readability, accuracy, and compliance with legal standards. To achieve this, the research establishes an evaluation framework based on text metrics and conducts user surveys to assess the accessibility and quality of AI-generated text compared with original and manually simplified versions. Looking ahead, the potential for refining and expanding this approach is substantial. Possibilities include generating pre-simplified texts directly from legal norms, introducing a compliance-evaluation framework, and developing collaborative workflows in which AI and human experts iteratively refine simplifications, combining automation with expert oversight. The experimentation on text simplification has been developed as a prototype and has successfully passed the evaluation stage. It is now transitioning into an operational business process within INPS and its technology partners, integrating a graphical interface to support a human-in-the-loop collaborative workflow.

title: Judicial Branch AI Management and Governance Model (Subnational: Mato Grosso)
description: The PJMT’s AI governance initiative was created to address the growing need for the structured, transparent, and accountable use of artificial intelligence within the Judiciary. As AI adoption expanded across different units, the absence of standardised processes posed risks to legal compliance, ethical use, resource allocation, and decision consistency. This initiative seeks to transform AI from isolated experiments into a coordinated institutional capability aligned with public value and regulatory requirements. The main objective is to establish a comprehensive governance model that ensures all AI initiatives follow defined processes for feasibility assessment, prioritisation, approval, development, and monitoring. This includes the establishment of strategic and operational committees responsible for decision-making and oversight, as well as the strengthening of the AI Center as a central unit that integrates technical development with governance practices. The model is aligned with CNJ Resolution No. 615/2025, ensuring adherence to legal, ethical, and accountability standards. The initiative currently encompasses a portfolio of ten AI projects under governance management, with six solutions in production and four in testing and development phases. In parallel, the AI Center has been proactively developing governance mechanisms to monitor key technical aspects such as token consumption, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) processes, and the management of data sources, ensuring efficiency, traceability, and responsible use of computational resources. User training is a mandatory prerequisite for AI adoption, reinforcing the importance of human oversight and responsible interaction with AI systems. This approach ensures that users are properly prepared to understand the limitations, risks, and appropriate use of the technology within judicial processes. Regarding implementation, the initiative is being institutionalised through formal governance structures, standardised workflows, and clear role definitions across the organisation. It is designed to scale by enabling multiple units to propose and develop AI solutions within a controlled framework, ensuring sustainability, interoperability, and continuous evolution of AI capabilities within the Judiciary.

title: Guideline on Artificial Intelligence for the Public Sector
description: The Guideline on Artificial Intelligence for the Public Sector (Garis Panduan Artificial Intelligence Sektor Awam) provides a common reference for government agencies in Malaysia to adopt and use artificial intelligence (AI) in a responsible, secure and effective manner. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into public-sector services and operations, the guideline seeks to support agencies in identifying opportunities for AI adoption while addressing associated risks, including those relating to governance, ethics, security, data and accountability. The Guideline on Artificial Intelligence for the Public Sector aims to strengthen the capacity of public-sector agencies to plan, develop, procure, deploy and manage AI applications in a manner that supports public value and aligns with broader government policies and requirements. It provides practical guidance on key considerations across the AI lifecycle, helping agencies establish appropriate governance, risk management, human oversight and safeguards when implementing AI. The Guideline forms part of Malaysia’s broader digital government and AI governance landscape and is intended to complement relevant national policies, guidelines, standards and legal requirements. As AI technologies and their applications continue to evolve, the Guideline can be further updated and refined to reflect emerging technologies, risks, standards and government priorities, supporting more consistent and scalable AI adoption across the public sector.

title: Law Overlap Detection System
description: The initiative addresses the complex challenge of legislative inflation and regulatory fragmentation in Albania. As laws are frequently updated or introduced, manual cross-referencing against the entire Official Gazette becomes prone to human error, leading to jurisdictional gaps or redundant requirements that stifle economic growth and public trust. The primary objective is to leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to scan, map, and analyse the interconnections between thousands of legal acts automatically via integration with the Official Gazette. The tool identifies where a new draft law might contradict an existing one or where multiple institutions claim authority over the same regulatory space. Currently, the tool is fully integrated into the legislative workflow, allowing for real-time analysis of proposed legal changes. Future evolution focuses on the use of AI to automatically verify whether each draft complies with the Code of Administrative Procedures and the Constitution. The system will also check every sub-law draft against its respective base law to ensure it does not exceed its delegated competences and that it fully addresses all obligations and requirements established in the parent legislation. Through these mechanisms, every draft will be subjected to a comprehensive and structured compliance checklist before approval. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has significantly reduced the time required for legal compliance checks, especially given that there are over 27,000 laws in the system. By using LLM-based semantic search, we have identified and flagged over 200 instances of critical legal overlaps that were previously undetected. These results are measured through comparative analysis between manual reviews and AI-generated reports. Looking forward, we expect to achieve a reduction in regulatory contradictions in new legislation, leading to a more stable and predictable legal environment. Tangible impacts include faster processing of draft laws and a measurable decrease in legal disputes arising from conflicting administrative instructions. Challenges and lessons learned A major challenge was the complexity of the Albanian language in legal contexts, given that it is a low-resource language. We also faced initial resistance regarding the “black box” nature of AI. We responded by implementing a “Human-in-the-Loop” system where AI findings are presented as recommendations for legal experts rather than final decisions. A key lesson is that data quality in the National Registry is paramount: AI is only as good as the archives it scans. Success requires a multidisciplinary team of AI specialists and senior jurists to bridge the gap between technical output and legal nuance.

title: Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Policy (Subnational: Newfoundland and Labrador)
description: As interest in artificial intelligence increased across government, the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador identified the need for a consistent framework to manage risks while enabling responsible innovation. AI presents opportunities to improve public services and internal operations, but also raises risks related to privacy, bias, transparency, accountability, and over-reliance on automated outputs. The Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Policy establishes a whole-of-government approach to governing AI. The policy applies to all departments and to all individuals working on behalf of government, including vendors and third-party service providers. It sets clear requirements related to approval, data handling, transparency, human oversight, accountability, fairness, security, and contestability, and aligns with existing information management and privacy legislation. A central component of the policy is the mandatory AI Impact Assessment (AIA), a structured process used to assess risks before implementing AI systems where required. The AIA evaluates the purpose, scope, data use, and potential impacts of AI technologies and informs decisions on approval and permitted use. Higher-risk use cases are reviewed through a Deputy Minister Artificial Intelligence Oversight Committee, providing senior-level oversight and consistent risk tolerance across government. Recognising that governance must be supported by capability, the policy also includes mandatory training requirements and OCIO-led education and awareness activities. These efforts help public servants understand AI risks, governance expectations, and their responsibilities, supporting responsible adoption as AI use evolves across the public sector. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has established a clear, government-wide framework for the approval and governance of AI use across departments. The AI Impact Assessment is being used to assess risks, clarify scope of use, and support consistent decision-making, while senior-level oversight provides accountability for higher-risk cases. The policy has improved clarity around acceptable AI uses, roles and responsibilities, and expectations for transparency, human oversight, and risk mitigation in public sector AI adoption. The policy is supported by an established review cycle, enabling the identification of improvements and updates over time while maintaining consistent governance and accountability for AI use across government.

title: Technical and Ethical Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Capital District of Bogotá (Subnational: Bogotá D.C.)
description: Bogotá adopted its technical and ethical guidelines on artificial intelligence in 2025 to respond to the rapid expansion of these technologies in the city and to ensure their safe, transparent and people-centred use across all public entities. The initiative emerged at a time when two in every ten residents already reported using AI and when the city’s development plan, Bogotá Camina Segura, set out the ambition to build a smart city grounded in data and evidence-based decision-making. With the approval of Agreement 3 of 2025 by the District Commission for Digital Transformation, Bogotá established a unified framework to guide everyday use of AI tools, the development of AI systems and the oversight of high-impact projects, under principles of legality, ethics, digital security and personal data protection. The guidelines set out clear rules and a common process for all entities, structured around a continuous improvement cycle that requires planning, validation, monitoring and adjustment. They introduce institutional maturity assessments, differentiated routes according to risk, obligations for algorithmic transparency, and both technical and legal audits. They also regulate the everyday use of generative tools by public servants, defining strict limits: AI may support routine, low-impact tasks, but it must never replace professional judgement or intervene in administrative, legal or rights-related decisions. As the document states, “artificial intelligence in the District must be used with clear rules: respecting the law, safeguarding digital security, protecting personal data and acting with ethics and responsibility.” The initiative seeks to close gaps in digital maturity, interoperability and specialised talent, while leveraging the opportunity to position Bogotá as a regional leader in public-sector innovation. Its implementation is aligned with the city’s data governance model, the broader data infrastructure strategy and the mandate to promote emerging technologies set out in Agreement 927 of 2024. Throughout 2026, the city will advance the dissemination and adoption of the guidelines, establish a community of practice for AI, deliver specialised training for public servants, strengthen the District CSIRT, and scale solutions such as Chatico, the citizen SuperApp and predictive systems in health, mobility and risk management. The guidelines will become a permanent policy for all entities, embedded in procurement, oversight, data management and impact assessment processes. Their design allows for future expansion into new sectors, the incorporation of emerging technologies such as advanced generative AI, and the strengthening of public trust through traceability, human oversight and robust risk controls. Through this initiative, Bogotá moves towards a model of smart governance in which AI is used responsibly to improve services, anticipate challenges and modernise public administration.
