title: AI eGovernment Chatbots
description: The initiative aims to strengthen the accessibility and efficiency of public services in Serbia through the deployment of sovereign AI assistants developed and operated by the Serbian Office for IT and eGovernment. The rollout began in 2025 with the introduction of an AI-based digital assistant on the national eGovernment Portal, enabling citizens to obtain information and guidance in clear, everyday language. Since its initial deployment, the initiative has expanded to support information provision for over 50 digital public services. Apart from the national eGovernment Portal, assistants have been implemented for the Ministry for Family Welfare, the property rights registration process, and the Foreigners Portal, where they provide support on topics such as visa applications and residence procedures. These deployments have demonstrated the system’s capacity to respond to high volumes of citizen enquiries across multiple service domains. The initiative is expected to evolve from primarily informational AI assistants towards transactional capabilities that allow users to complete administrative actions digitally. This next phase aims to further simplify procedures and improve digital accessibility. Supported by Serbia’s sovereign large language model development and ongoing infrastructure upgrades, the initiative is designed for institutionalisation across public bodies and scalable adoption throughout the public sector. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has delivered measurable improvements in service accessibility and administrative efficiency. Within two weeks of deployment, enquiries to the Contact Centre decreased by 20%. AI assistants now provide information for around 50 e-services and support high-demand domains, including family welfare, property registration and migration processes, with nearly 200,000 recorded conversations. These results demonstrate strong adoption and reduced manual workload. Future impacts are expected through transactional AI capabilities that will further streamline procedures and enhance service delivery. Challenges and lessons learned Early risks related to accuracy, user trust, and safeguarding personal data were mitigated through phased deployment, continuous model evaluation, and strict adherence to security and privacy standards. A major lesson learned is the importance of clear governance, strong coordination across public bodies, and transparent communication with users. Success requires reliable national infrastructure, access to high-quality local datasets, and sustained institutional commitment to responsible and ethical AI development.

title: VODOSTAI - Software platform for flood prediction and prevention based on artificial intelligence methods and IoT devices
description: The initiative addresses the problem of late and unreliable flood warnings caused by limited monitoring coverage, fragmented data, and slow analysis. It leverages the opportunity to combine low-cost river-level sensors with AI to produce faster, more consistent risk assessments. Its objectives are to: Improve flood prediction accuracy and lead time Provide clear, actionable alerts and dashboards for water authorities and emergency services Support prevention planning, including critical locations, thresholds, and response protocols Create a shared, auditable data and analytics layer that different institutions can rely on. In the next phase, the platform will be implemented through pilot deployments with river basin authorities and municipalities, then embedded into routine monitoring and emergency procedures via defined roles, SOPs, and data-sharing agreements. It is expected to scale by adding more sensor locations, integrating additional data sources, including weather forecasts, radar, and historical events, and standardising deployment as a repeatable package comprising hardware, software and training. Over time, VodostAI can be expanded to national coverage and adapted for related risks such as flash floods, landslides, and drought monitoring. Results, outcomes and impacts The main results are a working VodostAI prototype, comprising sensor data ingestion, AI forecasting and an alert dashboard, validated on historical flood events. Performance has been measured through back-testing against observed river levels, tracking forecast error and warning lead time versus baseline approaches. In future pilots, we expect earlier warnings, with a target of 2–12 additional hours of lead time where conditions allow, fewer false alarms, and faster response coordination. Impact will be monitored via operational logs, including alerts issued and acted on, event reviews, and reductions in reported damage and disruption in covered areas.

title: AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service 2025-27
description: The Government of Canada has used AI for many years. The recent explosion of AI capabilities demanded a coordinated approach to enable the government to benefit from AI while mitigating its risks. The AI Strategy was intended to ensure that the government’s AI adoption and use: Is aligned with the government’s values and ethics, objectives, and mandate to serve Canadians Prioritises uses that will meet the needs of and deliver the greatest benefits to public servants and those they serve Is developed efficiently and collaboratively with internal and external partners Is responsible, safe, and secure, mitigating threats, risks, and harms to people and the environment By responsibly adopting AI, the government can deliver world-class services to its clients, protect people and interests, achieve a more innovative and efficient workplace, and accelerate scientific discovery for the benefit of all. Results, outcomes and impacts The AI Strategy received positive feedback following its publication in 2025. Results are measured by progress made toward the key actions outlined in the AI Strategy. Teams across the federal government were tasked with completing and monitoring progress toward certain actions. Some completed key actions include the publication of a register of AI uses, the scaling of a secure machine translation project (GCtranslate) and collaboration on common capabilities with G7 governments. The AI Strategy is expected to result in increased AI use to support internal operations and service delivery, creating service improvements and operating efficiencies. Challenges and lessons learned The broad scope of programmes, services, department sizes, and AI readiness and maturity was challenging to address in a single strategy. This was addressed by including departments in its drafting and implementation. Preserving public trust in AI is another challenge. To address this, the government held public consultations on the Strategy, incorporating the findings in the Strategy in items such as the AI register. Developing the AI Strategy in the open, with ample public consultation, was a lesson learned. The team held in-person and virtual meetings with stakeholders, partners and AI experts across the country. This transparency resulted in a strategy that met public expectation.

title: Generative AI Literacy Programme
description: The Generative AI Literacy Programme at Anatel addresses the need to build practical skills and responsible habits for using generative AI in everyday public‑sector work. It responds to growing demand from civil servants for guidance on how to use these tools safely, ethically and effectively in real workflows. ​ The initiative offers workshops on prompting and good practices, an institutional Prompt Gallery, and governance guidance on risk mitigation in AI use. Its objectives are to develop essential digital competencies, promote responsible and ethical AI use, and support the adoption of AI in concrete tasks such as drafting and analysing texts. ​ Over time, the programme is expected to become part of regular capacity‑building and onboarding activities, expanding to more teams and use cases within the agency and potentially to other public bodies. Its modular, low‑cost design and close connection with existing tools such as SEI IA make it suitable for gradual scaling and institutionalisation as AI becomes more embedded in public administration. Results, outcomes and impacts The programme has led to high participation in workshops and growing use of the institutional Prompt Gallery, especially in conjunction with SEI IA, supporting safer and more efficient text and analysis tasks. Results are observed through user feedback and evidence of productivity gains in drafting and reviewing documents. In the future, the initiative is expected to further improve digital skills, strengthen responsible AI practices and support wider, more effective use of AI across the organisation and potentially other public bodies. Challenges and lessons learned A key challenge has been addressing risks related to privacy, bias and over‑reliance on AI, while motivating staff to change habits and adopt new tools. These risks are managed through clear governance guidelines, emphasis on human supervision and continuous training focused on safe, ethical use. Lessons learned include the importance of simple, hands‑on activities, concrete examples linked to real workflows and alignment with existing systems such as SEI IA. Conditions for success include leadership support, a clear policy framework, low‑cost and modular design, and ongoing opportunities for feedback and learning.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence Models in the Qualitative Evaluation of Responses - Avalia
description: The National Telecommunications Agency (Anatel) has sought to improve the relationship between consumers and regulated service providers, using advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) to analyse and evaluate the handling of consumer complaints through the Anatel Consumidor system. The main issue that the AvalIA system seeks to resolve is the need for a more assertive, efficient, and transparent diagnosis of how companies respond to consumer complaints, ensuring compliance with regulatory standards and promoting information quality in the sector. In addition, the initiative aims to take advantage of the opportunity to automate processes that currently depend on manual human analysis, making monitoring more robust and comprehensive. The objectives of the AvalIA initiative are clear and specific: to automate the process of Qualitative Response Assessment (AQR) by providers to consumer complaints, estimate the subjects of complaints, identify the enabled information indicators, and verify that these indicators have been properly addressed. This is expected to improve the effectiveness of resolving demands, increase transparency, and encourage continuous improvement in service delivery through each provider's Information Quality Index (IQI). The tool also ensures the anonymisation of personal data, guaranteeing the protection of sensitive consumer information. The expectation is that AvalIA initiative will evolve into a fully implemented and institutionalised system within Anatel, enabling the automated assessment of all complaints registered in the Anatel Consumidor system. This will allow for the inclusion of a larger number of providers in the process, faster assessments and more timely diagnoses, contributing to a more efficient and transparent regulatory environment. The tool can be expanded to cover other types of demands and indicators, as well as adapted to other complaint databases in the regulated sector, maximising its impact and reach. In summary, AvalIA represents a significant innovation in the way Anatel monitors and evaluates providers' response to consumer demands. By incorporating AI into the qualitative assessment process, the Agency strengthens the diagnosis of information quality, ensures compliance with consumer rights, and promotes the continuous improvement of services provided, consolidating itself as a benchmark for transparency and regulatory efficiency in the telecommunications sector.

title: AI-Based Linking of Ombudsman Submissions to Public Services
description: Fala.BR is the single-entry platform for ombudsman submissions to Brazil’s Federal Executive Branch. All federal institutions operate their ombudsman units through this centralised system, which has received more than five million submissions in the past five years. Despite this scale, fewer than 3% of submissions are currently linked to a specific public service. Without this connection, citizen reports cannot be systematically used to assess service performance or identify concrete opportunities for improvement from the user’s perspective. Manual classification at this scale is not feasible. The initiative seeks to automatically identify which public service each submission refers to and tag it in a structured way. By linking citizen messages to specific services, the solution enables targeted analysis of recurring problems, unmet expectations and service delivery gaps. This supports evidence-based improvements and reduces the distance between service users and service managers. As the central body of the Federal Executive Branch Ombudsman System (SisOuv), the Office of the Comptroller General (CGU) has system-wide visibility over submissions and is uniquely positioned to implement this solution. The AI model uses both official service descriptions from the Gov.BR portal and the text written by citizens to establish the most relevant match. The initiative covers both historical data and new submissions. It is being integrated into the Fala.BR platform so that, at the time of registration, citizens receive suggestions of the public service most closely related to their message, which they can confirm or adjust. This structured linkage will enable all federal institutions to access service-level analytics, strengthening monitoring, service evaluation and continuous improvement. The initiative complies with Brazil’s General Data Protection Law and existing ombudsman regulatory frameworks. Results, outcomes and impacts The AI model was validated on more than 61,000 ombudsman submissions across 227 public services, achieving 81% top-1 and 89% top-2 accuracy in service matching. For high-volume services (over 1,000 submissions), accuracy reaches 95.9%. Results are already used internally by CGU to support oversight and service monitoring. Once the five-million historical backlog is classified and real-time tagging is implemented, federal institutions will gain structured visibility into how citizen submissions relate to their services, strengthening evidence-based service improvement.

title: ANALIA: AI for Data Extraction and Analysis in Transport Infrastructure Supervision
description: The ANALIA initiative emerged in response to a critical operational problem in the supervision process of emergency maintenance of concessioned road infrastructure. In this process, the Supervisory Agency for Investment in Public Transport Infrastructure (OSITRAN) must analyse, within strict contractual deadlines, the information submitted by concessionaires to support the execution of activities such as the removal and transport of materials resulting from landslides and slope failures. This information is provided through heterogeneous PDF documents, including both handwritten records (Daily Dump Truck Transport Control Reports – PDCTV) and structured digital documents (Emergency Notification Forms – FNE). Until 2024, the extraction and incorporation of data into a structured database, as well as the processing and analysis of these documents, were carried out manually, generating a high operational burden, risk of errors, and bottlenecks in the issuance of technical decisions. In response, OSITRAN designed and implemented ANALIA as a solution based on artificial intelligence and process automation, using exclusively the tools available within its institutional environment, primarily Microsoft Office 365. The initiative integrates artificial intelligence models capable of capturing relevant data from both handwritten and digital documents, automated workflows to incorporate data into previously defined structures and process them, as well as mechanisms that automatically apply technical validation criteria established by the institution’s supervision teams. In this way, information is transformed into reliable and traceable data that directly supports technical analysis and regulatory decision-making. The main objectives of ANALIA are to significantly reduce the manual work associated with data registration and analysis, improve the operational efficiency of the supervisory team, strengthen process traceability, and ensure timely compliance with contractual deadlines. Additionally, the initiative seeks to free up technical specialists’ time so they can focus on higher-value-added tasks, such as in-depth analysis and comprehensive evaluation of contractual compliance. The initiative is currently operational and has demonstrated concrete results in terms of efficiency and quality within the supervision process. ANALIA has been designed with a modular and scalable approach, enabling its institutionalisation and potential replication across other concessions and supervision processes facing similar documentary information management challenges. In the future, the model may be expanded to other areas of OSITRAN’s supervisory function.

title: Impact Assessment Helper
description: Konsekvenshjälpen (“Impact Assessment Helper”) is a public-sector AI assistant which is responsible for guidance and training on regulatory impact assessments under the new Impact Assessment Ordinance (SFS 2024:183). We launched the service as a web-based prototype in 2025 to complement written guidance on the web and to provide on-demand, situation-specific support. The assistant supports civil servants and inquiry teams across government throughout the impact assessment workflow: framing the problem and objectives, planning the work, proposing and comparing policy options (including the “do nothing” option), identifying affected stakeholders, selecting suitable analytical methods, suggesting data sources, and reviewing drafts for clarity and compliance. title: Panoramic for the Conference on Social Protection for French Citizens Abroad
description: Objectives: To democratise access to information on a complex subject (international social protection) by offering all citizens a simple, clear and reliable tool for understanding the issues at stake; to promote informed citizen participation by allowing everyone to ask questions freely and obtain contextualised answers from public and verified sources; and to strengthen the inclusiveness of public debate by involving French citizens living outside France—who are often distant from participatory processes—in an innovative, transparent and accessible approach. Results, outcomes and impacts Panoramic has logged 963 total queries: 560 open-ended questions (58.2%). Some users conducted extended exchanges (more than 20 questions), indicating deeper exploration needs. The platform supported targeted, mostly on-topic information seeking and provided source-grounded answers based exclusively on the CNDP-validated corpus. Reported impacts include access to reliable information for hundreds of citizens, an innovative way to equip large-scale public debates, and making the topic more accessible, widening participation and giving a voice to people who often feel excluded. Measurement relies on platform analytics (volumes, open versus click-based actions, session depth) and answer-versus-no-answer categorisation by theme. Challenges and lessons learned Key risks and challenges included (1) handling questions outside the validated scope; and (2) addressing legitimate but sensitive or interpretive questions (feelings of unfairness, complex personal situations) that a strictly document-based assistant cannot always resolve. The response was to answer only from the CNDP-validated corpus and to refuse to answer when content fell outside it, avoiding approximations and reinforcing trust. Lessons learned: users often arrive with concrete personal questions and may engage in long conversational exploration, so the tool must support both quick Q&A and deep dives; credibility depends as much on knowing when not to answer as on answering well; and “critical” prompts need dedicated handling distinct from information requests. Conditions for success: a high-quality knowledge base, clear scope boundaries, and continuous monitoring of question types to keep answers clear, contextualised and verifiable.

title: Agroboost
description: Results, outcomes and impacts Agroboost is currently in its implementation phase. We are working with approximately 100 agricultural producers, training them in the use of Internet of Things (IoT) devices and basic data analysis to improve farm management and productivity. Progress is being monitored through participation rates, technology adoption levels, and improvements in decision-making practices. By 2026, the initiative is expected to expand to additional regions, scaling its impact and increasing the number of trained producers. Challenges and lessons learned Key challenges include a generational gap in digital skills and a gender gap that limits women’s participation. Many women producers are also primary caregivers, which restricts their ability to attend training sessions. Additional barriers include limited connectivity and initial resistance to adopting new technologies. To address these issues, the programme has adapted training formats, introduced flexible schedules, and promoted inclusive outreach strategies. Lessons learned highlight the importance of contextualised training, trust-building, and gender-sensitive design. Long-term success requires sustained technical support, local partnerships, and policies that reduce structural barriers to participation.

title: BolognAI - Urban Intelligence (Subnational: Bologna)
description: The Municipality of Bologna has framed responsible AI governance as a system of operational safeguards, rather than as a stand-alone pilot project. The objective is to balance speed of experimentation with robust control: before implementation, every AI initiative must be underpinned by adequate data, explicit accountability, the appropriate level of involvement, a risk assessment, and safeguards for citizens and employees. To avoid an approach that is either too slow (top-down) or too uneven (bottom-up), a hybrid model has been adopted (centralised and Hub & Spoke). A central co-ordination function defines shared standards and common approval gates (prioritisation criteria, risk levels, minimum requirements for data/security/transparency), while the identification and structured analysis of needs remain the responsibility of operational units to ensure alignment with day-to-day processes. Strategic oversight and final decision-making are ensured by the Integrated Directorate, which safeguards overall coherence. Key roles and functions are defined in the PDF file “organisational model roles and responsibilities ENG”: AI Ambassadors; Transformation Demand; AI Transformation Room; and BIS (Bologna Innovation Square). In addition, assets such as the Civic Digital Twin strengthen synergies for AI use in areas such as simulation and decision support, providing infrastructure and methodologies for data governance and for addressing ethical and regulatory challenges (e.g., a technical–regulatory sandbox). The model is designed to mature over time. Following an initial survey of around 4,000 people to map AI knowledge and perceptions, core governance capabilities (risk and impact assessment, use-case portfolio management) are expected to be progressively internalised. At the outset, these capabilities can be activated externally (via the AI Transformation Room) to accelerate delivery. As organisational maturity advances, a gradual decentralisation of responsibilities is envisaged. The operational core is an end-to-end process covering the lifecycle of AI initiatives (with a RACI and standardised deliverables): Intake and validation: request form, expected KPIs, data mapping, initial risk classification and assessment of alternatives (reuse, build/buy); Controlled experimentation: PoC with acceptance criteria, quality/robustness testing, checks on security/privacy/bias, and definition of human oversight; Go-live and scaling: go-live checklist, model/supplier register, continuous monitoring of performance and drift, incident logging, and periodic reviews. The demand phase is complemented by engagement actions (targeted training, guidelines, AI Ambassador communities) to embed compliance and responsibility directly into behaviours, making risk and data-assessment safeguards stable requirements integrated into the organisation’s ordinary pathways.

title: Rio de Janeiro State Artificial Intelligence Policy (Subnational: State of Rio de Janeiro)
description: Política de Inteligência Artificial Fluminense (PIAF) is Rio de Janeiro State’s public policy for artificial intelligence and data. It sets guidelines to strengthen the local AI ecosystem, improve public data management, and guide the ethical development, procurement, and use of data- and AI-based solutions in government. The initiative responds to both a problem and an opportunity. The State needs clear rules, responsibilities, and safeguards to use AI in a transparent, rights-respecting, and legally compliant way, while also using data and AI to improve services, public decisions, accessibility, and administrative capacity. PIAF also creates an implementation structure. It defines responsibilities for central, technical, and sectoral bodies; establishes monitoring through expected results, indicators, and targets; and creates practical instruments such as sector plans, training tracks, maturity assessments, ethical impact self-assessments, and digital systems for projects, data use, and solution mapping. It also creates two participatory and governance bodies: the AI Forum, which brings together government, universities, civil society, and the private sector to support the State’s AI ecosystem, and CEIA-RJ, a consultative council that helps guide the ethical use of AI in government. Over time, PIAF is expected to evolve through implementation across government, complementary rules, public monitoring, and periodic review as technology and regulation change. Results, outcomes and impacts So far, PIAF’s main results have been institutional and participatory: Rio de Janeiro created a Technical Working Group under the State Data Governance Committee, prepared the draft decree, formally instituted PIAF, the AI Forum and CEIA-RJ through State Decree No. 50.523 of 13 October 2026, and linked the policy to the State Digital Government Strategy. The process also engaged multiple sectors through a citizen perception survey, digital public consultation, formal consultation with state bodies, and about 20 expert interviews. Progress has been measured through policy design and governance methods; future impact is expected through implementation, public monitoring, and key performance indicators (KPIs), indicators, and targets.

title: JOSEIAS – AI Assistant for Administrative Processes in SEI (Electronic Information System) (Subnational: Municipality of Pedro Leopoldo)
description: JOSEIAS was developed to address the complexity of administrative procedures faced by public servants, particularly in Brazil’s Electronic Information System (SEI). Many government employees struggle with limited training, fragmented information, and time-consuming processes, which can lead to delays and inefficiencies in public service delivery. The initiative leverages artificial intelligence to provide real-time support, making administrative tasks more accessible and reducing dependence on manual support channels. It was developed using existing infrastructure and intellectual capital, leveraging Google Gemini, with no additional implementation costs. The main objective of JOSEIAS is to improve the efficiency and quality of administrative processes by empowering public servants with accessible, on-demand guidance. The system supports users with answers to procedural questions, step-by-step assistance, and access to personalised training materials, as well as local regulations and official documents. By doing so, it enhances staff autonomy, reduces errors, and contributes to more consistent and reliable public service delivery. The initiative is designed to be scalable and adaptable across different government contexts. While initially implemented within the Municipality of Pedro Leopoldo, JOSEIAS can be extended to other municipalities and public institutions that face similar challenges. Future developments include expanding its knowledge base, integrating with additional government systems, and strengthening its role as a continuous learning and support tool for public servants. Over time, JOSEIAS has evolved from a support solution into a broader model for AI adoption in local government, focusing on augmenting human capabilities rather than replacing them. It represents a practical approach to digital transformation, where AI is used to simplify processes, build institutional knowledge, and improve the overall effectiveness of public administration. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has improved the speed and consistency of administrative support by providing real-time guidance to public servants, currently reaching around 250 SEI users in the Municipality of Pedro Leopoldo. It is the first AI assistant of its kind implemented in the state of Minas Gerais, which has over 850 municipalities, and has reduced reliance on human support and increased staff autonomy. The initiative was highlighted at the SEI Municipalities Meeting in Minas Gerais, recognised at the Digital Cities Forum and presented at the IV ProPEN Network Meeting (2026). Results have been observed through user feedback and reduced support demand, with expected future gains in efficiency and scalability.

title: JULIO (AI PLATFORM)
description: The JULIO AI Platform is Peru's most ambitious digital transformation project in the public sector, designed to enhance registry services using artificial intelligence. Rather than replacing human judgment, it serves as a tool to optimise legal processes through three main pillars: Pillar 1: Specialised Consultation Modules: Use natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) to provide structured access to decades of legal precedents, technical resolutions, and plenary agreements. Pillar 2: Learning and Study Centre: Provides practical resources for staff, including AI manuals, optimised prompt libraries, and adaptive templates. It features an automated generator for official observation and rejection notices (esquelas) to ensure compliance with standards. Pillar 3: Integrated AI Access: Offers direct access to major AI applications with specialised guides tailored to specific registry contexts. Results, outcomes and impacts The main outcomes of the JULIO AI Platform are: a. Drastic time reduction: Decreasing the drafting time of registry entries from approximately 5 minutes to less than 45 seconds. b. Process standardisation: Ensuring that all registrars apply uniform criteria, regardless of their registry zone or level of experience. c. Error minimisation: Reducing errors of omission through tools that identify relevant data that might be overlooked during manual reviews. d. Capacity-building: Training registry staff in advanced digital competencies through the Learning and Study Centre. e. Citizen service improvement: Faster registrations without compromising technical quality, clearer and more complete observation notices (esquelas), and more complete responses. Challenges and lessons learned Implementation challenges: a. Resistance to change: Overcoming initial distrust of disruptive technologies through voluntary and collaborative adoption strategies. b. Training over 1,000 public servants across 14 registry zones with varying levels of technological familiarity. c. Effective prompt design: Developing methodologies so staff learn how to "converse" with the AI to obtain technically accurate responses. d. Template validation: Ensuring that entry (asiento) and observation (esquela) templates maintain the required legal precision. e. Technological integration: Co-ordinating the development and implementation of APIs and systems with the Information Technology Office. Lessons learned: a. Voluntary adoption works better than top-down imposition: Early adopters were enthusiastic volunteers who later became informal trainers for their colleagues.

title: Galileo (Subnational: Rio Grande do Sul)
description: The Galileu initiative was developed by the Regional Labor Court of the 4th Region (TRT-RS), in Brazil, to address procedural delays and workload pressures resulting from the large volume and complexity of judicial cases. Drafting decisions and conducting legal research require significant time and involve repetitive tasks, which contribute to delays in the delivery of justice. Galileu uses generative artificial intelligence to read case files, organise the issues in dispute, produce structured draft decisions, and provide reliable legal references, contributing to greater efficiency and legal certainty. The main objective of the initiative is to increase productivity and improve the quality of judicial decisions by reducing bureaucratic steps and allowing judges and staff to focus on more complex analytical work. The tool generates original content from case files, summarises the parties’ arguments, and suggests legal reasoning based on a closed and validated database, reducing the risk of inaccurate outputs. All suggestions remain fully editable, preserving judicial autonomy and the individualised analysis of each case. The solution was designed with strong attention to information security, data protection, and the mitigation of risks associated with generative AI. Data are anonymised, securely transmitted, and processed within a controlled environment, while the use of validated legal sources reduces the risk of “hallucinations.” Development followed a collaborative approach involving judges and technical teams, with gradual implementation and user training to ensure safe and effective use. Galileu has been institutionalised as a national tool within the Labor Justice system and continues to evolve to support different stages of judicial work. Adopted by the Superior Council of Labor Justice (CSJT) and made available to all Regional Labor Courts, the system is already in use, in addition to TRT-RS, by several other courts. Its expansion to the second instance now supports appellate judges and their teams in drafting decisions and organising procedural information, and the solution has also been extended to assist in the analysis of review appeals, structuring rulings and indicating relevant content based on prior decisions and case documents. This evolution demonstrates the maturity of the initiative, its adaptability to different stages of judicial proceedings, and its potential to strengthen efficiency, standardisation, and legal certainty, while laying the groundwork for future integration within the digital ecosystem of the Labor Justice system.

title: AI in Tender Evaluations
description: The Digital Marketplace Panel 2 (DMP2) supports Australian Government procurement of digital and ICT services. Evaluating supplier submissions for DMP2 involves reviewing large volumes of structured and unstructured information against defined criteria, which can be time consuming and resource intensive. The DTA is using an AI enabled tool to support evaluators by providing a check of an assessment as an AI check tool. The capability is used strictly as decision support and does not make automated recommendations or determinations. The objectives are to improve evaluation efficiency, promote greater consistency across assessment teams, and enable evaluators to focus more time on professional judgement, risk assessment and value for money considerations. Results, outcomes and impacts: The initiative is focused on testing feasibility and usability rather than delivering measurable efficiency gains. Initial observations suggest AI support may assist evaluators to navigate large and complex submissions and identify areas requiring closer review. Challenges and lessons learned: Key challenges include managing information security and privacy, avoiding overreliance on AI outputs, and ensuring alignment with procurement and probity requirements. These risks are mitigated by limiting AI use to decision support, requiring human validation of all outputs, and maintaining clear audit trails. A key lesson is that strong governance, clear guidance for evaluators, and careful prompt design and testing are essential. Success depends on transparency, human oversight, and clear communication that AI does not replace professional judgement.

title: Trending Topics in Ombudsman Submissions
description: Trending Topics in Ombudsman Submissions was developed to address the difficulty of summarising, in clear and comprehensive themes, the content of ombudsman submissions received by Brazilian Federal Executive Branch entities through the Fala.BR platform. Although the platform includes structured classification fields—such as type, subject and sub-subject—these are initially filled in by citizens, who may not be familiar with government structures and therefore often classify their submissions inaccurately. In addition, these predefined categories are not detailed enough to fully capture the issues raised. The most relevant information is contained in an open-text field, written in free form by citizens with diverse educational backgrounds and language styles. Given the high number of submissions received, it is not feasible for small ombudsman teams to manually produce aggregated and meaningful analyses that accurately reflect public concerns and their intensity. At the same time, the centralisation of all Federal Executive Branch ombudsman submissions within the Fala.BR platform—maintained and managed by the Office of the Comptroller General (CGU)—creates a unique opportunity for centralised access and large-scale analytical processing of this citizen feedback. The primary objective of Trending Topics is to identify common themes within the textual content of ombudsman submissions and to monitor how these themes evolve over time, including detecting sudden increases in related complaints or concerns. The initiative aims to strengthen the State’s capacity to listen to society in a structured way, to improve coordination and timeliness in government responses, and ultimately to enhance public trust in government institutions. Currently, the solution is used by the Office of the Ombudsman General (OGU) within the CGU (1) to produce periodic analytical reports for federal ombudsman units, (2) for its own supervisory activities, and (3) for senior leadership to monitor strategic public policies and services. In the future, the tool will be integrated directly into the Fala.BR platform, enabling individual ombudsman units to autonomously access and use the analytical functionality. The initiative is institutionally supported by Brazil’s General Data Protection Law (Law No. 13.709/2018), the Public Service User Protection Law (Law No. 13.460/2017), and Decree No. 9.492/2018, which established the Federal Executive Branch Ombudsman System.

title: Guidelines on using generative artificial intelligence to support and assist work in public administration
description: AI is here to stay, and not only does public administration need to keep informed about the changes reshaping our world, but it also needs to exploit these opportunities safely. AI is expected to increase the productivity of public administration in many ways. Functions where generative AI could bring productivity benefits include service provision, generation of knowledge and information, tools for sorting and summarising data, and process automation. AI could help information systems function more intelligently and offer more personalised services to improve user experience. AI can be programmed to work in partnership with people, and it can be developed to meet people’s needs. This guideline aims foremost to encourage ordinary civil servants as well as management to educate themselves, experiment with AI and consider the possibilities both in daily work and in administrative processes. The guideline is very high-level and is being used in public organisations as a starting point for more detailed instructions and guidelines. The guideline introduces and illustrates fundamental AI terms and concepts in order to help establish a common language for the public sector. Results, outcomes and impacts The guideline has been widely referenced and used in the Finnish public sector. As of today, the terms and vocabulary defined at the time can be seen as pioneering work. Challenges and lessons learned The guideline document is now one year old. The world around us has changed a lot and technological development has been fast (for example, AI agents were not properly addressed in the guideline). Even though the guideline is very high-level and does not go into detail, there will be an apparent need to critically examine the purpose and content of the guideline, since civil servants are increasingly familiar with basic concepts of AI. It is evident that AI is increasingly becoming part of civil servants’ everyday work.

title: AI Accelerator Program (Subnational: North Carolina)
description: The AI Accelerator programme promotes responsible use of artificial intelligence within government agencies by identifying urgent needs and demonstrating how AI can improve daily operations. Established by the Office of Artificial Intelligence and Policy at the North Carolina Department of Information Technology through an Executive Order issued by Governor Josh Stein on 2 September 2025, the programme has collected use cases from 15 state entities to explore AI-driven solutions. Its goal is to foster innovation, streamline processes, and enhance public service delivery. Each use case undergoes rigorous evaluation for feasibility, impact, and ethics using 32 criteria focused on public value, technical viability, and risk mitigation. The Office of Artificial Intelligence and Policy ensures data carries minimal risk and excludes personal citizen information. After initial review, submissions are vetted by two boards: one within the North Carolina Department of Information Technology (including Enterprise Security and Risk Management Office, Enterprise Architecture Office, Enterprise Collaboration Services Office, Legal Office, and Communications Office) and the AI Executive Leadership Committee, which includes the State Chief Information Officer and the Chief Operating Officer for the Office of the Governor. This multi-tiered process guarantees alignment with state objectives and ethical standards. Approved projects often involve vendor collaboration under a no-cost participation agreement that mandates responsible data handling and compliance. Once a vendor is selected, agencies engage in a 60-day sprint where problems are defined, data shared, and prototypes developed. Vendors provide hands-on testing opportunities, while the Office of Artificial Intelligence and Policy tracks success metrics and ensures compliance. At the end of the engagement, stakeholders review outcomes and decide on full-scale implementation. Vendor partnerships are central to success, offering technical expertise and innovative solutions that agencies might not otherwise access. title: AI Vision for Slovakia: Path to Digital Sovereignty and Efficiency
description: The "AI Vision for Slovakia" is a strategic framework responding to the "cognitive revolution" where AI becomes critical infrastructure. The initiative is driven by the urgent need for fiscal consolidation and the collapse of available skilled labour, positioning AI not as a luxury but as a necessity for state functionality. The strategy is built on six pillars: Infrastructure & AI Factories: Leveraging Slovakia’s competitive advantage in carbon-free energy (nuclear and hydro) to build data centres and AI computing hubs. Effective Public Administration: Moving from simple digitisation to automation. The strategy rejects building expensive foundation models from scratch, opting instead for a "sovereign adaptation layer"—secure fine-tuning of global models on state data. Economic Growth: Supporting the transition of industry to Industry 4.0 and aiding companies in moving from basic digitisation to AI adoption. Society & Ethics: Focusing on child protection in the online space and countering deepfakes. Education: Developing talent and adapting curricula for the AI era. International Co-operation: Active participation in EU initiatives (AI Factories, EuroHPC) to secure funding and computing power. A crucial component is the reform of governance. The initiative ends "departmental feudalism" by centralising methodological guidance and procurement under MIRRI SR to eliminate duplication and enforce interoperability. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative began with a comprehensive audit of state readiness in late 2025. Expected outcomes include the establishment of AI Factories using Slovakia's carbon-free energy and the deployment of a "sovereign adaptation layer" for secure government AI use. The strategy targets the automation of administrative processes to counter labour shortages and the creation of a centralised governance model to eliminate duplicate spending. Long-term impacts focus on digital sovereignty, increased GDP through AI adoption and enhanced protection of minors in the digital space. Challenges and lessons learned A major challenge identified is "departmental feudalism" and fragmented IT spending, where ministries previously built incompatible isolated solutions. The strategy addresses this by enforcing centralised methodological guidance and joint procurement. Another hurdle is the "data debt" (unstructured/low-quality data), which requires cleaning before AI deployment. The initiative explicitly rejects the costly "greenfield" development of foundation models, opting instead for a cost-effective "sovereign adaptation layer" (fine-tuning). Lessons learned emphasise that without centralised co-ordination and interoperability, public funds are wasted on incompatible systems.

title: AVAIL (Anomaly Validation using AI Learning) - Bridge Anomaly Detection Project
description: AVAIL addresses the challenge of extracting reliable insight from large volumes of time-series data generated by bridge monitoring systems. As sensor networks expand, sensor anomalies make manual data review time-consuming and reduce the data’s usefulness for engineering analysis and long-term planning. The initiative improves the quality and usability of structural health monitoring data by applying semi-supervised machine learning methods for anomaly detection and data cleaning. It isolates unreliable observations, producing cleaner datasets that support downstream structural integrity assessment, safety oversight and infrastructure lifespan extension. Developed by the Data Science and Major Bridges and Projects teams at HICC, AVAIL is expected to evolve by expanding to additional sensor types, increasing automation and integrating with analytical dashboards to strengthen data-driven analysis and eventual infrastructure decision-making. Results, outcomes and impacts The AI system enabled faster and more systematic identification of anomalous sensor readings, reducing reliance on manual data screening. By automating anomaly detection, the project improved consistency and traceability in how atypical data points are flagged and reviewed, producing higher-quality datasets in significantly less time. Overall, these results demonstrate AVAIL’s effectiveness in isolating data quality issues within large-scale sensor datasets. The cleaned outputs provide higher-quality data, forming a stronger analytical foundation for future assessments of structural integrity and long-term infrastructure management. Challenges and lessons learned Data labelling effort; sensor heterogeneity; and the importance of explainability and human oversight in safety-critical systems.

title: AI assistant of the Chancellery of the Riigikogu
description: The initiative was developed to address challenges in accessing and working with parliamentary and legislative information within the Estonian Government Office. Officials and legal experts regularly need to navigate large volumes of documents across multiple systems, including draft laws, background materials and prior inquiries. These tasks were previously handled manually, making the process time-consuming and difficult to manage, especially when responding to time-sensitive requests. The project uses advances in artificial intelligence to improve how this information is accessed, processed and used in daily work. The primary objective is to improve the efficiency and quality of legislative support processes by introducing an in-house AI assistant. The solution enables users to locate relevant parliamentary documents, ask structured questions about draft laws and related materials, and receive answers supported by references to source documents. By improving access to information and reducing manual workload, it supports more informed decision-making and more efficient internal workflows. The AI assistant is designed to be secure and aligned with government requirements, ensuring appropriate handling of sensitive information. It integrates with existing document systems and draws on multiple data sources, including legislative databases and related materials. The system is continuously improved based on user feedback and evolving needs, while also supporting capacity-building by enabling officials to use AI tools in their daily work. Looking ahead, the initiative is expected to be further embedded within the Government Office and potentially extended to other public-sector organisations with similar needs. Future development may include expanded functionality, integration with additional data sources and greater automation of routine tasks. Over time, the approach could inform wider use of AI to improve knowledge access and administrative efficiency across government. Results, outcomes and impacts The AI assistant has improved how officials access and analyse parliamentary information, replacing manual and time-consuming document searches with faster, more structured queries. User feedback indicates reduced effort in handling information requests and preparing legislative materials. Impacts have been assessed through qualitative feedback and observed usage patterns rather than formal quantitative measurement. Initial results suggest improved efficiency and more consistent access to information. Over time, the initiative is expected to further reduce administrative workload and expand functionality, including potential wider access.

title: Automated documentation
description: The initiative addresses administrative burdens and the risk of errors in manual documentation, journaling and minute-taking in municipalities and regions. It is expected to increase efficiency in relation to routine record-keeping tasks, thereby freeing up officials’ time for more complex tasks and citizen services. The objectives are to increase efficiency and accuracy in documentation processes, ensure timely documentation and enhance transparency and auditability across public bodies. A further objective is to test usability and governance requirements for the responsible use of AI in the municipalities and regions. If the use of AI for documentation tasks proves successful, then the initiative is expected to scale across municipalities and regions beyond the initial project participants and use cases. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative is still in an early phase; thus, no results have been observed so far. The goal of the initiative is that more than 50 municipalities will test AI assistants to help with documentation in relation to the employment sector. Additionally, more than 30 municipalities are expected to test AI assistants to help with documentation in relation to the healthcare sector. Finally, all four Danish regions are expected to test at least one use case where AI assistants are used in documentation-related tasks. Challenges and lessons learned The main challenges faced by the initiative relate to data, technology and organisational factors. Insufficient data or data of insufficient quality will make it challenging to train AI systems with the desired levels of accuracy and precision for tasks related to automated documentation. Closely related to this, even if the data is sufficient, there might be technological factors that create implementation challenges for the initiative. This might be a lack of access to AI systems of sufficient quality or a lack of technical resources to implement these systems within the desired public authorities. Additionally, organisational factors may have an effect on how the initiative develops. Without the right organisational setup and a plan for implementing automated documentation in specific processes, the impact could be lower than expected.

title: Alicia — AI-Assisted Severe Weather Detection and Nowcasting for the Caribbean
description: The Meteorological Department Curaçao (MDC) is the designated authority for aviation weather services within the Curaçao Flight Information Region (TNCF), covering approximately 200,000 km² of Caribbean airspace. MDC issues SIGMETs, aerodrome warnings and public severe weather alerts. Forecasters examine satellite imagery across multiple spectral channels, radar reflectivity at several scan levels, lightning observations and numerical weather prediction output, easily exceeding 300 images per analysis cycle. This makes systematic analysis of all data impractical for a single forecaster, and the process relies on subjective selection of which data to examine. Alicia addresses this by training a deep learning model to synthesise satellite observations into radar-equivalent reflectivity maps, extending the physical radar’s 225 km coverage across the entire FIR. The super-resolution U-Net takes 2 km satellite data from GOES-19 infrared, water vapour and lightning channels and produces 0.7 km radar reflectivity predictions, a 3.2× resolution enhancement. Training uses 24,535 co-located satellite-radar observation pairs collected over 211 days. The project has four phases. Phase 1, completed as a proof of concept, demonstrates pseudo-radar generation from satellite data. Phase 2 adds thunderstorm area identification using lightning as labels, validated against ground observations. Phase 3 introduces nowcasting to predict storm evolution 0–6 hours ahead. Phase 4 integrates the model into forecaster workflows to generate draft SIGMETs and warning products in ICAO-compliant formats. A Memorandum of Understanding with Blue NAP Americas provides GPU training infrastructure comprising four NVIDIA L40S units. Phase 2 continues this partnership with expanded datasets and revised training strategies. Curaçao’s C-band dual-polarisation radar has a historical archive extending back to 2015, with potential to support hydrometeor classification and hail detection. Central to the project is a meteorological training data lake: a versioned repository bringing government satellite, radar, lightning and numerical weather prediction data into a unified format optimised for AI training. Hosted on Blue NAP infrastructure, it enables Alicia to be trained in specialised modes as new data sources are incorporated. The initiative benefits aviation (improved SIGMETs, reduced weather-related delays), marine operations (search and rescue), public safety (earlier severe weather warnings), and regional meteorological research.

title: AI Community Juries and National Civic AI Governance Framework (ENIA)
description: The initiative addresses the growing gap between the technical deployment of artificial intelligence in the public sector and the social legitimacy of its use. While public administrations increasingly rely on AI for decision support, service delivery, and resource allocation, citizens often have limited visibility into how these systems affect rights, access to services, and fairness. The project creates a structured civic layer that complements legal and technical compliance with social and institutional evaluation. Its core objective is to integrate trained community panels into public-sector AI governance processes. These panels review real AI use cases, datasets, and deployment scenarios in collaboration with public authorities and technical experts. Their work results in formal reports and recommendations that support public procurement, regulatory sandbox activities, and ongoing monitoring of AI systems in sensitive domains such as urban management, social services, healthcare, and education. The initiative is designed to align with existing regulatory and standards-based approaches, including risk-based governance models under the EU AI Act, data protection impact assessments, and international AI management and risk frameworks. By doing so, it provides public institutions with a practical way to connect formal compliance requirements with public understanding and trust, helping to reduce institutional, legal, and reputational risks associated with AI deployment. Over time, the framework is intended to scale through partnerships with municipalities, regional authorities, and national bodies. Standardised training modules, evaluation templates, and reporting formats allow the model to be replicated across different jurisdictions. The long-term goal is to institutionalise civic review as a regular component of public-sector AI governance, supporting more transparent, accountable, and socially grounded use of artificial intelligence. Results, outcomes and impacts The first community juries were launched in October 2025 and have generated strong citizen engagement and institutional interest at the local level. Early results include the production of structured civic impact reports and formal recommendations that have been shared with participating public administrations to inform AI-related decisions and pilot projects. Impact is measured through participation rates, diversity of jury composition, number of AI use cases reviewed, and follow-up actions taken by public authorities. Expected future outcomes include expansion to additional municipalities and the development of standard indicators for trust, transparency, and public acceptance of AI in government services.

title: Karnataka Innovation Authority Regulatory Sandbox (Subnational: Karnataka)
description: The initiative by the Karnataka Innovation Authority seeks to address the challenge of regulating rapidly emerging technologies and frontier technologies like AI without stifling innovation. As Karnataka continues to position itself as a leading technology hub, innovators often face regulatory uncertainty while regulators struggle to anticipate and govern complex, evolving use cases of AI and such technologies that cut across different domains and sectors. This sandbox ecosystem aims to resolve this tension by creating a controlled environment where innovative products and services can be tested with temporary regulatory relaxations. This approach leverages Karnataka’s strong start-up and technology ecosystem to promote responsible innovation while ensuring risks are identified and mitigated early on. Additionally, emerging technologies increasingly cut across different domains and sectors like health, finance, mobility, climate, etc. A sector-agnostic regulatory sandbox is therefore essential. It will allow for cross-sector experimentation with a unified oversight mechanism, lowering compliance ambiguity for innovation companies and enabling anticipatory governance for the regulators. The primary objectives of the initiative are threefold. First, it seeks to enable innovators to test new technologies in a live but limited market environment, thereby reducing time-to-market and identifying technical or operational gaps before full-scale deployment. Second, it aims to generate evidence-based insights for regulators by allowing monitoring of sandbox participants and activities to identify risks and pitfalls of new technologies. Third, it fosters collaboration between innovators and regulators, promoting transparency, compliance and trust in the application of emerging technologies. Aapti Institute has been supporting the government through technical inputs on process design and policy in the implementation of the regulatory sandbox. The design of the sandbox framework has been informed by rigorous research, stakeholder consultations and comparative analysis of global best practices for sandboxes. In the future, the initiative is expected to evolve through structured implementation and institutionalisation under the Karnataka Innovation Authority Act. A notified sandbox operator will oversee performance, compliance monitoring and overall administration, ensuring accountability. Over time, learnings from successive sandbox cohorts can be codified into formal regulatory guidelines, standards and best practices. As the model matures, it could scale across sectors by continuously embedding iterative learning into the regulatory process and institutionalising adaptive governance that keeps pace with technological change.

title: Electronic SIN Automation (eSIN)
description: In 2024–25, the Government of Canada (GC), through Service Canada, issued over 2.6 million Social Insurance Numbers (SIN). A SIN is a unique nine-digit number issued by the GC to Canadian citizens, permanent residents and temporary residents with work to enable them to access employment and essential government programmes, services and benefits. Citizens can apply for a SIN in person at a Service Canada Centre, via mail, online (eSIN) or through provincial newborn registration. Until recently, Client Service Officers (CSOs) would process these applications manually through a time-consuming and resource-intensive process. With the manual processing of an eSIN application, it would take five days for a client to receive their SIN versus the same day if they applied in person. To accelerate eSIN processing and encourage online applications, eSIN Automation (eSINa) was developed and launched. It is a custom programme that automates application processing, approval and SIN issuance. eSINa relies on the Document Verification Service (DVS), an artificial intelligence (AI) solution built to automate ID document verification and comparison. The DVS uses optical character recognition (OCR) to extract text from scanned ID documents. Documents are then authenticated using rules-based validation, layout analysis, and logo detection. This new eSINa solution reduces workloads for the SIN programme, while also reducing wait times to minutes. Results, outcomes and impacts In operation since October 2025, the eSINa platform currently supports nine ID documents out of the 12 documents selected for automation, with support for the complete set of ID documents to be available in 2026. Once fully completed, eSINa is anticipated to save thousands of hours of manual processing annually, reduce in-person visits to Service Canada Centres and improve client experience. This initiative contributes to operational efficiencies, modern service delivery, and data innovation. Challenges and lessons learned The project, although still underway, brought together many teams across the organisation to successfully deploy the first releases of eSINa. The OCR performance, measured by word accuracy across various identification documents, is quite consistent at 96.8%. Moving forward, the team is identifying opportunities to adapt and scale up the use of the DVS solution to further improve the processing of information in other programmes. Lessons learned include improving documentation, strengthening communication, adopting more agile practices and involving key stakeholders earlier to design more scalable and clearly scoped solutions.

title: ASAN AI HUB
description: The ASAN AI Hub was established by the Innovation Centre of the State Agency for Public Service and Social Innovations under the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan to serve as a national platform for advancing artificial intelligence development and collaboration. Within a short period since its launch, ASAN AI Hub has built a growing ecosystem for applied and responsible AI. The initiative responds to the growing need for co-ordinated AI ecosystem building, innovation support, and skills development in Azerbaijan. It brings together public institutions, private-sector actors, researchers, start-ups, and individual innovators within a unified digital platform. The Hub operates across four main activity areas: open innovation, research and talent development, business solutions, and AI literacy and skills development. Through open innovation mechanisms, it connects government bodies with technology providers and start-ups to facilitate AI-driven solution development. It supports applied research and international collaboration, fostering knowledge exchange and strengthening institutional AI capabilities. In addition, the platform promotes AI-ready business solutions and integration opportunities while enhancing co-operation with international partners. A strong emphasis is placed on AI education and capacity-building, offering training programmes and learning opportunities to improve AI literacy among public servants, professionals, and the broader community. The ASAN AI Hub is designed to institutionalise AI ecosystem co-ordination within the public sector while maintaining alignment with responsible AI principles. By combining collaboration, experimentation, and skills development, the initiative contributes to strengthening national AI readiness and fostering sustainable AI innovation in public service delivery.

title: AI-Enhanced Forensic Evidence Management Using Wearable Technology (Subnational: Mato Grosso State)
description: This initiative introduces wearable artificial intelligence into forensic workflows within a public forensic laboratory in Brazil. The technology enables continuous audiovisual recording, automatic transcription, and structured organisation of forensic examinations in real time. It was developed to address inefficiencies in traditional forensic processes, which rely heavily on manual documentation and are time-consuming and prone to information loss. The primary objective is to improve the reliability, traceability, and efficiency of forensic evidence production. By integrating AI into the examination process, the initiative enhances documentation quality and supports forensic experts in capturing detailed, contextualised information without interrupting their workflow. This contributes to stronger chain of custody practices and more transparent judicial processes. The initiative is currently active and being progressively expanded within the laboratory. It is expected to evolve through increased adoption, refinement of AI capabilities, and integration with digital forensic systems. The model is scalable and can be replicated across different forensic domains and jurisdictions, particularly in contexts facing high demand and limited human resources. Results, outcomes and impacts Preliminary results based on approximately 55 forensic examinations show significant improvements: up to 67% reduction in examination time, 75% reduction in pre-report preparation time (from 2 hours to 30 minutes), and up to threefold increase in processing capacity per forensic expert. These results were measured through comparative time analysis between traditional and AI-supported workflows. The initiative reduces backlog, improves efficiency, and enhances the reliability and timeliness of forensic evidence delivered to the justice system. Challenges and lessons learned Key challenges included adapting workflows to integrate AI without disrupting established forensic procedures, ensuring data security, and maintaining the central role of the forensic expert in decision-making. Initial resistance to technological change was addressed through training and gradual implementation. Lessons learned highlight the importance of human-centred design, clear governance, and incremental adoption. Successful implementation requires institutional support, capacity-building, and alignment with legal and ethical standards, particularly regarding transparency and accountability in the use of AI.

title: Official Gazette Intelligence (Subnational: Public Management Innovation Consortium)
description: The Public Management Innovation Consortium (CIGA) operates the Municipal Official Gazette (Ciga Diário), a critical transparency tool for over 295 Brazilian municipalities. With more than 100,000 documents published annually by 4,500 different users, manual oversight of every publication was historically impossible. This high volume, combined with the stringent requirements of the Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD) — which is closely modelled after the European Union's GDPR — created a significant risk of privacy breaches and administrative errors. CIGA Diário Intelligence was developed to bridge this gap, leveraging AI to provide a layer of security and intelligence that ensures transparency does not come at the cost of data privacy or legal integrity. Although the Gazette system has successfully operated for over a decade, the integration of artificial intelligence in 2025 marked a transformative evolution. The initiative was catalysed by the need for regulatory compliance, a pro-innovation internal culture, and the increasing accessibility of high-quality AI models. The platform now operates across four strategic pillars: automated privacy analysis to detect sensitive data, AI-generated summaries to improve citizen accessibility, intelligent legislative compilation to track legal impacts, and content integrity monitoring. This shift from a simple PDF repository to an intelligent governance hub allows public managers to handle complex documentation with greater precision. The impact of the initiative is already measurable, particularly in risk mitigation. Previously, responsibility for content accuracy rested solely on individual users, which occasionally led to the publication of incorrect or sensitive information. Today, AI provides real-time moderation. In a recent high-stakes incident, the system demonstrated its value by identifying and blocking malicious publications attempted by a hacker who had compromised user credentials. By acting as a proactive guardian rather than a reactive archive, the tool prevents legal and reputational damage to the municipalities, proving that AI-assisted oversight is essential for modern public administration. Looking ahead, CIGA is focused on the full institutionalisation of these features. While malicious content detection is already active for all users, the remaining functionalities are being phased in, with the goal of 100% adoption by the end of 2026. The current strategic focus is the continuous refinement of these models to ensure maximum reliability and accuracy. By providing this technology as a shared service through a public consortium, CIGA demonstrates a scalable and sustainable model for how small and medium-sized municipalities can access cutting-edge AI tools to improve local governance without the need for individual high-cost investments.

title: Lina
description: Brazil faces the challenge of providing clear, consistent, and easily accessible information on foreign trade procedures, as required under the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement. For many years, this role was fulfilled through “Comex Responde”, a human-operated service that responded to questions from businesses and citizens. However, users had to submit forms and wait an average of four days for a response. This process led to delays, repeated inquiries, and difficulties navigating a complex regulatory environment, particularly for small businesses and individual traders. To address these challenges, the Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services (MDIC) launched “Comex Responde 2.0” and, in 2025, introduced Lina, an AI-powered virtual assistant integrated into Brazil’s national trade single window (Siscomex). Lina uses natural language processing to understand users’ questions and provide immediate responses, available 24/7. It relies exclusively on official sources, such as legislation, manuals, FAQs, and technical guidelines. When a response is insufficient or the issue is complex, users can request expert support and are redirected to the human service channel, ensuring continuity and accuracy of assistance. The initiative aims to address three main challenges: long response times, repetitive questions that consume public administration resources, and the complexity of Brazil’s trade regulatory environment. By providing instant and standardised answers, Lina reduces uncertainty, enhances transparency, and lowers compliance costs for companies, customs brokers, and citizens, helping them meet regulatory requirements more efficiently. It also enables public servants to focus on more complex cases rather than routine and repetitive inquiries, thereby strengthening the overall quality of public service delivery. Future development will focus on strengthening accuracy and governance. This includes continuous curation of the knowledge base, supervised learning based on real interactions, improved fallback mechanisms, and structured collaboration among technical departments and regulatory agencies. The goal is to institutionalise a permanent model of digital knowledge management within the Ministry. As the architecture matures, it may be expanded to other policy areas, allowing the platform to serve as a broader foundation for AI-supported public information services. By combining artificial intelligence with clear governance and official sources, the initiative enhances regulatory predictability and reinforces Brazil’s commitment to transparency in foreign trade.

title: Estratég.IA Thon - AI Strategy Hackathon for Public Organisations
description: Organised by the Conexão Inovação Pública network, the Estratég.IA Thon was an intensive, online marathon positioned at the intersection of strategic foresight and artificial intelligence governance. The programme aimed to democratise access to advanced strategic planning methodologies, specifically focusing on how public institutions can strategically adopt and implement AI. Multidisciplinary teams were provided with a comprehensive "Toolkit" and a curated list of "Prompts" to guide AI models (such as Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude) as co-pilots in generating AI adoption scenarios, strategic visions, and actionable implementation plans. Over the course of the event, participants learned how to apply rigorous foresight frameworks to design robust AI strategies tailored for public organisations. Results, outcomes and impacts Observed results include 17 comprehensive AI strategies (919 pages, 67 projects, 74 minutes of video) tailored for government bodies. Measured via an AI-assisted impact assessment, the intellectual capital generated is valued at approximately BRL 4.25 million, compressing 3–5 months of traditional consulting work into a short agile event. Expected future impacts are substantial: these strategies could directly impact more than 200 million citizens and influence sectors managing approximately BRL 4.5 trillion per year of the national GDP, demonstrating the potential of AI to accelerate public-sector modernisation with a focus on Responsible AI. Challenges and lessons learned A primary challenge was ensuring that participants designed specific, viable AI strategic plans rather than generic technological proposals. To mitigate this, the organisers developed and distributed a highly structured "Toolkit" and a specific framework of "Prompts" to guide the human-AI interaction. A key lesson learned was that using generative AI as a co-pilot dramatically enhances the speed and depth of creating AI strategic plans in government, but its effectiveness relies heavily on users being adequately trained in both prompt engineering and foundational strategic planning concepts.

title: Do it with AI
description: Do it with AI is a national public-private initiative that seeks to promote the adoption of generative artificial intelligence in the Chilean workforce, with an emphasis on the public sector. It offers free, online, asynchronous courses designed around work tasks to facilitate the practical and responsible incorporation of AI. The programme stems from a study on the impact of generative AI on the 100 occupations with the greatest weight in the Chilean economy, which showed that almost 48% of their tasks could be accelerated with AI. On this basis, it was designed as a scalable training solution to translate this potential into improvements in productivity and institutional efficiency. The programme incorporates a diagnostic tool that allows participants to be guided towards personalised training itineraries based on their expressed interests in the use of artificial intelligence in their work tasks. These itineraries integrate AI literacy content, principles of responsible use, and specialised modules, with a focus on the needs of the public sector. The initiative offers 18 courses aimed at the public sector, focusing on the integration of generative artificial intelligence into key government functions. These contents address specific applications such as process automation, data analysis and visualisation, public policy design and evaluation, and institutional communication. The initiative has developed a strategy for co-ordination with the public sector, in collaboration with the Ministries of Labour, Economy, and Science, aimed at integrating Do It with AI into the government's training policies. Within this framework, work was carried out with Servicio Civil, the institution responsible for training public officials, which incorporated the programme into its training recommendations. Due to high institutional demand, the training path was adapted for the public health sector, incorporating an additional profile aligned with its specific needs. Approximately 30,000 public officials are expected to undertake training through Do It with AI, reflecting the programme's growing relevance for strengthening state capabilities and supporting the modernisation of the public sector. In the long term, Do It with AI seeks to consolidate AI capacity-building as part of the country's job training strategies, strengthening productivity, the quality of public services, and the implementation of public policies.
