title: Justice Practical Guide
description: The Justice Practical Guide (Guia Prático da Justiça – GPJ) was created to address a persistent challenge in the justice system: citizens often struggle to understand legal information and the steps required to solve common justice-related issues. By simplifying and centralising information about procedures – such as contracts, family matters, consumer rights, mediation, and peace-court processes – the GPJ helps reduce informational barriers and prevents unnecessary travel to justice services. It builds on the principle that access to justice begins with clear, accessible information that helps people make informed decisions about their rights. The initiative’s main objective is to offer a single, intuitive digital channel where citizens and businesses can quickly obtain answers written in clear, everyday language. To achieve this, in a few months, the GPJ will aggregate content from approximately 190 services available on the Digital Portal of Justice (Plataforma Digital da Justiça) and transform complex legal concepts into simple explanations. It is an AI‑based engine – built, until now, on GPT‑4 models and reinforced with a curated legal knowledge base – providing natural‑language responses validated by justice experts to ensure accuracy and reliability. This combination of structured content and expert‑supervised AI aims to reduce information asymmetry and make justice services more understandable for all. Over time, the GPJ has evolved from a static guidance tool into an intelligent conversational assistant (“Bot”), capable of helping users identify the correct service or procedure for their situation. The new version also incorporates mechanisms for user feedback, enabling continuous improvement and reinforcing human oversight in the decision‑making loop. By integrating with systems such as Google Maps and SIGA (platform for scheduling onsite appointments), the GPJ strengthens interoperability across justice services and enhances the user experience across web and mobile channels. Looking ahead, the initiative is designed to scale. Future development includes expanding coverage to all 190 justice services, improving content governance processes, and ensuring regular updates as legislation and procedures evolve. Internally, the project is becoming institutionalised through structured governance models, dedicated teams, and alignment with wider digital-transformation programmes within the Ministry of Justice. As the platform matures, it is expected to extend it’s reach, support multilingual interaction, and serve as a model for replicating AI-enhanced public-service guidance across other sectors of government.

title: National Data Infrastructure (NDI)
description: The National Data Infrastructure (NDI) was created to address a long‑standing challenge in Brazil’s Federal Public Administration: public data is often dispersed across different systems, formats, and technological standards, limiting its usefulness for evidence‑based policymaking, efficient service delivery, and transparent information sharing. Fragmentation and limited interoperability have historically prevented government bodies from fully realizing the value of the information they collect and maintain. The NDI aims to transform this landscape by promoting the strategic use of data across the federal government. Its purpose is to ensure that public bodies can discover, access, and integrate data securely and responsibly, turning information into actionable insights for policy development. The initiative supports the interoperability, privacy, security, and protection of public data, helping institutions improve services, empower citizens, and foster economic and social development. It also contributes to national sovereignty and federative integration by establishing a trusted environment for data use while rationalizing public-sector costs. In aligning itself with international best practices, the NDI strengthens Brazil’s capacity for data-driven decision-making and technological innovation. Formally instituted by Decree No. 12,198 on September 24, 2024, the NDI represents an evolution of the National Open Data Infrastructure established in 2016. While the earlier initiative focused primarily on open data, the NDI expands the scope to include interoperability, governance, security, privacy, and digital public goods, reflecting a more comprehensive approach to public-sector data management. NDI initiatives are integrated into the Federal Digital Government Strategy, which is updated annually. Its ongoing implementation is supported by several mechanisms. These include the development of data‑governance and sharing policies, which undergo public consultation; the adoption of common technological models such as the Government Cloud, which standardizes infrastructure and data integration practices; the expansion of interoperable national data catalogs to organize and make thousands of datasets reusable; and the consolidation of specialized roles, such as data executives, within government structures. Together, these measures support a gradual, scalable rollout that can expand to additional levels of government and new data partners.

title: AI Security Institute (formerly AI Safety Institute, AISI)
description: The AI Security Institute was established following the Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit in November 2023, building directly on the Foundation Model Taskforce which had operated from April 2023. It was the first government-backed AI safety body in the world and served as the model for equivalent institutions subsequently established in the United States, Japan, Canada, France, South Korea and Singapore under the International Network of AI Safety Institutes (INAIS). In January 2025, the incoming Labour government renamed the Institute the AI Security Institute, broadening its mandate to encompass AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, offensive AI capabilities, and adversarial uses of AI systems alongside the original focus on frontier model safety evaluation. Core activities include: conducting pre-deployment and post-deployment evaluations of frontier AI models from developers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta and others; publishing public-facing safety reports and evaluation methodologies; developing benchmarks and tooling for model assessment; contributing to international AI safety standards through INAIS, the OECD, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 and G7/G20 processes; and conducting research into systemic risks from advanced AI including misuse potential, deceptive alignment and emergent capabilities. The Institute operates the AI Safety Evaluations Platform (AISEP), an infrastructure enabling both UK government and invited international partners to run standardised model evaluations.

title: AI STRATEGIC WORKFORCE PLANNING
description: The strategic workforce planning initiative aims to strengthen evidence‑based human resource management across public administration. It responds to long‑standing difficulties in anticipating staffing needs, managing demographic change, addressing skills mismatches and aligning workforce capacity with organisational priorities. By drawing on increasingly available HR, performance and administrative data, the initiative supports a shift from reactive staffing decisions toward forward‑looking workforce planning. The initiative treats workforce planning as a strategic management function rather than an administrative task. It supports policymakers and managers in planning both the quantity and quality of the public‑sector workforce by identifying current and future staffing gaps, analysing skills requirements and assessing the impact of technological, demographic and economic change on roles and competencies. This approach strengthens alignment between organisational objectives and available skills over the medium to long term. To enable this, a dedicated digital workforce‑planning platform has been developed. The platform integrates demographic information, retirement trends, skills profiles and operational needs, and generates alternative staffing scenarios over a five‑ to ten‑year horizon. Users can compare different policy options, such as accelerated recruitment, internal mobility or targeted reskilling, making the platform a practical simulation tool for evidence‑based workforce‑strategy discussions. Artificial intelligence and predictive analytics are used strictly as decision‑support tools. They analyse large datasets to identify patterns and forecast potential skills shortages, supporting structured assessment of hiring, mobility and reskilling options. All strategic and operational decisions remain under human responsibility. The initiative is aligned with broader HR digitalisation and performance‑management reforms, ensuring consistency with goal‑setting, evaluation and incentive frameworks. The platform has been developed and piloted in nine public entities, allowing real‑world testing of data integration, scenario generation and usability. Progress has been assessed through validation of data inputs, evaluation of scenario outputs and qualitative feedback from participating policymakers and managers. These pilots provided practical insights and supported refinement before wider deployment.

title: Public Procurement Directive No. 44/2026 for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Projects
description: ChileCompra’s Public Procurement Directive No. 44/2026 provides guidance to public entities incorporating data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) into their procurement processes, updating and expanding the guidance first issued in 2023 under the Ethical Algorithms project led by Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, in which ChileCompra participates. The update responds to changes introduced by the modernization of the Public Procurement Law and its new regulation, with a focus on maximizing the public value of these technologies while safeguarding legality, ethics, and information security. The directive applies to all procurement modalities, with particular emphasis on projects involving personal data processing, high technological complexity, or automated decision-making. It identifies common risks—such as lack of algorithmic transparency, bias in AI models, and cybersecurity vulnerabilities—and establishes recommendations to mitigate them, including rigorous planning, the formation of multidisciplinary teams, and prior ethical, legal, and technical assessments before initiating the procurement process. It also proposes specific contractual clauses, such as algorithmic audits, data protection impact assessments, and information security measures. These aim to ensure standards of transparency, fairness, and accountability throughout the project lifecycle, from design and award to operation and closure. A cross-cutting principle is explainability: decisions derived from the use of AI must be understandable and explainable to people, strengthening public trust and enabling oversight and continuous improvement. Through these guidelines, the directive supports effective planning and procurement of data and AI projects, enhancing their positive impact on public management and on the design of more efficient and inclusive public policies. Given its recent publication (March 12, 2026), results are primarily expected: improved quality and consistency in AI-related tender documents, reduced risks of bias and opacity, and enhanced data security and governance. An increase in algorithmic audits, data protection impact assessments, and explainability clauses in contracts is anticipated. The expected impact is a more responsible and trustworthy adoption of AI in government, leading to better services and greater public trust.

title: BridgeAI (Innovate UK)
description: The Regional AI Adoption Hubs form part of the UK's AI Opportunities Action Plan, which identified the geographic concentration of AI benefits as a key challenge. The hubs are designed to ensure AI-driven growth reaches all parts of the UK, particularly those with historically lower AI adoption. Delivered through Innovate UK's BridgeAI programme (launched April 2023, expanded at Autumn Budget 2025), the hubs are implemented in partnership with Digital Catapult, the Alan Turing Institute, the Hartree Centre, and the British Standards Institution. Their activities include: (1) connecting businesses with AI experts through innovation networks; (2) funding the development of new trusted AI services and technologies through co-creation between AI developers and end-users; (3) upskilling organisations through training programmes and the AI Skills Hub; and (4) providing access to AI adoption frameworks and scientific advice. The programme is structured around a series of open competitions and challenge calls, with grants typically ranging from GBP 25,000 to GBP 350,000 for SMEs and research organisations. The Technology Adoption Review 2025 reinforced the hub model as a key mechanism for sector-specific AI support. The hubs also feed into the broader AI Assurance Innovation Fund.

title: UK AI Assurance Innovation Fund
description: The AI Assurance Innovation Fund was announced in September 2025 as part of DSIT's Trusted Third-Party AI Assurance Roadmap, which sets out the UK Government's vision for a credible and scalable AI assurance market. The fund is designed to address the challenge that transformative AI will present novel risks requiring continuous innovation in assurance methods and tools. It will issue £11 million to support research, pilot projects, prototypes and novel assurance methodologies, with a focus on scalable and adaptive solutions for highly capable AI systems. The fund is focused on the eight industrial strategy sectors and will work alongside the AI Security Institute's existing efforts on advanced AI security risks. DSIT will also explore opportunities for the fund to support the UK's AI Adoption Hubs by providing funding to pilot innovative assurance solutions alongside cutting-edge technologies. The initiative is part of a broader roadmap that also includes professionalisation efforts and skills development and information sharing guidelines.

title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation
description: The Blueprint for AI Regulation outlines the United Kingdom’s proposed approach to regulating artificial intelligence through a flexible and pro-innovation framework. Rather than establishing a single central regulator, the blueprint builds on existing sector-specific regulators and provides them with guidance and tools to oversee AI applications within their respective domains. A key component of the blueprint is the proposed AI Growth Lab, a regulatory experimentation platform designed to test innovative AI products and services under controlled regulatory conditions. The Growth Lab would function as a cross-sector regulatory sandbox, allowing companies to pilot AI technologies while regulators monitor outcomes, evaluate risks and adapt regulatory frameworks accordingly. The initiative aims to reduce regulatory uncertainty, accelerate market entry for new AI applications and generate evidence for future rule-making.

title: NEDO Deep-Tech Startups Support Program (DTSU)
description: Administered by the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO), the DTSU programme (officially: Deep Tech Startup Support Fund / Deep Tech Startup Support Program) was established for FY2023–FY2032 with a total budget of JPY 93B. A companion programme for Green Transformation (GX) deep-tech startups runs FY2024–FY2032 with a FY2025 budget of approximately JPY 30B. DTSU targets startups developing breakthrough technologies that: require long-term R&D and large-scale funding; are assessed as having high technical and commercial risk; and contribute to solving major economic and social challenges (carbon neutrality, resource circulation, economic security). The programme provides non-dilutive grants in three sequential phases: (1) STS (Seed-stage Technology-based Startups): early-stage proof-of-concept R&D funding; (2) PCA (Practical application and late-stage Commercialization Research): prototype and pilot development, up to JPY 1B per project; (3) DMP (Demonstration for Mass Production): mass production readiness and overseas demonstration, up to JPY 3B per project. Each project undergoes Stage-Gate reviews between phases; public recruitment is open approximately four times per year (2023–2027). Venture capital partners are embedded in the programme structure, providing investment alongside NEDO grants and participating in commercialisation mentorship. IP rights arising from the programme are retained by the startup. Eligible sectors include AI, advanced manufacturing, biotech, quantum computing, materials science, space, robotics, and clean energy. Approximately 50 companies are active across both DTSU and GX streams as of 2025.

title: Automated web request management process
description: The initiative addresses the inefficiency of the previous manual process used to route citizens’ requests submitted through the INPS Risponde web channel. In the past, all messages were reviewed by contact centre operators and forwarded to back-office staff where necessary, meaning that most requests were handled twice and resolved with delays. The initiative leverages the opportunity offered by artificial intelligence to automate this routing process and improve service delivery. The main objective is to reduce processing steps and response times by automatically directing each request to the appropriate operational level, either the Contact Centre or back-office units. Additional objectives include improving the accuracy of request classification, reducing unnecessary work for operators, and ensuring compliance with data-protection rules through an internally managed system. The initiative is expected to evolve through its integration into ordinary operational processes and its progressive extension to additional request categories. Over time, the initiative has evolved from an experimental automation tool into a structured system based on supervised artificial intelligence models. The main technology used is a BERT Transformer. The models are retrained weekly through a defined workflow that includes data collection, preprocessing, training, testing, benchmarking against the production model, and feedback generation. At the end of each training cycle, a report is produced highlighting any components that require manual updates. The system is trained exclusively on internal INPS data, organised by thematic area, and operates in compliance with GDPR requirements. The entire solution is built on open-source technologies and hosted on the organisation’s own infrastructure, ensuring full control over both data and operational processes. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has led to faster and more accurate handling of citizens’ requests and a reduction in unnecessary work for first-level staff. The system automatically analyses all incoming messages and routes them to the appropriate level, so first-level operators handle only requests appropriate to their level. Results have been measured through system logs and operational statistics. Since 22 April 2024, more than two million requests have been processed by AI, and approximately 30% have been automatically routed directly to second-level staff. In the future, further improvements are expected in response times, automation rates and resource efficiency as the system is extended to additional request types and services.

title: National Digital Decade: Roadmap of the Slovak Republic
description: The National Roadmap for the Digital Decade is Slovakia’s primary strategic document for implementing the European Union’s Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030. It provides a detailed analysis of the current state of digitalisation and sets ambitious national trajectories to meet EU-wide targets. A key component of the roadmap is the acceleration of AI uptake, with a specific target for 25% of Slovak enterprises to use AI technologies by 2030. The roadmap integrates various existing strategies and new measures into a cohesive plan. For AI, it emphasises the development of high-performance computing infrastructure (including participation in the EuroHPC JU), support for Digital Innovation Hubs to assist SMEs in adopting AI, and the implementation of the "AI in Government" agenda to improve public service efficiency. It also addresses the need for advanced digital skills to support the AI ecosystem. The initiative is monitored through a robust governance mechanism involving regular reporting to the European Commission. It is designed to be a living document, subject to periodic reviews and adjustments based on technological advancements and progress towards the defined KPIs. By aligning national efforts with EU goals, the roadmap ensures that Slovakia contributes effectively to Europe’s digital leadership while addressing specific local challenges such as the digital divide and the need for modernisation in public administration. Results, outcomes and impacts The primary expected outcome is the achievement of the 2030 targets, specifically increasing AI adoption in enterprises from the current baseline to 25%. The roadmap has already established a clear governance structure and a monitoring framework to track progress annually against the Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI) indicators. Early impacts include the launch of support schemes for Digital Innovation Hubs and the initiation of projects for high-performance computing infrastructure, which are foundational for AI development. The ultimate impact will be a digitally transformed economy and public sector with high levels of AI integration.

title: Gov.pt virtual assistant
description: The Gov.pt virtual assistant is a generative-AI chatbot embedded in the Portuguese single public services portal. Using a curated public-services knowledge base and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), it answers questions by text or voice and can also be used through a chat interface with an animated avatar. It supports 12 languages, according to the nationalities that most frequently use Portuguese public services (Portuguese; Brazilian Portuguese; English; Spanish; French; German; Italian; Bengali; Hindi; Nepali; Mandarin; Ukrainian; Russian) and covers information for more than 2,300 services, helping users to quickly identify requirements, administrative steps, service delivery channels and where to go next. It tackles a core opportunity in digital government: reducing information asymmetry and navigation complexity that drive in-person visits, repeated calls and abandoned processes. The main objectives are to (1) provide consistent, accessible, multilingual guidance 24/7; (2) shorten the time to find the right service and reduce errors when preparing the documents and information needed in advance to access a specific service; (3) improve inclusion for non-Portuguese speakers, people with lower digital literacy and users with accessibility needs; and (4) generate evidence (analytics + feedback) to continuously improve the Gov.pt portal content. Implementation combined iterative delivery with strong quality controls: a 2023 pilot on a limited scope, a Minimum Viable Product to test languages and accuracy with content and language experts, front-end integration and document ingestion, guardrails for tone and follow-up questions, performance metrics, stress testing and deployment in late 2024. The virtual assistant operates within Gov.pt’s governance framework, with ARTE and partner agencies working together to keep source information and content accurate and updated. From 2026 onward, the roadmap expands from informational support to assisted completion of services: broader scope, transactional capabilities, process tracking and appointment scheduling with public bodies. The modular design allows scaling to more services and deeper integrations while maintaining human oversight, privacy safeguards and continuous monitoring to sustain trust and institutionalise the solution across agencies.

title: Remote Video Identification Service for Citizen Digital Identities
description: The Spanish Royal Mint (FNMT‑RCM) has deployed a remote video identification service to meet the growing demand for secure digital identity in an increasingly digital society. Until now, obtaining a qualified electronic certificate required citizens to appear in person at a registration office. This new service applies advanced artificial intelligence to offer a legally compliant, secure, and user‑friendly alternative that fully meets the requirements of the European eIDAS framework. The initiative aims to expand the reach of digital public administration, reduce barriers linked to physical mobility, and improve the efficiency of public resources. The system uses biometric algorithms to perform liveness detection and to match the user’s facial image with the photograph on their identity document in real time, ensuring that the applicant is the legitimate holder of the ID. The service has been designed with scalability in mind. As digital interaction with public authorities becomes standard practice, the FNMT plans to continue improving the underlying AI models, broaden support for additional international identity documents, and progressively integrate the solution into Spain’s future European Digital Identity Wallet. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has demonstrated strong results, with approximately 14% of all qualified electronic certificates now issued through the remote video identification channel. In 2025, the service reached nearly 700,000 completed video identifications, marking a significant milestone in its adoption. Its main impact has been the substantial reduction in travel time and physical queues for citizens, thereby improving the overall accessibility of digital public services. Performance is monitored through real‑time issuance statistics and user completion rates, which provide continuous insight into system efficiency and user experience. Looking ahead, a steady increase in uptake is expected, with the goal of making it the preferred option for users. Challenges and lessons learned One of the main challenges was ensuring the security and authenticity of identity documents in a remote environment. To mitigate risks like "presentation attacks" (using photos or masks), the FNMT implemented sophisticated biometric algorithms and a human-in-the-loop verification process. A key lesson learned is that user experience (UX) is vital; the process must be intuitive, providing clear instructions for lighting and camera positioning to ensure high-quality biometric capture. Success requires a robust legal framework that recognises remote identification as equivalent to physical presence, alongside a high-performance technological infrastructure capable of processing large volumes of video data securely.

title: AuditSearch: AI-Powered Search System for Internal Government Audit
description: Before AuditPesquisa, searching for information in Brazil's internal government audit reports was manual, time-consuming, and inefficient. The CGU's Federal Office of Internal Control (SFC) maintained over 3,000 audit reports but lacked a system to interpret textual content, identify patterns, or connect similar findings across audits. As government demands for faster, evidence-based analysis increased, there was a critical need for an intelligent solution that could understand context and meaning—going far beyond simple keyword searches. The AuditPesquisa initiative pursues five primary objectives: 1. Facilitate Access to Audit Knowledge: Enable auditors and government managers to rapidly access insights embedded in 3,000+ historical audit reports through semantic understanding rather than keyword matching. 2. title: DIMO – Governing Data and Artificial Intelligence in Local Government. Pre AI data governance (Subnational: Alicante)
description: Local governments increasingly rely on data to design and implement public policies, yet administrative information is often fragmented across organisational silos and managed under heterogeneous standards. This limits institutional capacity, increases legal risk and constrains the responsible use of advanced analytics and artificial intelligence. At the subnational level, these challenges are particularly acute for small and medium-sized municipalities with limited technical and organisational resources. Without clear data governance, the introduction of AI risks reinforcing inconsistencies rather than improving public decision-making. This context highlighted the need for a co-ordinated governance approach before expanding the use of artificial intelligence in public administration. Results, outcomes and impacts The initiative has strengthened data quality, interoperability and analytical capacity across local administrations. It has enabled more consistent and evidence-based public decisions, reduced legal and operational risks and improved co-ordination between institutions and municipalities. DIMO has also supported fairer policy design, increased transparency and contributed to higher levels of citizen trust. Beyond operational results, the initiative has fostered a cultural shift towards evidence-based governance within public administration. Challenges and lessons learned Key lessons from the initiative include the importance of establishing data governance before deploying artificial intelligence, and recognising that trustworthy AI is primarily an organisational challenge rather than a technical one. The initiative also demonstrated the value of shared governance models in reducing territorial inequalities and supporting smaller municipalities. Institutional trust increased when public servants clearly understood how data and analytical insights were generated. These lessons highlight that governing with AI requires long-term institutional commitment and continuous learning.

title: "Services Publics+" : Using AI to improve the quality of public services and re-humanize public services
description: The French Government’s Services Publics+ (SP+) programme is a nationwide initiative designed to restore the fundamentals of public service and improve the daily experiences of 45 million citizens interacting with 2.5 million public servants. Historically, citizens have faced frustrations such as long wait times, complex forms, and a lack of transparency. To resolve these issues and leverage the capabilities of emerging technologies, the Government has integrated generative AI into the SP+ platform—specifically through its citizen feedback feature, "Je Donne Mon Avis" (I Give My Opinion). This transforms how user feedback is collected, analysed, and actioned across major public services, from police stations to social benefit desks. The primary objective is to drive continuous improvement at all contact points, making services more efficient while freeing up civil servants to focus on strategic, high-value tasks. To achieve this, the initiative deploys three core AI components: speech-to-text capabilities to ensure accessibility for mobile users, individuals with disabilities, and those facing digital illiteracy; automated drafting assistance that provides civil servants with proposed responses to citizen feedback, which they can easily review and refine before sending; and real-time semantic analysis of user feedback across the public services, creating summaries that detect weak signals, pinpoint administrative difficulties, and suggest concrete action plans. These summaries can also be generated for a specific irritant. These technological integrations are already demonstrating measurable value. The initiative currently yields three main benefits: improving public satisfaction and civic engagement; streamlining service delivery by reducing the time civil servants spend on trivial or repetitive tasks; and reducing response times to make the administration more agile. As the programme matures, the key challenge for the Government is comprehensively assessing and quantifying the long-term impact these AI tools have on the actual quality of service experienced by both users and civil servants. Looking forward, the initiative is set to scale by deeply institutionalising these AI insights into both local governance and public transparency. The AI-generated feedback summaries will soon be provided directly to local préfets (State representatives), enabling them to closely monitor and quickly resolve specific bottlenecks within their départements. Additionally, these overviews will be made publicly available, giving the general public a transparent, aggregated view of what their fellow citizens think about each public service. This evolution is intended to ensure a continuous, transparent loop of civic feedback and administrative modernisation.

title: The Data and Digital Government Strategy
description: The Strategy combines data and digital into a single strategy, recognising the opportunities of aligning the use and management of data and digital technologies. It puts people and business at the centre of its vision ensuring everyone’s experience with the Australian Government is inclusive, accessible and responsive to their needs. Digital services are the first way that many people engage with and experience government, while government-held data informs decisions that affects peoples’ lives. For these reasons, the quality and implementation of the Government’s data and digital capabilities can build public trust – or erode it. The Strategy was developed in consultation with people, community and advocacy groups, academia, industry, state and territory governments and the APS. The Strategy is accompanied by an annual Implementation Plan that sets out achievements in the past year, as well as key actions and initiatives that will drive the Strategy’s missions over the next year. The 2025 Implementation Plan outlines four key priority areas for the Australian Government over the next year, including AI. Capturing the opportunity of AI is vital to enhancing the Government’s ability to build world class data and digital capabilities, improve productivity and economic resilience, and deliver better policy and services for all people in Australia. Harnessing the opportunity of AI and sharing its benefits is expected to help the APS improve standards of living in Australia. Realising the benefits of AI in Government requires a culture of innovation, accelerating the safe and responsible use of AI across all government agencies while maintaining the trust and confidence of the public. Results, outcomes and impacts: The 2025 Implementation Plan includes supporting metrics that demonstrate progress towards the Strategy’s 2030 vision, and outlines AI solutions, such as GenAI assistants, that increase productivity. 2025 metrics on AI include: • 12.4% of APS staff were in data and digital roles – up from 10.4% in 2024, reflecting strong growth in digital capability across the service. • 78.6% of APS staff agreed their workgroup had the right skills and knowledge to perform effectively, reinforcing confidence in the APS’s ability to deliver in a digital-first environment. • Over 70% of APS agencies have identified specific opportunities where AI can deliver measurable benefits to their work, and 81% have systems in place to monitor the effectiveness of AI.

title: BI Dave - Natural Language Processing Assistant
description: ‘BI Dave’ is an internal initiative created to help staff make better use of large volumes of written information collected through everyday interactions with businesses. Before ‘BI Dave’, understanding this information required staff to manually read, sort and summarise thousands of notes and reports. This was slow, resource‑intensive, and made it difficult to respond quickly, especially during busy periods or when urgent advice was needed. As a result, valuable insights were often under‑used. The initiative was developed to improve how efficiently insights could be turned into reports and briefings without relying on more staff. Since going live in March 2024, ‘BI Dave’ has been used frequently and has reduced report drafting time by more than 50 per cent, improving the speed and consistency of reporting. This enables faster, more evidence-based policy and program decisions for government and ensures public feedback is integrated more consistently. Impacts have been measured through before‑and‑after comparisons of drafting effort, operational testing, and staff feedback during routine use. This has also enabled analysis of large volumes of written information that were previously impractical to process manually. Further efficiency and insight gains are expected as similar capabilities are applied to other information sources across the department. Key challenges included inconsistent data quality, privacy risks from identifying information in free‑text records, and the effort required to prepare data for analysis. Early testing showed variable accuracy across large and mixed datasets, including missed identifiers and occasional mis‑categorisation, requiring controls to prevent inappropriate outputs. These risks were mitigated through staged, batch‑based testing using a “test–train–repeat” approach, with manual review of outputs and incremental refinement before broader operational use. The initiative highlighted the importance of human oversight, strong quality assurance, and active involvement of business users. Lessons learned include starting with a focused use case, accepting iterative improvement, and embedding governance early. Success depends on reliable internal data, clear accountability, skilled reviewers, and organisational support for AI as an assistive capability rather than an automated decision‑maker.

title: Whole of Australian Government Occupation Coding Service
description: Australia’s labour market intelligence depends on consistent occupation coding to the Occupation Standard Classification for Australia (OSCA) 2024, and the Australian and New Zealand Standard Classification of Occupations (ANZSCO) Australian Update 2022. Today, many agencies still rely on labour intensive manual processes and varied local practices, fragmenting data and slowing policy, research, and service delivery. The Whole of Australian Government (WoAG) Occupation Coding Service resolves this by providing a secure, AI/ML powered cloud service that automatically codes free text job titles and tasks in real time via API or at scale in batch. Objectives. The initiative aims to (1) lift coding consistency and coherence across the public sector; (2) reduce effort and cost by maximising automated coding rates; (3) offer controllable and explainable models (hierarchical SVM as the primary method, with support for LLMs as appropriate); (4) provide secure, standards aligned access for agencies; and (5) improve the quality and timeliness of labour market data for decisionmakers and communities. The service is implemented on ABS-operated cloud infrastructure with segregated training/inference accounts, static models that do not learn from user inputs, and documented assurance under the Australian Government AI and security frameworks. Current outcomes. The platform is live and already used by numerous agencies, enabling fast, consistent coding for surveys, forms, and enterprise datasets. Within the ABS, data from the 2021 Census of Population and Housing is being recoded to OSCA 2024 and the forthcoming 2026 Census will require substantially fewer clerical coders, freeing resources for targeted quality assurance and yielding significant productivity gains. The cloud-hosted service is able to serve multiple models efficiently, supporting single record real time calls and batch processing of millions of records. The service has delivered major efficiency gains, with agencies coding 100,000 records in minutes rather than weeks and Census reducing temporary coding workforce needs while maintaining quality. Automated AI/ML models increase consistency across datasets and support adoption of updated classifications. Early use shows faster processing, improved comparability, and staff effort redirected from manual coding to quality assurance. Future impacts include broader uptake, reduced duplication, and more coherent labour market insights across government.

text_raw: Whole of Australian Government Occupation Coding Service. Australia’s labour market intelligence depends on consistent occupation coding to the Occupation Standard Classification for Australia (OSCA) 2024, and the Australian and New Zealand Standard Classification of Occupations (ANZSCO) Australian Update 2022. Today, many agencies still rely on labour intensive manual processes and varied local practices, fragmenting data and slowing policy, research, and service delivery. The Whole of Australian Government (WoAG) Occupation Coding Service resolves this by providing a secure, AI/ML powered cloud service that automatically codes free text job titles and tasks in real time via API or at scale in batch. Objectives. The initiative aims to (1) lift coding consistency and coherence across the public sector; (2) reduce effort and cost by maximising automated coding rates; (3) offer controllable and explainable models (hierarchical SVM as the primary method, with support for LLMs as appropriate); (4) provide secure, standards aligned access for agencies; and (5) improve the quality and timeliness of labour market data for decisionmakers and communities. The service is implemented on ABS-operated cloud infrastructure with segregated training/inference accounts, static models that do not learn from user inputs, and documented assurance under the Australian Government AI and security frameworks. Current outcomes. The platform is live and already used by numerous agencies, enabling fast, consistent coding for surveys, forms, and enterprise datasets. Within the ABS, data from the 2021 Census of Population and Housing is being recoded to OSCA 2024 and the forthcoming 2026 Census will require substantially fewer clerical coders, freeing resources for targeted quality assurance and yielding significant productivity gains. The cloud-hosted service is able to serve multiple models efficiently, supporting single record real time calls and batch processing of millions of records. The service has delivered major efficiency gains, with agencies coding 100,000 records in minutes rather than weeks and Census reducing temporary coding workforce needs while maintaining quality. Automated AI/ML models increase consistency across datasets and support adoption of updated classifications. title: Good Practice Guide for the Identification, Prevention and Mitigation of Gender Biases in the Life Cycle of Artificial Intelligence
description: The development of this guide of good practices aligns with the objectives outlined in CONPES 4080 of 2022, "Public Policy on Gender Equity for Women: Towards the Sustainable Development of the Country". This policy aims to "create the conditions necessary for the country to advance toward gender equity and ensure the economic, social, cultural, participation, and health rights of women, as well as the possibility of living a life free from gender-based violence, with a horizon extending to 2030." In accordance with this policy, the National Planning Department (DNP) is responsible for preparing and disseminating good practices guide to promote gender equity and mitigate biases in the application of artificial intelligence (Action 1.17).The development of the good practices guide incorporates multiple components, including:i) the conceptualization of gender equity within the ecosystem and life cycle of AI systems, as well as the mapping of initiatives (e.g., tools, ethical frameworks, recommendations) that promote gender equity in this context; andii) the creation of a comprehensive guide of good practices, complemented by a catalog of tools and a decision tree aimed at identifying, preventing, and mitigating gender biases in the development and adoption of AI systems. To develop practical tools, qualitative information was gathered from national and international stakeholders within the AI ecosystem. This approach ensured that the design and validation of the products incorporated a participatory process, fostering inclusivity and relevance across diverse contexts.

title: Law n. 4961/2022 Emerging information and communication technologies and societies, enhancing digital governance and other provisions
description: Greek Law 4961/2022 addresses the need for a structured framework to manage the rapid adoption of advanced technologies like AI, IoT, and 3D printing. It aims to modernize public services, enhance digital governance, and promote Greece's digital transformationObjectives:Ensure lawful, safe, and secure use of emerging technologies.Enhance public service efficiency and data protection.Promote innovation and digital transformation.The law will be implemented through sector-specific regulations and horizontal guidelines, ensuring adaptability and scalability. It will be institutionalized by establishing control mechanisms and enforcement bodies. Since its enactment, the law has seen updates to align with the EU's AI Act and other international standards, ensuring continuous improvement and relevance. Specifically on AI, law 4961/2022 defines:Algorithmic Impact Assessment (Article 5) - Requires public bodies to provide technical information and assess the impact of AI systems on rights, freedoms and social groups before implementation.Transparency obligations (Articles 4, 6) - Requires public sector entities to provide information about the operation, characteristics and decisions of AI systems.AI contractor obligations (Article 7) - Contractors developing AI for public entities must disclose technical details and ensure that systems comply with human rights legal frameworks.Registry of AI systems for public entities (Article 8) - Requires public entities to maintain and update a registry of AI systems in use, detailing their purpose, date of commissioning and measures for safe operation.Disclosure of AI use in the workplace (Article 9) - Requires private entities to inform employees and job applicants about the use of AI in decision-making processes affecting employment.Ethical data use policy (Article 10) - Requires large and medium-sized private entities to maintain a policy on the ethical use of data in AI applications, including procedures and measures for ethical compliance.AI Coordination Committee (Article 11) - A committee responsible for the implementation and improvement of the national AI strategy. It ensures the alignment of national efforts with the strategic objectives.National AI Strategy Oversight Committee (Article 13) - Oversees the implementation of the national AI strategy and ensures the alignment of activities of all stakeholders. It focuses on implementation and compliance.AI Observatory (Article 14) - Collects data, monitors AI-related activities and provides key performance indicators for AI initiatives in the country. It identifies opportunities and assesses the impact of AI on fundamental rights.

title: Regulatory Framework for Automated Vehicles in Australia
description: On 11 February 2022, at the meeting of Infrastructure and Transport Ministers (ITMM), transport ministers from all Australian jurisdictions agreed that the future Automated Vehicle Safety Law will be implemented through Commonwealth law. This agreement built on a 2020 agreement to work towards establishing a national approach to regulating automated vehicles when they are commercially deployed on Australian roads. Earlier work (from 2016-2018) focused on a safety assurance system for automated driving systems, to ensure the safety of automated vehicles when they are first supplied to the market.The initiative has the following objective(s):The purpose of this paper is to present proposals on the end-to-end regulatory framework for the commercial deployment of automated vehicles. This framework consists of existing Commonwealth and state and territory frameworks, frameworks already agreed by ministers as part of automated vehicle reforms, and recommendations for in-service safety. The NTC undertook targeted consultation with key stakeholders to understand whether the regulatory framework will achieve national outcomes, potential gaps, and how it will impact on different sectors. The framework presented in the paper includes recommendations on the detailed content of the proposed in-service Automated Vehicle Safety Law. It also identifies further work on the reform program, focused on amendments to state and territory law to accommodate automated vehicles.

title: Grants4Companies
description: Business grants are an important tool for steering and supporting the economy. In addition, they can be used to quickly react to and counter crises. However, the search for suitable business grants can be a challenge for businesses in Austria, due to the large number of available business grants from a multitude of different providers. While there are dedicated search engines, businesses often are simply not aware of the existence of grants on a specific topic, and hence cannot use these engines in a targeted search. This is the starting point for the application Grants4Companies.Grants4Companies aims to provide a better visibility for business grants by suggesting grants in the context of the Unternehmensserviceportal (USP), supplementing existing dedicated search engines. This is achieved by listing relevant business grants for the company or business logged into the USP. Most importantly, whether a grant is relevant for the particular business is evaluated using methods of symbolic AI based on the data on that business available from the registers of the public administration. The grants for which the business satisfies the formal eligibility criteria, e.g., concerning the location or type of business, are shown more prominently. Of course the data used to evaluate the grants for a particular business is retrieved only after an explicit consent, and is visible only for this specific business. The employed methods of symbolic AI yield a higher transparency and explainability, since the ranking of the business grants is achieved by rule-based and hence explicitly explainable evaluations. These explanations as well as the relevant data are shown explicitly. For more information on the specific grants as well as the actual application process the user is referred to the websites of the funding agencies.The main benefit achieved by Grants4Companies for businesses is the better visibility of relevant and potentially interesting business grants and hence by easier discoverability of funding possibilities. But the employed methods and technologies also yield benefits for political institutions, public administration and funding agencies. In particular, the underlying machine-interpretable description of the business grants can be used in the future for formal and automated analyses of the considered grants, helping, e.g., to discover gaps in funding or multiple funding in the form of overlapping business grants. This was demonstrated in a proof of concept implementation using standardised AI programming languages.Standards are a prerequisite for optimal cross-border cooperation between European Member States, companies and developers. The Austrian government therefore endorses and participates in the development of international standards and reference systems for symbolic AI programming languages such as ISO/IEC 13211-1:1995 (Prolog) which are needed to implement AI services reliably, and to ensure digital sovereignty and vendor independence.

title: Law as Code for Procedures of Public Administration
description: Following the žLaw as Code-approach (or rules as code approach), several international initiatives aim to introduce transparent and explainable methods for the creation and execution of regulations and legal texts in public administration. Examples include initiatives in Canada, social benefit calculators in Barcelona or New Zealand, or a recently established research centre for Computational Law in Singapore. Advantages of this approach are in particular increased transparency and explainability of the computations and evaluations based on these regulations in public administration, as well as the possibility of automatized procedures based on the underlying logic-based formal rules using methods of symbolic Artificial Intelligence.The successfully completed žLaw as Code for procedures of public administration-initiative aimed to provide a basis for such an approach in the context of Austrian public administration. This included both a theoretical analysis of current approaches and their suitability in this context, as well as a proof of concept implementation of an end-to-end workflow. The workflow started with a tool for extracting a logic-based formal rule representation close to the logic programming paradigm from legal texts given in natural language, followed by a tool for viewing these rules, comparing them to the original texts and modifying the extracted formal rules where needed. The resulting rule base could then be used for evaluating business cases using a rule execution engine.When employed on a broader basis, the formulation of legal texts and regulations in a logic-based language as envisioned in this initiative would enable a high degree of automation of processes in public administration with transparent, explainable and predictable results. In addition, it would enable also a more comprehensive analysis of laws and regulations with respect to their mutual relations as well as possible overlaps and conflicts. Ideally, such a formal representation would be developed already in the law-making process itself, to ensure that the intent of the texts is captured exactly.Wherever possible, the initiative employed standardised representations and methods. Standards are a prerequisite for optimal cross-border cooperation between European Member States, companies and developers. The Austrian government therefore endorses and participates in the development of international standards and reference systems for symbolic AI programming languages such as ISO/IEC 13211-1:1995 (Prolog) which are needed to implement AI services reliably, and to ensure digital sovereignty and vendor independence.

title: National Consultative Committee on Digital Ethics and AI
description: The French National Pilot Committee for Digital Ethics was set up in December 2019 under the aegis of the National Consultative Ethics Committee for Health and Life Sciences (CCNE) at the request of the Prime minister. It is composed of 27 members from different backgrounds (academics, digital specialists from the private sector or from civil society organisations, etc.) and seeks to address the ethical issues raised by digital technology. Its role is both to formulate opinions on the subjects referred to it and to maintain ethical oversight in order to elucidate individual and collective decision-making. In 2022, the CCNEN becomes the CCNEN-IA to better take into account AI-related ethics issues.

title: AI Governance Center
description: The AI Governance Center (AIGC) was established to address the growing risks and ethical challenges associated with AI adoption in Thailand while positioning the country as a leader in AI governance. With AI becoming integral to various sectors, issues such as bias, privacy risks, and transparency gaps require robust governance. AIGC leverages this opportunity by developing comprehensive guidelines, risk assessment tools, and policy frameworks to ensure responsible and sustainable AI deployment. Additionally, it strengthens Thailand's alignment with global AI governance standards, facilitating international cooperation and investment.The initiative's key objectives include developing AI governance guidelines and toolkits, fostering AI ethics awareness, and enhancing testing frameworks to mitigate AI-related risks. By engaging policymakers, businesses, and researchers, AIGC ensures practical implementation of responsible AI principles. It has also introduced AI ethics education through training programs such as the AI Executive Program (AIX), AI Change Agent Program (AICA) and knowledge sharing, reaching over 20,000 participants in 2024. International collaboration is another priority, with Thailand serving as a key contributor to OECD AI governance initiatives and ASEAN AI ethics frameworks, reinforcing its regional and global leadership.Looking ahead, AIGC will continue to expand its impact by institutionalizing AI governance across sectors. It is set to co-host the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI 2025, further elevating Thailand's presence in AI policy discussions. title: National Convergence Plan for the Development of AI
description: Belgium has three regions: the Flemish Region, the Brussels-Capital Region and the Walloon Region. These regions have already had ambitious AI plans approved by their governments, which they are currently implementing. Several institutes, such as FARI in Brussels, have been created to support large-scale projects within the framework of territorial priorities, programs such as the DigitalWallonia4.ai project have been set up, initiatives like AI4Belgium have been created. Given the societal stakes, the challenges to be met and the multiplicity of actors involved, the integration of the potential of AI at the Belgian national level can only be done in synergy with the federated entities.The initiative has the following objectives:To promote a trustworthy AI.To ensure cybersecurity.To strengthen Belgium's competitiveness and attractiveness through AI.To develop a data-driven economy and an efficient infrastructure.To promote AI at the heart of health.To support more sustainable mobility. To preserve the environment. To promote better and lifelong learning. To provide better services and protection to citizens.

title: The Bhashini Initiative (National Language Translation Mission)
description: The Bhashini initiative, evolving from the National Language Translation Mission (NLTM), marks a pivotal shift towards leveraging technology for linguistic inclusivity in India. While NLTM focused on making government documents accessible in multiple Indian languages, Bhashini aims to build a comprehensive ecosystem for Indian language technologies. It utilizes artificial intelligence and machine learning to facilitate translation, speech recognition, and content creation across India's languages, aiming to eliminate linguistic barriers in accessing digital services and information. This strategic move towards technological solutions for language inclusivity signifies a broader effort to ensure digital empowerment for all, making the digital revolution accessible across India's diverse linguistic landscape.

title: Definition of a Model of Indicators for Monitoring the Potential of Ai Deployment in Slovenia
description: The initiative has the following objectives:- Definition of a model of indicators and a methodology for assessing the uptake of AI in Slovenia (in the private and public sectors). The methodology should relate to methodologies and analyses already defined at EU level.- review and assess the state of play of the deployment of AI in Slovenia according to a prepared methodology (by sector, by size of organisation, etc.) in the private and public sectors, based on a representative sample of stakeholders in Slovenia (public and private organisations) that use or intend to deploy AI in their business (to improve and optimise their own operations and business processes, or to create new innovative services and products for their users, suppliers or customers);- Analysis of factors influencing the ability and interest to accelerate the deployment of AI, including internal factors within organisations (e.g. human resources, financial resources, computerisation of internal operations, computerisation of operations with external partners in the value chain, availability and accessibility of data, changes in work processes, employee readiness for change, etc.), market factors and other factors (e.g. regulatory compliance, ethical compliance).

title: Public Sector Artificial Intelligence Observatory
description: The creation of the Artificial Intelligence Observatory was established in Commitment 1.6 of the Fifth National Action Plan for Open Government 2021-2024, undertaken by Agesic and the Unit for Access to Public Information (UAIP).The Observatory is focused on:Promoting and encouraging the ethical, responsible, safe, and reliable use of AI technology.Strengthening the AI ecosystem in Uruguay.Promoting access to information about AI applications in the State.The Observatory was created by integrating contributions from various actors in the public sector, private sector, academia, and civil society, who participated in specific exchange workshops for its design and in dialogue tables as part of the process of reviewing the Artificial Intelligence Strategy and developing the National Data Strategy. The first survey of AI application in the State was conducted from December 2023 to May 2024 through a questionnaire sent to the directors and general managers of organizations, as well as to IT and e-government sector leaders in various branches of the Central Administration, Decentralized Services, Autonomous Entities, and Departmental Governments. It was also sent to some non-state public entities, such as the National Agency for Research and Innovation (ANII) and Ceibal, as well as the Judicial Power and Legislative Power.The survey form consists of 3 sections:Section 1: Introduction, explaining the purpose of the survey and some considerations for reporting initiatives, as well as examples of what is considered AI applications for the purposes of the survey. It specifically asked for cases or initiatives that have identified the problem to be solved and are included in the strategic plan of the responding organization.Section 2: Identification of the organization.Section 3: Identification of the system or initiative to report, including: description, technical development data, information about the team working or who worked on the initiative, decision-making data, and the main challenges encountered.Additionally, a questionnaire was included for cases where the organization does not have AI applications, to identify potential areas or applications of interest that could be developed.This survey was the initial step for the first version of the Observatory, which will be updated periodically with new reported cases.

title: Mechanisms for Attracting Foreign and Returning Domestic Experts to Strengthen Slovenia's Position in Global Digitisation Trends
description: Initiative relates to implementation of 2nd strategic goal of National AI programme ensuring proper Education and strengthening of human resources.The initiative has the following objectives:- Inventory and analyse in depth the activities carried out by European and other countries to cooperate more actively with experts abroad and to help them return to their home countries.- Develop a multi-dimensional index that assesses for each activity the transferability and needs of the activity, and its adaptation to enable the activity to be introduced in the Republic of Slovenia.- Use the multi-dimensional index to carry out a comparative and cost-benefit analysis of a list of activities in other countries in order to make recommendations for the Slovenian situation and specificities. Identification of solutions that would allow the implementation of appropriately adapted activities in the Republic of Slovenia in a way that would enable their widespread and effective use.- In-depth study and evaluation of programmes based on the example of the State of Israel, with a focus on digital entrepreneurship, industrial and high-tech disciplines (e.g., The Israel Brain Gain Programme, Back to Tech, Israeli Houses, Study in Isreal and other programmes). Emphasis on the study of programmes aimed at attracting foreign professionals to Israel and programmes aimed at supporting the return of Israelis living abroad.- Examine the criteria for the implementation of programmes in Israel and, as a consequence, identify the real needs, opportunities and benefits for the adaptation and transfer of the selected programmes to the Republic of Slovenia.

title: Innovation Strategy for Smart Specialisation 2021-2027
description: Results-based management of ISSS 2021-2027 is a priority in the current programming period as it shall build upon the achievements of ISSS 2014-2020. The strategic and operational objectives of ISSS 2021-2027 have been updated in a way that allows taking further steps in specific directions (areas) in order to maximize the potential of the innovation ecosystem on the basis of the results achieved so far, the identified regional strengths and weaknesses.During the previous programming period 2014-2020, ISSS was implemented at NUTS II level (six regions in Bulgaria) with limited impact on the regional innovation capacity. In ISSS 2021-2027, each district (28 districts in Bulgaria) has consulted various stakeholders in order to identify the relevant thematic areas (2 + Clean technologies, circular economy and low carbon economy) for smart specialisation in the respective NUTS III region. Strategic objectives:I. To develop and position Bulgaria as a centre of medium- and high-tech innovation in strategic areas (the five thematic areas) where the country has established capacity and market positions, as well as recognised competencies to compete in the global market, enhancing the country's national and regional innovation performance. To support the deployment and establishment of a sustainable, modern, dynamic, inclusive, data-driven and globally connected research, innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem in Bulgaria. Operational objectives: 1) Improve the research system and innovation performance of enterprises. 2) Increase the technological capacity of enterprises, increase the environmental friendliness and internationalisation of Bulgarian products and services. 3) Improve human resource capacity in the field of new technologies and innovation.

title: Panhellenic Educational Robotics Competition
description: The National Competition on Educational Robotics is designed to integrate educational robotics and the broader STEM approach into mainstream education. It serves as a platform where students, teachers, and schools can explore hands-on learning, creativity, and problem-solving through robotics projects. The competition’s objectives include: Introducing robotics into classrooms as part of the official curriculum Promoting STEM as a teaching methodology for compulsory education Defining clear ways for students to acquire 21st-century skills , such as critical thinking, collaboration, and digital literacy Through national-level contests and activities, students gain practical experience in building and programming robots while learning scientific principles. Teachers receive guidance on how to integrate STEM concepts into their lessons, creating a pipeline of future innovators and technology-savvy professionals. Looking ahead, the competition aims to expand participation across regions , strengthen partnerships with schools, and further embed STEM-based learning in the education system to enhance the country’s innovation capacity.

title: Reform of Higher Education for a Green and Resilient Transition to Society 5.0
description: Slovenia is actively working to modernize its higher education system by supporting the digital transformation of teaching and learning. The goal is to equip both students and educators with the skills needed to succeed in a world shaped by advanced technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, and blockchain. This reform addresses the urgent need to update digital skills and teaching methods so that graduates are prepared for the demands of the modern labor market, especially in fast-growing tech sectors. As part of a broader education reform, guidelines and an implementation plan were developed to enhance digital competencies through pilot projects and targeted training. The initiative focuses on advanced digital skills such as AI, blockchain, and cybersecurity, and aims to strengthen digital teaching abilities in higher education. A key element is the introduction of micro-credentials, enabling universities to respond flexibly to evolving labor market demands, particularly in emerging tech fields like AI, though funding for AI-specific actions is still being finalised. These micro-credentials provide a way for students and professionals to gain recognition for specific skills in a short time, helping to keep pace with rapid changes in technology and industry needs. The reform includes pilot projects that test new approaches to teaching with digital tools and technologies in Slovenian universities. Educators receive focused training to better incorporate these advanced subjects into their courses. Collaboration among universities, government bodies, and industry stakeholders ensures that the curriculum remains relevant and aligned with the skills required in the workplace. By embedding these practices within higher education, Slovenia aims to create a learning environment that balances theoretical knowledge with practical application of digital technologies. Looking to the future, this initiative is expected to grow as additional funding becomes available, especially for AI-related activities. The use of micro-credentials offers a flexible, scalable solution that allows universities to quickly adapt and introduce new programs aligned with the evolving needs of the digital economy. Through these efforts, Slovenia is building a foundation for ongoing improvement in digital education, helping students and educators stay ahead in a rapidly changing technological landscape.

title: Pumice
description: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more common in daily life, there is growing need for students—not just in technical fields—to understand how AI works and how it affects the world around them. Many students encounter AI only through media or social platforms, with limited opportunities to explore its educational value. To change this, the Slovenian Ministry of Digital Transformation is co-funding a project aimed at introducing AI into primary and secondary school classrooms—not as a separate subject, but as a tool to enhance learning in a wide range of subjects. The main goal of the project is to create educational content and practical examples that show how AI can be used in the teaching of existing subjects. This includes disciplines such as Slovenian language, history, chemistry, biology, and art. Instead of treating AI as something only for computer science classes, the project focuses on how it can support learning across the curriculum. For example, AI tools might be used to help students explore historical data, analyse language patterns, or generate visual representations in art lessons. This approach helps students see AI as a useful and relevant part of their education, not just a complex or distant technology. The project is being carried out in partnership with educators, content developers, and experts in both AI and pedagogy. These teams are working together to design and test new teaching materials that use AI in ways that are meaningful, age-appropriate, and aligned with national learning goals. Special emphasis is placed on practical demonstrations, making sure teachers and students can directly see how AI adds value to their lessons. The Ministry provides financial support and strategic guidance, helping to ensure that the content developed is both high quality and suitable for broader adoption. In the future, the results of this project may lead to a wider rollout of AI-integrated teaching practices across Slovenian schools. If successful, the content and methods developed could be included in national guidelines, teacher training programmes, or even embedded in digital learning platforms. By starting with small-scale, subject-based integration, Slovenia is taking a measured and inclusive approach to preparing young learners for an AI-influenced world—where understanding and applying these technologies will be increasingly important across all areas of life and work.

title: DiTEdu
description: The goal of the national project “Support for the Digital Transformation of Education” (DiTEdu) is to create innovative teaching methodologies for preschools, primary schools, and secondary schools that will reflect the latest trends in digitalisation. It builds upon the project of the National IT Academy along with partners, the Pavol Jozef Šafárik University in Košice (UPJŠ) and Comenius University in Bratislava (UK), Ministry of Education, Science, Research and Sport of the Slovak Republic (MŠVVaM SR), to create study materials for new and innovative subjects in the field of artificial intelligence, including topics such as Introduction to Neural Networks, Neural Networks, Artificial Intelligence, and Programming Languages for Artificial Intelligence. The activity “Support for the Digital Transformation of Education” will be implemented, divided into nine sub-activities with nationwide impact. These will involve formal and informal education of school digital coordinators, principals, teaching and professional staff of kindergartens, primary and secondary schools, students of teaching programmes at universities, updating and creating innovative methodologies, networking schools and staff, certifying the quality of digital schools, and popularization. Educational research aims to improve the quality of the provided support, ensure the safety of digital transformation considering its risks, and communicate the acquired knowledge with the international community. The activity is divided into 9 sub-activities: 1. Education and continuous methodological support for school digital coordinators. 2. Adaptation of the EU DigCompEdu framework into undergraduate education and professional development of teaching and professional staff of kindergartens, primary and secondary schools. 3. Creation and use of methodological materials to support the digital transformation of education. 4. Establishing a community of cooperation with other organisations and departments of the Ministry of Education, the academic community, primary and secondary schools, public administration and self-government bodies, other entities, and the public in the field of utilising and exchanging experiences of practitioners in the field of digital transformation of education. 5. Creation of analyses, expert opinions, standards, recommendations, criteria, and mechanisms for implementing measures in the field of digital transformation of education. 6. Implementation and support of educational research in the field of digital transformation of education. 7. Preparation, implementation, and certification of the quality of educational content, teaching methods, and schools of digital excellence. 8. Experimental verification of a new study programme “Gymnasium” with a focus on informatics. 9. Popularisation activities and support for public awareness of the needs of digital transformation of education.

description: The Slovenia e-Farming, Food and Forestry Project is a comprehensive digitalisation programme consisting of eight sub-projects under the national Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRF). Its goal is to enhance efficiency, innovation, and sustainability in agriculture, food production, and forestry by introducing digital tools and practices. By integrating multiple sub-projects under a single programme, it provides a coordinated approach to technology-driven transformation. Future outlook: Expansion of digital tools and smart farming solutions across Slovenia Strengthened research and development capabilities in food and forestry sectors Improved collaboration between industry, academia, and public institutions for innovation and competitiveness

title: Smart Specialization Technologies for Agro-ecology and Forestry (PNRR) in the context of the National Forest Strategy 2030
description: The National Forest Strategy 2030 sets out to strengthen Romania’s capacity for sustainable forest management and environmental protection . It targets the smart specialisation subdomain of “Smart Specialisation Technologies for Agro-ecology and Forestry” by supporting the establishment of innovation and technology centres . The flagship investment under this strategy is the creation of an integrated IT system to: Support sustainable development and improve environmental quality Protect nature and preserve biodiversity Supervise and control forest integrity and the transport of wood This investment is implemented in two phases : Installation and configuration of the IT system, including security solutions for confidentiality and training of personnel Operationalisation of a platform for investigations and alerts The system will be integrated with SUMAL 2.0 , the Romanian wood traceability system currently under development. It will monitor: Compliance with legal obligations on wood harvesting Timely forest regeneration Forest health and habitat conservation status Climate change impacts and adaptation of different forest ecosystems All data centres for this system will comply with the European Code of Conduct on Data Centre Energy Efficiency , ensuring sustainability and high operational standards. Future outlook: Increased transparency and control of Romania’s forest resources Enhanced data-driven decision-making for forest conservation Stronger alignment with EU environmental and climate objectives

title: R&D projects for ICT and specific economic purposes
description: In 2022, the Ministry of the Economy, Tourism and Sport launched a public call for R&D project proposals, with the following strategic objectives: Contributing to the green transition, supporting sustainable and environmentally friendly solutions. Increasing investment in research and development, to strengthen Slovenia’s innovation capacity. Enhancing productivity, including material and energy efficiency, through advanced technologies. Boosting the competitiveness of the economy, particularly by fostering innovation-driven growth. From this initiative: 95 R&D projects carried out by consortia of companies received public co-funding. 18 projects specifically focused on the application of artificial intelligence, underscoring the growing importance of AI in economic transformation. AI was integrated not only within the ICT programme, but also partially into nine other sectoral programmes overseen by the ministry. This initiative illustrates how Slovenia is embedding AI into broader economic development and innovation strategies, ensuring that digital technologies contribute to sustainability, competitiveness, and long-term growth. Looking ahead, these measures are expected to stimulate AI adoption across industries, foster cross-sectoral innovation, and further align national R&D with EU green and digital priorities.
