title: SFI Research Centres and Spokes Programme
description: These new programmes by Science Foundation Ireland, replace the Centres for science Engineering and Technology and the Strategic Research Clusters. The Research Centres Programme is one of Science Foundation Ireland's (SFI) main funding programmes. It replaces the CSETs and SRCs. The Research Centres was introduced in 2012 and the Spokes Programme in 2013. Achievements include: +300 Collaborations with industry; 52 Coordinations of Major EU Research Projects; 19 ERC Awards; +EUR 132m Funding from non-exchequer sources. Science Foundation Ireland announced in 2017 that it will invest EUR 87 million over the next six years in five new world-class SFI Research Centres in Ireland. The new SFI Research Centres will be supported by 80 industry partners who will provide an additional EUR 52 million to support cutting-edge basic and applied research with strong industry engagement, economic and societal impact. The five new SFI Research Centres announced will address the following:Smart manufacturing IT and industrial automation systems, led by Prof Conor McCarthy, University of Limerick;Biological resources as alternative materials to finite fossil resources, led by Prof Kevin O'Connor, UCD;Innovative techniques and processes in Additive Manufacturing, led by Prof Denis Dowling, UCD;Diagnosis, monitoring and treatment of chronic and rare neurological diseases - led by Prof David Henshall, RCSI.Fundamental and translational research for precision pasture-based dairying - led by Professor Donagh Berry, Teagasc.The initiative has the following objectives:To achieve, maintain and enhance research excellence and leadership, as measured through indicators such as publication in top-tier journals and conferences, citations, editorship of top-tier journals, and giving invited lectures at top-tier conferences.To deliver significant economic and societal impact - research excellence with impact - which will be aligned with areas of strategic opportunity for Ireland, including the 14 National Research Priority areas and including the six broad enterprise themes outlined in Innovation 2020.To increase the level of industrial and commercial investment in R&D activities with existing Ireland-based companies, and furthermore to attract large Foreign Direct Investments in corporate R&D laboratories.To spin out new, high-technology start-up companies that have the potential to raise external angel or venture funding.To transfer technology, through licences, to Multinational Companies (MNCs) and Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) based in Ireland.To transfer knowledge, expertise and know-how to MNCs and SMEs based in Ireland.

Institutionalization may involve creating long-term partnership agreements between universities, research institutes, and industry stakeholders. Expanding the initiative could include broader participation of private sector partners and integration with wider European and Asian scientific networks, enhancing its impact and sustainability.Since its inception, the initiative has progressively expanded its scope and depth, reflecting the increasing strategic importance of international scientific cooperation. Regular reviews and updates help align the activities with emerging global trends and priorities, ensuring the partnership remains relevant and effective. This dynamic approach enables continuous adaptation, fostering a robust platform for scientific excellence and innovation between Poland and Taiwan.

title: Danish e-infrastructure Consortium (DeiC)
description: DeiC was created to ensure that researchers and universities across Denmark have access to the digital tools they need for modern scientific work. Today’s research depends heavily on powerful computing, secure data storage, and fast networks. Without a coordinated effort, these resources could be unevenly distributed or too expensive for individual institutions. DeiC brings all Danish universities together to share and develop this national digital infrastructure. The main goal of DeiC is to provide reliable access to computing power, data services, and high-speed connections for all researchers in Denmark. This supports tasks like running complex simulations, managing large datasets, and collaborating internationally. DeiC also sets standards and works with partners across Europe to keep Denmark’s research connected and competitive. DeiC is a collaboration between Danish universities, supported by the Ministry of Higher Education and Science. It also connects with European initiatives like the European Open Science Cloud, ensuring Danish researchers benefit from international cooperation. Each university both contributes to and benefits from this shared infrastructure. DeiC is expanding to support better data management and secure platforms, especially as research grows in areas like AI and climate science. The initiative plans to scale up services and deepen its role in European research networks to meet future digital needs.

title: Hansken
description: Hansken is a digital forensics platform for fast filtering, searching and analysing millions of digital traces from seized computers, smartphones and other devices. Thanks to an intuitive user interface, case investigators can search digital data without specialist knowledge, while Hansken also offers numerous specialised tools for more advanced and complex analyses. In this way, Hansken facilitates collaboration between case investigators, digital experts and data scientists. Hansken streamlines digital forensic investigations and makes them more targeted, effective and efficient. The platform is suited to finding and correlating relevant information within massive amounts of data. Cases range from significant bank fraud and money-laundering schemes to environmental crimes. Hansken also plays a crucial role in intelligence investigations and searches of crypto-communication servers. Each investigative service can run its own Hansken platform and control the forensic data in its own domain. The solution has delivered digital evidence and forensic substantiation in thousands of cases. Data are processed transparently, and traces can always be traced back to the seized devices. Hansken thus registers and monitors both the chain of evidence and the chain of custody from crime scene to court. All user actions are logged unequivocally and can be retrieved by security and audit systems. Hansken also supports inspection and reporting functionality for defence lawyers and the judiciary. In our ‘digital law enforcement race’, Hansken can quickly implement new requirements and wishes. As an integration platform, Hansken uses leading third-party core components and focuses its own development on specialist forensic search, reporting and AI-based analysis innovations. Via the available APIs and the associated Software Development Kit, customers and partners can develop their own plug-ins and use them directly within Hansken. The Hansken platform is developed and maintained by the Netherlands Forensic Institute (NFI), one of the world’s leading forensic laboratories, and is only delivered to law enforcement agencies. Via the Hansken Community, partners can exchange knowledge and jointly develop, share and deploy plug-ins. In this way, law enforcement agencies combine their expertise and join forces to boost digital forensics. Hansken is all about powerful digital investigation, leading innovation and sharing forensic knowledge. Some 20 partners around the world currently use Hansken, and the community is still expanding.

title: IRT SystemX
description: IRT SystemX is a not-for-profit research establishment (Institut de Recherche Technologique) co-funded by both the public sector and private industry. Its mission focuses on digital engineering of complex systems, with special emphasis on mobility, autonomous transport, simulation, safety, and system validation. Here are some of the key autonomous mobility projects it leads: SVA – Simulation for the Autonomous Vehicle Safety Launched in 2015, this project develops methods and tools using digital simulation to validate the safety of autonomous vehicles. It addresses issues like sensor failures, environmental disturbances (rain, glare, etc.), and challenges in interpreting road features. 3SA – Simulation for the Safety of Systems in Autonomous Vehicles Started in 2019, this continues and extends SVA. It builds on simulation tools, sensor modeling, scenario libraries, and result analysis to deepen the safety demonstration of autonomous driving systems. SVR – Vehicle Robots and Autonomous Shuttles Scenarios Also launched around 2019, SVR looks specifically at autonomous shuttles and robot-taxis. It aims to define shared test scenarios, build a national reference system, and use both digital simulation and infrastructure-based validation for operational safety. Expected outcomes and benefits include: More robust methods for validating autonomous vehicle safety without relying only on physical tests. Shared scenario libraries & simulation frameworks to reduce duplication of effort across industry. Better alignment between regulatory authorities and technology developers in safety protocols. Enhanced public confidence in autonomous and robotic transport systems. Future directions may involve scaling up these simulation platforms, improving the realism of test scenarios (weather, traffic, infrastructure variety), integrating regulatory approval processes, and extending results to other autonomous mobility contexts globally.

description: TœBITAK ULAKBIM started the high-performance computing studies with the 128 PCs purchased in 2003 with the budget of the institution and then realized the TUGA (Turkish National Grid Infrastructure/TR-Grid) project with the demand from national researchers as well as the experiences and achievements achieved in international projects. The infrastructure was supported and expanded significantly between 2006 and 2008 within the scope of the TUGA project supported by TARAL with the approval of the TœBITAK Science Board. In 2009, the project TR-Grid Research e-Infrastructure Strengthening was presented by applying to the Research Infrastructure Project Call of DPT (State Planning Organization). Within the scope of this project, TRUBA, formerly called TR-Grid, was supported by DPT until the end of 2011. Within the scope of the Turkish National e-Science e-Infrastructure Strengthening project, which is a continuation of the previous project, the infrastructure is being expanded and updated with the current technologies with the support of the Ministry of Development.The initiative has the following objectives:- To provide high-performance computing, data-intensive computing, scientific data warehouses and cloud computing services.

title: Investments for the Future Programme
description: Since 2010, the National Agency for Research (ANR) is the main operator of the state for the PIAs higher education and research actions.The Investments for the Future Programme was set by a Finance Law of March 9, 2010. The goals of this programme and the amount budgeted are structured in accordance with the 2009 report and recommendations issued by a consultative commission chaired by two previous French Prime ministers, MM. Juppe and Rocard. The ambition of the PIA is to increase the long-term growth potential of the French economy, by strengthening investment in four priority sectors: higher education and research, industries and SMEs, sustainable development and digital economy. Until this day, the PIA consists of three phases: - The first phase (PIA 1) covers the period 2010-2020 with a total budget of USD 40.9 billion PPP (EUR 35 billion) allocated to five priority axes: Higher education and training Research Industrial sectors and SMEs Sustainable development Digital economy - The second phase (PIA 2) covers the period 2013-2025 with a total budget of USD 14.3 billion PPP (EUR 12 billion). Its objective is to improve the growth potential of the French economy by organising technological research activities in global excellence clusters.- The third phase (PIA 3) with a total budget of EUR 10 billion was set by the Finance Law for 2017 of December 26, 2016. Of the EUR 10 billion, EUR 5.9 billion will benefit the teaching, research and development of it. This phase includes, for example, calls for projects to support the development of digital technologies. In particular, a part of the Innovation Contest is allocated to support innovative digital technologies such as artificial intelligence, internet of things, blockchain, big data, etc.The initiative has the following objectives:Encourage the excellences of higher education and research on large campuses with the best international standards in terms of governance and academic level. During the first and the second phases of the Investments for the Future Program, the ambition of the .« Initiatives dexcellence / Initiatives - Science “ Innovation “Territoires “ Economie .» action (IDEX / I-SITE) is to allow best campuses to promote their specific advantages in order to increase their international visibility and attractiveness.In particular, the IDEX / I-SITE action selected :- IDEX in order to create world-leading research universities with leading scientific power and impact in broad areas of knowledge ;- I-SITE so as to help universities with more concentrated, distinctive and internationally recognized thematic scientific assets to emerge. These assets are a point of support for their strategy of development and partnership with the economic world.

title: AI-specific research and innovation programme administered by Vinnova, Sweden’s innovation agency
description: Vinnova , Sweden’s government agency for innovation, plays a central role in financing AI-related research, innovation, and adoption across the country. Since 2009, it has administered more than 800 projects in artificial intelligence , ranging from basic research to applied solutions across industry and society. Since 2019, much of this work has been organised under the “Advanced digitalisation – future solutions in Swedish industry” programme. This initiative seeks to accelerate Sweden’s digital and AI transformation by funding projects that bridge the gap between research and innovation, especially in the industrial sector. Key features of the programme include: Targeted funding calls with AI-specific themes , such as: “AI – from research to innovation” “AI in the service of the climate” “AI for Advanced Digitalization” Strong support for SMEs , both as providers and adopters of AI solutions. Large-scale investments – approximately SEK 1.3 billion of SEK 1.5 billion since 2019 directed to SMEs. Through these initiatives, Vinnova is fostering a vibrant AI ecosystem where start-ups, SMEs, academia, and larger companies can collaborate, innovate, and scale solutions. The focus on sustainability , climate-friendly applications , and industry-driven innovation helps ensure that AI contributes to Sweden’s long-term competitiveness and societal benefit.

title: Research Tax Credit
description: Administered by the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation (MESR) and the Direction Générale des Finances Publiques (DGFiP), the CIR has been a permanent fixture of French innovation policy since 1983 (reformed significantly in 2008). The credit is calculated at 30% on qualifying R&D expenditure up to a threshold of EUR 100M per year, and at 5% for expenditure above that threshold. The credit is fully payable as a cash refund to newly created companies, SMEs, and companies in financial difficulty within the first 3 years; other companies may carry it forward up to 3 years and then receive a cash refund. Qualifying expenditure includes: personnel costs (researchers and technicians), depreciation of R&D equipment, subcontracted R&D (to approved organisations), patent costs, costs of technology monitoring, and can include certain AI-related data and compute costs where they form part of an eligible R&D project. AI companies using the CIR typically claim on: AI model development and training; algorithm R new AI product or process development; and AI-driven scientific research. In 2022 approximately 24,000 firms claimed CIR, generating approximately EUR 7B in annual tax credit. Young Innovative Companies (JEI) benefit from additional exemptions on top of CIR.

text: Research Tax Credit. Administered by the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation (MESR) and the Direction Générale des Finances Publiques (DGFiP), the CIR has been a permanent fixture of PLACE innovation policy since 1983 (reformed significantly in 2008). The credit is calculated at 30% on qualifying R&D expenditure up to a threshold of PLACE 100M per year, and at 5% for expenditure above that threshold. The credit is fully payable as a cash refund to newly created companies, SMEs, and companies in financial difficulty within the first 3 years; other companies may carry it forward up to 3 years and then receive a cash refund. Qualifying expenditure includes: personnel costs (researchers and technicians), depreciation of R&D equipment, subcontracted R&D (to approved organisations), patent costs, costs of technology monitoring, and can include certain AI-related data and compute costs where they form part of an eligible R&D project. AI companies using the CIR typically claim on: AI model development and training; algorithm R new AI product or process development; and AI-driven scientific research. In 2022 approximately 24,000 firms claimed CIR, generating approximately PLACE 7B in annual tax credit. Young Innovative Companies (JEI) benefit from additional exemptions on top of CIR

title: ZIM – Central Innovation Programme for SMEs
description: Administered by the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energie (BMWE), ZIM (Central Innovation Programme for SMEs) was established in 2008 and is the cornerstone of Germany's SME innovation funding landscape. It is open to all technologies, industries, and sectors without thematic restriction. Eligible entities are SMEs with fewer than 500 employees (with up to 1,000 employees allowed if cooperating with an SME) and research institutions partnering with businesses. Three funding pillars: (1) Individual R&D projects (single company); (2) R&D cooperation projects (at least two companies, or company and research institution); (3) Innovation networks (consortia with network management funding). Funding rates range from 25–60% of eligible R&D costs depending on company size and project type; maximum grant per project is up to EUR 336,000 per partner. Applications are accepted continuously (no fixed deadlines). A new ZIM guideline with optimised conditions was launched in 2025. In 2024, a positive independent evaluation confirmed ZIM's significant leverage effect: for every EUR 1 of ZIM funding, companies spend an additional EUR 0.90 on R&D. Annual budget is approximately EUR 536M. AI projects are among the most active areas of ZIM applications.

description: BMFTR focuses on collaborative research projects in which SMEs collaborate with research partners on application‑relevant research questions. The funding is technology‑ and application‑agnostic within the thematic area. AI‑driven project ideas in the application context of different domains and sectors are increasingly in focus. description: Typical UK PhD students take three years to complete their doctoral research (or four years in cohort training programmes) under the guidance of an academic supervisor or small supervisory team and tend to be located within an existing research group. Initially, CDTs were regarded as a strategic mechanism for increasing capacity in interdisciplinary research activities such as the life sciences interface and complexity science, areas that were difficult to locate within a traditional University's departmental organisation. title: The Wallenberg AI and Transformative Technologies Education Development Program
description: As artificial intelligence continues to develop rapidly, having access to powerful computing resources is essential for researchers aiming to push the boundaries of AI. To meet this need, Denmark began collaborating with NVIDIA in 2024 to create the Centre for AI Innovation. This new centre will host Gefion, one of the world’s most powerful AI supercomputers, designed to support large-scale AI projects. This initiative addresses the challenge of providing Danish researchers from both public institutions and private companies with advanced tools and infrastructure necessary for innovative AI work. The primary objective of this collaboration is to offer widespread access to state-of-the-art AI computing power, along with software platforms, training, and expert support. Gefion will enable users to work with extensive datasets, develop sophisticated AI models, and explore new applications that require significant processing capabilities. The centre aims to accelerate AI research and development across Denmark by equipping researchers with the resources and knowledge needed to succeed. The centre brings together stakeholders from Denmark’s public research sector, private industry, and technology partners. NVIDIA provides the supercomputing technology and technical expertise, while Danish universities, research institutions, and companies contribute projects, data, and skilled researchers. This partnership creates a collaborative environment that promotes knowledge sharing and innovation within Denmark’s AI community. Since its launch, the centre is expected to grow both in capacity and influence. As more researchers and organizations utilize Gefion and the related services, Denmark plans to expand training programs, software tools, and support services to keep pace with evolving AI demands. This growth will help maintain Denmark’s position as a leading country in AI research and innovation.

title: EU AI Office
description: The EU AI Office was established by European Commission Decision on 24 January 2024, ahead of the formal entry into force of the EU AI Act (August 2024), in recognition of the need for a dedicated EU-level body to coordinate AI Act implementation and provide specialised technical and governance expertise. Its mandate is broader than enforcement alone: the AI Office serves as the EU's primary institutional voice on AI policy, representing the Commission in international AI forums including the OECD, G7, G20, the Council of Europe, ISO/IEC, and the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. The AI Office has four main functions. First, AI Act implementation and enforcement: it is the sole competent authority for supervising GPAI model providers across the EU, including conducting conformity assessments, requesting model evaluations, issuing warnings and, where necessary, imposing fines (up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global annual turnover for GPAI violations). Second, standards and guidance: it coordinates with European standards bodies (CEN/CENELEC, ETSI) on harmonised standards for AI Act compliance and publishes guidelines, codes of practice and technical documentation requirements. Third, the Office leads the multi-stakeholder drafting process for the GPAI Code of Practice, a key implementation instrument for GPAI model providers under Article 56 of the AI Act. Fourth, AI research and safety: the Office conducts and commissions research on AI safety risks, including systemic risks from GPAI models, and maintains the EU's scientific capacity for AI evaluation. It also manages the Apply AI Alliance under the Apply AI Strategy and coordinates AI Factories network development under InvestAI.

Second, standards and guidance: it coordinates with European standards bodies (CEN/CENELEC, ETSI) on harmonised standards for AI Act compliance and publishes guidelines, codes of practice and technical documentation requirements. Third, the Office leads the multi-stakeholder drafting process for the GPAI Code of Practice, a key implementation instrument for GPAI model providers under Article 56 of the AI Act. title: Innovation Tax Credit (ITC)
description: Introduced in 2004, the Jeune Entreprise Innovante (JEI) status and its more research-intensive variant Jeune Entreprise Innovante de Recherche (JEIR, introduced in 2022) offer a package of fiscal and social exemptions to qualifying French startups. To qualify as a JEI, a company must: be an SME under EU definition; be fewer than 8 years old; be independent; and spend at least 15% of total tax-deductible expenditure on qualifying R&D. JEIR requires 30% R&D intensity. Exemptions include: full exemption from employers' social security contributions on wages of researchers, technicians, and project managers involved in R&D (under certain ceilings); 100% corporation tax exemption in the first profitable financial year; 50% corporation tax reduction in the second profitable year; and exemptions from certain local business taxes (CFE and CVAE). From 1 January 2024, the social exemption is capped and tapered: full exemption applies for salaries up to 4.5 times the minimum wage (SMIC); and companies retain JEI status until the financial year they reach 8 years of age. The combined benefit can amount to several hundreds of thousands of euros per year for a typical AI deeptech startup with a significant R&D team. The JEI/JEIR regime is widely used by French AI startups and is actively promoted by Bpifrance as complementary to CIR. The current regime is extended until 31 December 2028.

title: Component 7, Reform 1 of the curriculum reform of the Slovak education system
description: Slovakia is taking steps to better prepare its students for a future where artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly important role in everyday life and the job market. The current education system has not yet fully adapted to the rapid changes brought about by digital technologies, including AI. Many young people lack the skills needed to understand or work with these tools. To address this, Slovakia is focusing on making changes in how digital and technical topics are taught in primary schools, secondary schools, and vocational training programmes. This effort is part of a broader plan to ensure students have the foundational knowledge needed to navigate a society shaped by digital technologies. The main goal of this initiative is to improve digital and technical education, with a special focus on AI. Rather than introducing AI as a completely separate subject, the plan is to include it within broader areas like computer literacy, digital citizenship, and media literacy. This way, students will learn not only how AI works in a basic sense, but also how it affects the way we live, communicate, and make decisions. The reforms also aim to help students understand both the opportunities and the risks that come with using digital tools and AI systems. To make this happen, Slovakia is updating its national curriculum and revising textbooks to reflect modern technological developments. These changes will apply to different levels of the school system, including primary education (for younger children), secondary education (typically ages 12–18), and vocational schools that prepare students for specific careers. Teachers will be supported through training and new teaching materials, ensuring they can confidently deliver this updated content. The government is working together with education experts, curriculum developers, and possibly EU partners to align these reforms with European standards for digital and AI education. Looking ahead, the changes are expected to be rolled out gradually over the coming years. The long-term aim is to create a more modern education system that prepares young people not just to use technology, but to think critically about it and contribute to its development. As the reform progresses, there may also be efforts to share resources and teaching models with other countries, or to expand the programme into lifelong learning initiatives for adults. This approach reflects a recognition that AI is not just a technical topic for specialists, but a societal issue that everyone needs to understand to some degree.

title: BIFAP
description: Spain's BIFAP (Base de Datos para la Investigación Farmacoepidemiológica en Atención Primaria) is an electronic database comprising anonymised medical records from primary care settings. Managed by the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS), BIFAP serves as a critical resource for pharmacoepidemiological studies, enabling the evaluation of medication safety and effectiveness within the Spanish population. Key Features: Data Source: BIFAP aggregates anonymised clinical data from primary care physicians across Spain, focusing on medication prescriptions, patient demographics, and health outcomes. Research Applications: The database supports a wide range of pharmacoepidemiological research, including post-authorisation safety studies, risk-benefit analyses, and the identification of adverse drug reactions. Collaboration and Oversight: Developed and funded by AEMPS, BIFAP operates with the support of professional medical societies such as the Spanish Society of Family and Community Medicine (SEMFYC), the Spanish Society of Rural and General Medicine (SEMERGEN), and the Spanish Association of Primary Care Paediatrics (AEPAP). Scientific Advisory: A scientific committee oversees the project, ensuring methodological rigor and ethical compliance in research activities. International Collaboration: BIFAP collaborates with international pharmacoepidemiological research initiatives, contributing to global efforts in medication safety surveillance.

title: IPA MITOU Program
description: The MITOU Program (Exploratory IT Human Resources Project; officially 未踏IT人材発掘・育成事業) was launched by METI in FY2000 and is operated by the Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA). The programme's mission is to discover and develop exceptional young IT creators capable of driving innovation in AI, robotics, big data, and other frontier digital technologies. As of April 2025, the programme has developed over 2,300 'Creators'. The MITOU Programme has three tracks: MITOU IT Program — for IT talents under age 25 (approx. 9 months); focuses on big data, AI, robotics, and novel digital products; MITOU Advanced Program — for aspiring IT entrepreneurs of all ages (approx. 8 months); adds business advisors alongside technical project managers; targets commercialisation and startup creation; MITOU Target Program — for specialists of all ages (up to 18 months); targets specific frontier technology areas designated annually (past themes include quantum computing, AI, reservoir computing). All tracks share a core model: 'Project Managers' — prominent Japanese IT innovators from academia and industry — select promising individuals from applicants, mentor them intensively through weekly one-to-one sessions, and guide project development. Creators retain IP rights from their projects. Outstanding performers are designated 'Super Creators' by METI. Graduates have founded over 250 businesses and commercialised numerous AI products. The MITOU Foundation (established 2014 by alumni) extends the programme's community and runs MITOU Junior for innovators aged 17 and under. Annual programme budget is not publicly itemised but sits within IPA's total budget (JPY 146.4B as of April 2025 across all programmes).

title: Fondo di Garanzia PMI
description: The Fondo Centrale di Garanzia per le PMI (FGPMI) has been operational since 2000 under Law 662/1996 and is administered by MIMIT through the fund manager Mediocredito Centrale. It provides public guarantees to banks on loans to SMEs and innovative startups, reducing lenders' credit risk and enabling businesses that would otherwise lack sufficient collateral to access finance. For innovative startups and certified incubators, the guarantee is free, priority-processed, and covers up to 80% of the loan (maximum guaranteed amount: EUR 5M per company; simplified assessment with no additional credit evaluation beyond the bank's own). For standard SME investment operations (including AI and 4.0 technology purchases), the guarantee is also 80% (maintained under Budget Law 2025 and extended through 2026 under Budget Law 2026). For liquidity operations, the guarantee was reduced to 50% from 2025. The fund can also be used to secure Nuova Sabatini loans. An extension to mid-cap companies (up to 499 employees) was approved, subject to EU authorisation. Between 2013 and 2023, the fund managed 18,053 operations for innovative startups, mobilising approximately EUR 3.4B in financing. For innovative PMEs (PMI innovative), access is free but subject to minimum creditworthiness thresholds. Total financing mobilised across all SME operations exceeds EUR 3.8B for startup/innovative SME categories alone.

title: The Public Attitudes to Science Survey
description: While the quantitative survey has always been the core of PAS the mix of methods has changed each time. For this iteration it was decided to use additional question modules and online dialogues looking at four current science topics (mostly supporting our industrial strategy grand challenges - the Future of Mobility, Ageing Society, the Future of Mobility and AI). title: Genome Canada
description: To date, the Government of Canada has provided over CAD 1.5 billion (including investment income) to Genome Canada, including CAD 100.5 million through Budget 2019. Genome Canada has matched this significant federal commitment to date with an additional CAD 2.1 billion raised from other partners, both domestically and internationally. The federal funding enables Genome Canada to continue to invest in and launch new large-scale research competitions; provide access to leading-edge technologies; support continued participation by Canadian genomics researchers in national and international partnership initiatives; and maintain Genome Canada's operations and the operations of the regional Genome Centres. In addition, Genome Canada also supports the translation of genomics discoveries into practical applications and research projects aimed at studying and analyzing the ethical, environmental, economic, legal and social issues related to genomics (GE3LS).The initiative has the following objectives:To respond to societal needs by generating genomics discoveries and accelerating their translation into applications.To attract greater investment in genomics research from a broad range of stakeholders, in particular the private sector.To enhance the impact of genomics by transforming knowledge of the ethical, environmental, economic, legal, and social challenges and opportunities into sound policies and practices.To enhance the recognition of the value of genomics by increasing stakeholder appreciation of genome science, its applications and implications.

description: The AI Boost programme, hosted within one of Denmark’s seven government-approved Research and Technology Organisations (GTS institutes), is designed to transfer cutting-edge research knowledge into practical applications for industry and society. title: EXIST Program
description: EXIST (Existenzgründungen aus der Wissenschaft) is administered by the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) with co-funding from the European Social Fund (ESF). It was launched in 1998 and has supported over 5,000 startups to date. The programme has three main components: EXIST-Gründerstipendium — funding for individual founders and small teams (up to 12 months) to develop a business plan for a knowledge-intensive innovation; EXIST-Forschungstransfer — a two-phase programme supporting teams conducting proof-of-concept R&D (Phase 1: up to EUR 250,000; Phase 2: up to EUR 180,000) with a commercial application in mind; and EXIST-Potentiale — funding for universities to build startup ecosystems and entrepreneurship culture. For AI ventures, EXIST-Gründerstipendium provides monthly stipends for founders (from EUR 1,000 for students to EUR 3,000 for senior scientists), plus up to EUR 30,000 in material costs and coaching. AI has been among the fastest-growing EXIST application areas in recent years. The programme is particularly relevant for AI startups emerging from Germany's AI Competence Centres, DFKI, and university AI groups.

title: Co-operative Research Centers Program
description: The CRCs program is one of the main Australian providers of competitive grants. It has two streams: - CRCs undertake industry-led, high quality collaborative research for up to 10 years. CRCs must have at least one Australian industry entity and one Australian research organisation as partners. CRCs have no set funding limit.- CRC Projects (CRC-Ps) undertake industry-led collaborative research for up to three years with grants capped at AUD 3 million. CRC-Ps must have at least two Australian industry entities (at least one of which is an SME) and one Australian research organisation as partners. To date, the Government has committed over AUD 4.8 billion to support the establishment of 225 CRCs and 111 CRC-Ps. Participants have committed a further AUD 14.9 billion in cash and in-kind contributions. There are currently 23 active CRCs and 96 active CRC-Ps. CRCs and CRC-Ps provide industry-focused education and training opportunities for Australian students. Since the program was established in 1991, over 4,000 PhD graduates have been supported by the CRC Program. CRC Projects with a focus on AI Announced in the 2018-19 Budget, the Australian Government committed AUD 25 million in additional funding for the Co-operative Research Centres (CRC) Program to support additional CRC Projects with a specific focus on artificial intelligence (AI). CRC-P funding is available for a duration of up to three years and CRC-Ps may request a maximum of AUD 3 million of Commonwealth funding. The minimum grant amount is AUD 100,000. Each CRC-P must include and maintain amongst its project partners at least:- two industry entities including at least one SME; and- one research organisation. All partners must contribute resources to the CRC-P. Funding for the AI priority round has now been committed and the AI projects supported are now underway.The initiative has the following objective(s):The CRCs program is designed to create a more collaborative research culture between Australian business and other end-users of research and the higher education sector. The scheme provides financial support for collaborations between researchers and industry in specific fields selected after annual rounds.

title: OTP-Emese
description: OTP-Emese is a specialized high-performance computing (HPC) system built to meet the increasing demands of training deep learning language models. As natural language processing (NLP) technologies grow more complex, traditional computing systems often lack the capacity to handle the massive data and processing needs. OTP-Emese addresses this by offering an estimated 27 PetaFlops of computational power, making it suitable for training large-scale models like GPT. Its main purpose is to support both commercial and research efforts in AI language model development. By providing a powerful and stable infrastructure, it helps developers and researchers train models faster, more efficiently, and with better results. Users include AI engineers, data scientists, and academic institutions working on NLP tasks such as machine translation, text generation, and chatbots. The system is actively maintained and optimized for deep learning workloads. Although its current focus is language models, the platform’s capacity makes it adaptable for other advanced AI tasks.

title: Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Credit
description: Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program, administered by the Canada Revenue Agency, is a tax-based incentive that supports businesses conducting research and development in Canada by allowing them to claim a portion of eligible R&D costs through their corporate tax filings. Companies receive either a 35% fully refundable credit on up to CAD 6 million in annual qualifying expenditures (primarily for Canadian-controlled private corporations and, more recently, certain public firms) or a 15% partially refundable credit for other businesses. Eligible activities include experimental development, applied and basic research, and supporting work such as software engineering and AI development, provided it involves genuine technical uncertainty and systematic experimentation. Recent updates have expanded eligibility to include capital expenditures like equipment, raised thresholds so more mid-sized firms can access enhanced rates, and introduced faster, AI-assisted claim processing. In addition to the federal incentive, most provinces offer supplementary credits, allowing companies to recover a significant share of their R&D investment.

title: IMEC Core Funding
description: In February 2016, the merger was announced between the strategic research centres Imec and iMinds, which was completed in October 2016, when iMinds vzw was disbanded to become one of Imec's business units. The renewed Imec confirms its role as the world's leading research centre for nanoelectronics and digital technology. It brings together nearly 3,500 researchers from all over the world and has a unique infrastructure, with the most advanced equipment for research into next-generation IC technologies, and state-of-the-art bio, network and imaging labs. This includes 12,000 square meters of cleanrooms (of which the most recent 4000 square meeters 300mm facility was inaugurated in March 2016).Imec is also a driver of theCity of Things' project, that builds a Smart City Internet of Things' (IoT) living laboratory in Antwerp. IoT is a network of digitally connected objects and infrastructure via wireless gateways that exchange data using embedded sensors. Companies, researchers, residents and local authorities can experiment with smart technology through the participation in IoT and share information on mobility, energy consumption and air quality as part of a major urban digital project.The initiative has the following objectives:Confirms its role as the world's leading research centre for nanoelectronics and digital technology.

title: Austrian Society for Artificial Intelligence (ASAI)
description: The current revolution of AI, which is about to change our world in all areas of life, is determined by an unprecedented speed of translation of basic academic research into immediate applications in real life. The recent events surrounding the crisis triggered by COVID-19 have triggered a real boom in the successful implementation of AI and ML methods in virology and epidemiology, but also, for example, in economic research and other fields. This shows the universal applicability and superiority of the underlying AI and machine learning (ML) technologies.The Austrian University Conference (uniko), together with a spontaneously founded working group, drew up a position paper with concrete and comprehensive measures to strengthen Austria as a research location and called for their timely implementation in order to further strengthen Austria's competence in the field of AI and ML and, above all, to anchor Austria as a research location in the international AI community, in particular in the European networks ELLIS and CLAIRE.The cooperation in the uniko working group has united the different scientific perspectives on the broad field of AI in their interests for a common Austrian AI strategy. As a result, the almost 40 year old Austrian Society for Artificial Intelligence (–GAI) has been reorganized under the English name "Austrian Society for Artificial Intelligence (ASAI)".Starting from the uniko position paper, among others ASAI's agenda addresses:- Strengthening research excellence in Austria in an international context- Support in setting up international lighthouse projects- Increasing the attractiveness of the location for young researchers- Consultation for all relevant ministries

text: Fraunhofer Society. The Fraunhofer Society, with 76 institutes across PLACE, plays a crucial role in transferring AI research into business applications. Three Fraunhofer Institutes are particularly relevant for the transfer of AI research: i) Fraunhofer Institute for Intelligent Analysis and Information Systems (IAIS); ii) Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Engineering and Automation (IPA) (Fraunhofer IPA, 2024[318]); and iii) Fraunhofer Institute for Industrial Engineering (IAO). Through their AI Innovation Centre, IPA and IAO offer companies support in exploring, assessing, and implementing AI solutions, including proof-of-concept projects. To date, over 250 companies, including many SMEs, have participated in these programmes, with 30% of them implementing operational AI systems
